Title: Validation of a SEU simulation technique for a radiation hardened 64-bit MIPS processor.
Publication: IAC 2005 congress proceedings, 56th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  16–21 October 2005, Fuduoka, Japan
Abstract:
Single event upsets (SEUs) are a potential threat to the reliability of digital circuits in the space environment. They are the result of the impact of high-energy particles with sensitive areas of the processors, and are responsible of transient changes, generally called “bit flips” or “upsets”, in bits of information stored within an integrated circuit.
Unlike other radiation effects, SEUs can be caused only by a single particle, that although doesn’t damage permanently the device, it can produce unpredicted consequences ranging from erroneous results to system crashes. 

To avoid these effects, space agencies have traditionally used radiation hardened processors specifically designed for the space environment. However, the increasing demand of more powerful processors that the new space missions requires, together with the complexity and high cost of a custom design, makes the use of Commercial Off-The-Shelf (COTS) based solutions highly attractive. They rely on advanced commercial technology and the use of hardware and software techniques to reduce the radiation effects. 

One of the aims of the QLF group is to study new techniques and tools for the validation and hardening of complex processors operating under radiation. Currently the author is working with the first 64-bit radiation hardened processor designed for space applications, that has been developed by HIREC and the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) for its new satellite programme. It is a modified Toshiba TX49 commercial processor, based on the R4000 MIPS RISC architecture, that includes some typical radiation hardening techniques such as an EDAC (Error Detection and Correction) and a parity bit. 

One objective is to test some software hardening techniques in this processor. Another objective is to be able to predict with high accuracy, the error rate caused by SEU’s over this processor when it is running any program, without using this program in the radiation tests. This is possible if we combine the results of a static radiation test with the use of a Code Emulation and Upset (CEU) fault injection method applied on the program considered.  

A static test estimates the sensitivity to SEUs by loading all the storage accessible elements of the processor with a predetermined pattern, whose corruption  by SEUs is identified by periodically reading out the exercised memory area and comparing it with the expected values. This provides a very worst-case estimation because when the processor is running a real application, the SEUs can affect its results only when they change the values of registers that, in this instant, have useful information for the program. 

CEU method is a SEU simulation technique that consists basically in the injection of bit flips into random memory cells at random instants using interrupt requests. Our group has developed a hardware platform to obtain the results of this method in a systematic way.  A daughterboard with the processor is inserted into a motherboard with all the features needed to realize also the ground radiation test.

Validation of  a SEU simulation technique for a microprocessor family architecture enables the study of Software Implemented Fault Tolerance (SIFT) techniques without requiring the use of expensive satellite and ground radiation test experiments. Using previous experiences we expect to present the results of current SIFT techniques applied to this processor family, and the results of a SIFT technique that exploits 64 bits architecture when running 32 bits applications. Therefore this work aims to be a contribution to the current discussion between the use of radiation hardened or COTS solutions.

Title: A DATA TREATMENT TOOL FOR A SATELLITE THRUSTER TEST FACILITY
Publication: IAC 2003 congress proceedings, 54th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  29 September–3 October 2003, Bremen, Germany
Abstract: This work introduces and discusses CATPA (Computer Aided Thruster Performance Analysis), a user friendly data treatment software specially developed for INPE’s Satellite Thruster Test Facility. This facility is a ground-based structure that can emulate the space environment for testing and qualifying satellite thrusters and satellite propulsive loops. A structure like this requires the prompt availability of data treatment tools which must be extensible to encapsulate the particular needs of the customers. The original data treatment package supplied by the test bench development team required some effort to customize the available features. However several constraints were imposed on the overall system such as: a) support for low amount of data; b) large time slices were required for processing the acquired data; c) poor final output quality; d) specific hardware requirements; e) non portability; f) specific language used for coding the scripts; etc. The CATPA came up to override these constraints and to make data treatment easier and much more powerful. It uses modern concepts like design patterns and standard template library, making the reuse of code and the rapid application development easier to be reached.

Title: A PLATFORM APPROACH TO SMALL SATELLITE DESIGN
Publication: IAC 2003 congress proceedings, 54th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  29 September–3 October 2003, Bremen, Germany
Abstract: Small satellites designed for various missions can be made more affordable by utilizing a modular, platform approach to the spacecraft architecture. A platform approach is used most commonly in the auto industry to identify where commonality in design versus variance from the common design makes the most sense. By applying this platform approach to five generic design reference missions for small satellites, it is expected that the conceptual design study will yield a cost effective, yet flexible small satellite architecture. This paper addresses the process of determining platform architecture for small satellites. As context, a survey of the small satellite industry to determine typical uses of small satellites and emerging trends in mission requirements has been completed. These typical mission requirements can now be generalized to characterize the design reference missions further. Also explained are how Utah State University’s involvement of manufacturing early in the process is influencing its spacecraft design and the promise of advanced manufacturing techniques.

Title: COVERAGE OPTIMIZATION OF ELLIPTICAL SATELLITE CONSTELLATIONS WITH AN EXTENDED SATELLITE TRIPLET METHOD
Publication: IAC 2003 congress proceedings, 54th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  29 September–3 October 2003, Bremen, Germany
Abstract: The design of a satellite constellation is often driven by coverage objectives. Many methods have been developed to evaluate the coverage efficiency of a constellation pattern, but they are often restricted to continuous global coverage analyses of satellites on circular orbits. Unfortunately, a global coverage of the planet is not always the most cost effective paradigm. In many cases, it is better to optimize a constellation according to zonal coverage objectives rather than a global one. Moreover, to further improve the zonal coverage of the satellites, we should switch to elliptical orbits to allow the satellites to stay for a longer time in view of the zonal targets around their apogee. In this paper, we will show that with some modifications we can still use Walker’s coverage analysis algorithm based on satellite triplets to assess the coverage efficiency of satellite constellation patterns on elliptical orbits. As an illustration of the method, we will present the most suited symmetrical patterns to cover the Northern hemisphere. These patterns are an extension of the classical Walker constellations. To limit the search domain, but also because of their remarkable stability, we will use only elliptical orbits with a frozen perigee.

Authors: ['K. Kruijff', 'E.J. v.d. Heide', 'E. Dragoni', 'D. Castagnetti', 'S. Ferretti']
Title: Concept selection and design of the inherently safe re-entry capsule for YES2
Publication: IAC 2003 congress proceedings, 54th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  29 September–3 October 2003, Bremen, Germany
Abstract:
features An Inherently-safe Re-entry vehicle (AIR). AIR is lighter than any previous re-entry vehicle design, and has an extremely low ballistic coefficient. Therefore it will decelerate very early in the re-entry (at 80 km rather than typical 50 km) and will remain relatively cool, in its turn allowing for a lightweight thermal protection system. The low terminal velocity of the vehicle (soccer ball impact energy) and inherent safety may allow it to land Western Europe. Such a capsule can return samples from Space Station quickly and directly to the customer.
The design of AIR started with a design brainstorm in which 18 universities around Europe participated, based on a minimal set of requirements: weight, inherent safety,
recoverability, payload capability. About 25 concepts were entered, in various levels of detail. The paper discusses the concept evaluation logic, design approach and prototyping.
The preferred concepts for further study were the inherently safe “cold re-entry” vehicles, very light (few kg) or single-stage inflatable without any hard parts (except for ~1 kg payload and recovery system). If inflation is performed, it is done already before re-entry. Most of the support systems are released before atmospheric entry, further reducing the capsule’s weight. The vehicle is axially symmetric, is uncontrolled and has no lift to reduce landing site errors.
The remaining designs that satisfied the requirements were (temporarily) stripped of all particular features that add complexity, and were merged into 3 high-level concepts (COLD, MOLD, FOLD). Mock-ups for each concept were tested with drop test and aerodynamic measurements. Next, at least one flight-prototype per concept will be built. For the detailed design, the main design driver is manufacturability, so a material search and characterization was a large part of the initial design activity. Heat resistant fabrics and lightweight insulators such as Nextel, Pyrogel and Alumina were selected and tested in a re-entry simulation chamber.
Because the inflatable for re-entry purposes is a new technology and the flexibility of the vehicle
interacts with the aerodynamic performance, an iterative CAD/FEM/CFD design is required, which has to be verified by test. Results of aerodynamics, stability analysis and re-entry simulations are used to optimize the shape within limits of manufacturability. Production of flight- scale prototypes has started.

Title: ELECTRIC PROPULSION DEVELOPMENTS FOR INTERPLANETARY FLIGHT
Publication: IAC 2003 congress proceedings, 54th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  29 September–3 October 2003, Bremen, Germany
Abstract:
With the advent of the Deep Space 1 (DS1) mission Electric Propulsion (EP) has moved from providing station keeping capability for spacecraft to being its primary propulsion system. In this paper the trends and expectations for the future development in EP for interplanetary flight is discussed. Three paths are explored. First the path opened by DS1 is treated, covering the relative near future between now and 2005. Three future developments based on the DS1 baseline design are presented: 1) Improved performance derivatives, i.e. engines with better efficiencies, lower dry mass, and greater service life capability; 2) The Multiple Mission EP system, a system that can be used for a range of deep-space missions; 3) Scaled-down DS1 systems, following the trend toward smaller scientific spacecrafts. Emphasis is put on the background for these developments and the how they will improve deep space exploration. The second path is the development of higher power EP systems, in particular Direct-drive TAL systems and Variable Isp Propulsion Systems (VIPS). These are developments that are expected to be available in the mid-term time frame, i.e. between 2005-2020. The paper discusses the fundamental aspects behind these systems and the possible gain that can be achieved. Finally, a general discussion on mass savings possibilities and the trend in the future
EP development in Europe is given.

Authors: ['Jens Krieger', 'Jörg Bernhard Multhoff', 'Josef Betten', 'Luís Eduardo Vergueiro Loures Loures da Costa']
Title: FINITE ELEMENT ANALYSES OF COMPOSITE PRESSURE VESSELS SHOWING THE INFLUENCE OF SOME MAJOR PRODUCTION AND DESIGN PARAMETERS FOR AN APOGEE MOTOR
Publication: IAC 2003 congress proceedings, 54th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  29 September–3 October 2003, Bremen, Germany
Abstract: The failure mechanisms of composite pressure vessels are studied by means of a detailed Finite Element model. Layered volume elements are used to create a high-resolution model. This model is conceived to analyze the stress distribution under internal pressure and to predict the burst load for parameter variations. The model was verified by comparison with results from hydraulic burst tests of the Solid Rocket Motor S44 which is also used as the 4th stage of the Brazilian satellite launcher VLS. The motor case is manufactured with aramid fibers and epoxy resin by means of wet filament winding and acts essentially as a pressure vessel. The structural qualification was performed by ground tests and the final qualification was achieved by a successful flight. The influence of production process and various design factors on the structural performance of the S44 motor case are studied using the qualified model. The first focus is on the cool down after curing, which has an tremendous influence on the dome deformation behavior. Together with the dome wall thickness distribution, linked to the used winding pattern, the stress distribution of the domes is greatly influenced. With a more balanced stress state in the caps, composite pressure vessels can be significantly improved.

Authors: ['A. van Dijk', 'M. Kruijff', 'E.J. van der Heide', 'J.P. Lebreton']
Title: LEBRETON, A LIGHTWEIGHT BARE ROTATING TETHER SYSTEM FOR JOVIAN ATMOSPHERIC ENTRY
Publication: IAC 2003 congress proceedings, 54th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  29 September–3 October 2003, Bremen, Germany
Abstract:
This paper reports the initial results of a study of a lightweight system that could enable (multi-)probe release into the Jovian atmosphere at low entry velocity. LeBRETON (Le Bare Rotating Electrodynamic Tether for jOvian eNtry) is a new intrinsically stable concept based on a simple aluminium tether without insulation and not requiring an active plasma contactor. The Lorentz drag force on LeBRETON in orbit around Jupiter could be used to de-orbit one or more small atmospheric probes with low mass impact on the host Jupiter orbiter. The LeBRETON design, in all its simplicity, avoids excessive heat dissipation and instability. The initial idea not to use an active contactor would not only reduce the hardware required, but also intrinsically guarantees that the (base) current and therefore heat dissipation will not be excessive and can be dealt with in a practical manner.
Around Jupiter, due to the high velocities and strong magnetic field, even without an active device to emit electrons, a significant current will flow, the circuit being closed by ion collection. Furthermore LeBRETON makes use of the Jovian environment to create its own stability in a passive manner, which is necessary in the absence of a significant gravity gradient. LeBRETON’s particular distribution of Lorentz force over the tether and resulting torque is such that, if given an initial rotation, this rotation will self-accelerate, keeping the tether taut through centrifugal force and stable through the gyroscopic effect.
A simple analytical derivation of the LeBRETON concept is provided, together with initial results from multi-segmented bare tether simulations including models of the Jovian environment. The effect that (passive) current enhancement will have is qualitatively discussed.

Title: MODEL BASED DEVELOPMENT AND VERIFICATION ENVIRONMENT
Publication: IAC 2003 congress proceedings, 54th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  29 September–3 October 2003, Bremen, Germany
Abstract:
The use of simulators modelling the functional behaviour of satellite systems plays an increasingly significant role in the design, development and verification process of current and future satellites.
In the past, simulation only required to verify the feedback control algorithms and performance of the attitude and control subsystem, and to support development of flight operation procedures and team training for mission operation. In most recent and future satellite projects, simulation is an important asset to the design and development process in general. With today's technologies in computer hardware and software it is possible to accomplish by use of numerical simulators important tasks of the satellite development which traditionally are verified by means of a dedicated engineering model spacecraft. The real time capabilities have to allow inclusion of hardware in the loop so that manufacturing of engineering model units can be limited to technologically critical items such as the scientific and Earth observation payload.
Within the last years Astrium GmbH has implemented a new simulation based system engineering process along with a standard infrastructure supporting it, which is called the „Model-based Development & Verification Environment^ - or „MDVE“ for short. The MDVE is consistently applied from early development stages to satellite Assembly Integration and Verification (AIV) and also for mission operation support. This paper describes
• the satellite design process being supported by the MDVE
• the different MDVE constellations applied for design refinement, onboard software verification, checkout system configuration, spacecraft AIV and finally for use in the ground segment
• the components of MDVE, their hardware and software features
An overview of MDVE project applications and a critical reflection of the experiences and the trends for future improvements concludes this paper.

Title: NEXT GENERATION LAUNCH TECHNOLOGY OXYGEN-RICH STAGE COMBUSTION PROTOTYPE ENGINE
Publication: IAC 2003 congress proceedings, 54th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  29 September–3 October 2003, Bremen, Germany
Abstract: The National Aeronautics and Space Administration has undertaken the Next Generation Launch Technology (NGLT) Program to develop the technologies that will provide an order of magnitude improvement in safety with an order of magnitude decrease in operations cost. Key enabling technologies have been identified for a number of potential launch system architectures. Technologies that require immediate risk reduction and apply to a large cross-section of vehicle architectures have been selected for further development. The RS-84 Lox-hydrocarbon engine was one of the selected technologies in the NGLT program. This project will design a prototype engine of over 1 million pounds sea level thrust using an oxidizer-rich staged combustion engine cycle. If selected for advancement the project will fabricate and test the prototype engine design. The design was initiated in June, 2002 and is supported by component testing and culminates in a prototype engine test in 2007. Data and analysis provided by the design and test program will enable an informed Reusable Launch Vehicle full-scale development decision in 2009. This paper describes the overall program plan, the design philosophy, and the ongoing effort associated with the RS-84 engine system.

Title: SPACE ON LINE A vision of living in space
Publication: IAC 2003 congress proceedings, 54th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  29 September–3 October 2003, Bremen, Germany
Abstract:
“SPACE ON LINE” is a vision of a space hotel. It was the winning design at a inter- disziplinary studends competition called “early bird”, initiated in 2001 by the German Aerospace Society DGLR e. V. in cooppera- tion with the Technical University of Darmstadt. This contest was directed towards students of architecture.
The basic system of “SPACE ON LINE” is a tether-structure. It stabilizes itself towards the earth’s centre and, if affected on external forces, will level itself out. A construction can be created consisting of ropes and textile elements. For a rope-length of about 500 km the acceleration due to gravity gradient effects amounts to 0,1 m/s2 at the ends. Because of this limitation of gravitational force, permanent readjustment for a visitor between earth’s gravitational pull and weightlessness is not necessary. Gravitation is only an aid for handling many things in an easier way.
The center of the station - the continuum - (a timeless, floating area) is an inflatable structure with a diameter of 20 m and made of joint textile elements. Inside it is organized with interchangeable function- pins and planes.
In contrast to the continuum the centers are separated and organized in three areas with a time-shift of 8 hours, to optimise use of technical equipment and to enable travel to the station from three places on earth without time shift.
The living-spheres are situated alongside of the service-centers and pick up the guests. The spheres are concurrently “elevators” to move the whole system along.

Title: THE AURORA MARS SAMPLE RETURN MISSION
Publication: IAC 2003 congress proceedings, 54th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  29 September–3 October 2003, Bremen, Germany
Abstract:
The paper reports the results of an ESA internal assessment study of a Mars Sample Return mission.
The mission architecture proposed by the study foresees two Ariane 5 ESC-A launches in 2011 bringing two separate composite spacecrafts to Mars.
The composite launched as first, features an Orbiter inserted into low Mars orbit and an Earth Return Capsule. The Orbiter acts as Data Relay in the communications between Mars surface and Earth and performs a rendezvous with a Mars Ascent Vehicle (part of the second launch) carrying the sample container from Mars surface.
The second composite has a Carrier and a Descent Module for landing the Mars Ascent Vehicle and the platform that performs the sample collection.
The entry into Mars atmosphere is from hyperbolic interplanetary trajectory.
After sample collection, the sample is sealed within a container and the container is transferred to the Mars Ascent Vehicle that
carries it into Mars orbit. There, the upper stage of the ascent vehicle docks to the Orbiter. The sample container is mechanically transferred inside the Orbiter to the Earth Return Capsule. When all these operations have been performed, the Orbiter returns back to Earth and after the sealing of the container has been checked, releases the Earth Return Capsule into an Earth re-entry trajectory. The Earth Return Capsule, designed for a parachute-less descent and a hard landing, is finally recovered.
The paper describes the trade-offs leading to the selected mission architecture and the design of all the elements and the operations of the mission.

Title: THE SIMULATION TOOL OF WIDEBAND MULTIMEDIA MOBILE SATELLITE COMMUNICATIONS SYSTEM
Publication: IAC 2003 congress proceedings, 54th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  29 September–3 October 2003, Bremen, Germany
Abstract: The developing trend of modem communications system leans to personality, multimedia and be moveable. In despite of needs of wider band, flexibility access, convenience and rapid services, the development and operation cost of such system must be not very expensive so that it can be accepted by market. There are many uncertain features for such system considered technologies development in the future, and it makes high risks in developing such system. The satellite communications technology lias developed for many years, there are some technical options which can be selected and combined for a certain system. When these options and user requirements, conunercial features and other uncertain features are considered comprehensively, it becomes very complexity and difficult to make a final decision. In tliis paper, a digital simulation tool is presented, which is adapted to investigate the satellite conununications system, specially adapted to study wideband multimedia mobile communications satellite system developed in future. This simulation tool is a set of software packages developed based on commercial software, and lias a hierarchy. The actual using of tliis simulation tool proved that is an effective way in conception design period.

Title: The Dynamical equations in terms of Relative orbit Elements for Satellite formation Flying
Publication: IAC 2003 congress proceedings, 54th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  29 September–3 October 2003, Bremen, Germany
Abstract: The characteristics of relative orbit motion are studied deeply in previous researches. Imitating the traditional orbit elements, the six relative orbit elements defined therein are as follows: difference in semimajor axis, modulus of difference in eccentricity vector, modulus of vector of non-coplanarity, argument of vector of non-coplanarity, angle from vector of non-coplanarity to vector of eccentricity, and initial argument or moment at epoch. The second to fifth items are equivalent to components of difference in eccentricity vector, and vector of non-coplanarity. These relative orbit elements are convenient for analysis and design of the pattern and space mission of formation flying. Based on theory of orbit perturbation, two groups of dynamical differential equations in terms of relative orbit elements are derived and presented by strict mathematical method in this paper. On the right side of these equations are relative forces including real perturbation and control force. So that the equation for perturbation and equation for control are unified in form. The establishment of dynamical equations of relative orbit elements is beneficial for mission design, perturbation analysis and control realization oriented to mission of multi-satellite formation flying.

Authors: ['E.J. Van der Heide', 'M. Kruijff', 'A. Avanzini', 'V. Liedtke', 'A. Karlovsky']
Title: Thermal Protection Testing of the Inflatable Capsule for YES2
Publication: IAC 2003 congress proceedings, 54th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  29 September–3 October 2003, Bremen, Germany
Abstract:
The YES2 (2nd Young Engineers’ Satellite) project employs An Inherently safe Re-entry (AIR) vehicle that will be de-orbited by the means of a 30 km polyethylene (Dyneema) tether. Low mass, large drag area concept design options are pursued for the reentry vehicle. In these concepts, the mass of the capsule is kept to several kilograms only through strongly reduced payload requirements, as well as through jettison of most instrumentation and structure shortly before entry. Due to the low ballistic coefficient the capsule will decelerate in the upper layers of the atmosphere, thus reducing aerodynamic and thermal loads. This approach allows for new lightweight materials (Nextel, aerogel, foams) and inflatable structural design concepts. A matrix of lightweight flexible Thermal Protection System material assemblies have been tested at the AMTT test house in August 2003. Two testing facilities have been used: the newly developed Re-entry Simulation chamber and the Universal Testing Machine.
This paper lists the first results of the first YES2 TPS material testing campaign, of which the objectives are twofold. Firstly to characterize the gradient/conductivity of the assembled TPS for the YES2 re-entry vehicle concepts in a high radiation, low pressure, hot gas environment (impact different materials, multi-layer, surface porosity etc.). Secondly to determine non-documented break strength & strain of material fabrics.

Title: Unique Space Educational Organization - Challenges of University Space Engineering Consortium (UNISEC) -
Publication: IAC 2003 congress proceedings, 54th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  29 September–3 October 2003, Bremen, Germany
Abstract: UNISEC is a Non-Profit Organization that aims at development of human resource and technology through supporting student activities to design, fabricate, launch and operate satellites and rockets. This paper describes the features and organizational structure of UNISEC, and then discusses the future prospects of UNISEC’s contribution to society beyond the space engineering community. The intent of UNISEC is for universities to become one of the key players in space development, and it is expected that similar organizations will be formed in many other areas of the world. UNISEC one day hopes to collaborate with these sister organizations. Education is equal to creation. UNISEC will contribute to the creation of unique paths to space development through education.

Title: A study of annular flow film characteristics in microgravity and hypergravity conditions
Publication: IAC 2002 congress proceedings, 53rd  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  10–19 October 2002, Houston, United States
Abstract: Annular flow is an important flow regime in many industrial applications. The need for a better understanding of this flow regime is driven by the desire to improve the design of many terrestrial and space-based systems. Gravity is a complicating factor in the studies and modeling of two-phase flows on earth. Experimental data on the annular flow film characteristics was collected in microgravity aboard the Novespace Zero-G Airbus microgravity simulator. The gravitational effect on the film thickness characteristics was examined by collecting data using an air-water mixture during the microgravity and pull-up (hypergravity) portions of each parabolic flight. Previously reported trends in annular flow average film thickness values for normal gravity are observed in microgravity and hypergravity conditions. The change in gravitational acceleration has little effect on the average film thickness and the film thickness time trace. However, the wave characteristics vary significantly.

Title: An advanced In-Situ Resource Utilization (ISRU) production plant design for robotic and human Mars mission
Publication: IAC 2002 congress proceedings, 53rd  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  10–19 October 2002, Houston, United States
Abstract:
The ability to produce the necessary consumables, rather than relying solely on what is brought from Earth decreases the launch mass, cost, and risk associated with a Mars mission while providing capabilities that enable the commercial development of space. The idea of using natural resources, or “living off the land”, is termed In-Situ Resource Utilization (ISRU). Trade studies have shown that producing and utilizing consumables such as water, breathing oxygen, and propellant can reduce the launch mass for a human or robotic mission to Mars by 20-45%. The Johnson Space Center and Lockheed Martin Astronautics are currently designing and planning assembly of a complete collection-to-storage production plant design for producing methane (fuel), oxygen, and water from carbon dioxide (Martian atmosphere) and hydrogen (electrolyzed Martian water or Earth-originated), based on lessons learned and design enhancements from a 1st generation testbed. The design and testing of the major subsystems incorporated in the 2nd generation system, including a carbon dioxide freezer, Sabatier reactor, water electrolysis unit, and vacuum-jacketed, cryogenic, common-bulkhead storage tank, will be presented in detail with the goal of increasing the awareness of the readiness level of these technologies. These technologies are mass and power efficient as well as fundamentally simple and reliable. These technologies also have potential uses in Environmental Control and Life Support System (ECLSS) applications for removing and recycling crew-exhaled carbon dioxide. Each subsystem is sized for an ISRU-assisted sample return mission, producing in an 8-hour period 0.56-kilogram (kg) water and 0.26 kg methane from the Sabatier reactor and 0.50 kg oxygen from electrolyzed water. The testing of these technologies to date will be discussed as well as plans for integrating the subsystems for a complete end-to-end demonstration at Mars conditions. This paper will also address the history of these subsystem technologies, the issues involved with the interfaces between these subsystems, the storage of the products, and the benefits for the contined study of ISRU related technologies.

Title: Contact sensors on ceramic ball bearings
Publication: IAC 2002 congress proceedings, 53rd  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  10–19 October 2002, Houston, United States
Abstract: Integration of micro contact sensors onto a ball bearing is a critical technology necessary for online bearing health monitoring in an aeronautical harsh environment and evaluation of the bearing performance and design. The current planner fabrication methods offered by the MEMS technology restrict the possibility of integrating micro sensor onto a double contoured bearing surface in a traditional manufacturing environment. We have developed an unique technique to directly fabricate micron-sized pressure and temperature sensors onto a miniature ceramic ball bearing. A complete fabrication process, based on sensor design, surface preparation, sputtering parameters optimization, photolithographic techniques and sensor posttreatment, is described. Pressure and temperature measurement results on a miniature ceramic ball bearing have shown good indictors of the states of thermal elastohydrodynamic lubrication and bearing working condition.

Title: Definitions of relative orbits elements of spacecraft formation flying for purpose of orbit design
Publication: IAC 2002 congress proceedings, 53rd  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  10–19 October 2002, Houston, United States
Abstract: Much effort has been made to the research concerning the dynamical characteristics of spacecraft formation flight. The problem can be deduced to the issue of relative orbit motion of one satellite called companion satellite around another called reference or central satellite. It is known that the relative motion is completely determined by initial state of relative motion (called state parameter or parameter set 1). On the other hand the relative motion is caused by difference in eccentricity vector and non-coplanarity vector and influenced by the angle between the two vectors (called vector parameter or parameter set 2). Now the authors try to define relative orbit elements determining all geometrical and kinematical properties of the relative motion and having clear physical meaning similar to traditional orbit elements. Based on deep study of the dynamical characteristics we decide to define three sets of relative orbit elements as follows: (1) based on relative motion states; (2) based on orbit elements and their difference; (3) based on shape of pattern of satellite formation flight. Then the relations among the three sets of relative orbit elements are given, and relative orbit perturbation is primary researched in this paper.

Authors: ['Y. Tsuda', 'N. Sako', 'T. Eishima', 'T. Ito', 'Y. Arikawa', 'N. Miyamura', 'K. Kanairo', 'S. Ukawa', 'S. Ogasawara', 'S. Ishikawa', 'S. Nakasuka']
Title: Educational pico satellite project CubeSat - University of Tokyo's CubeSat XI and its operation plan
Publication: IAC 2002 congress proceedings, 53rd  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  10–19 October 2002, Houston, United States
Abstract: Our laboratory ISSL is proceeding with a project to design and fabricate a nano satellite named ” XI” as ’’CubeSat” project. This project was initiated at USSS’99 as a Japan-US joint venture to make satellites for educational purpose. CubeSat is, as can be imagined from the name, a 10 cm and 1kg cubic size satellite. XI is going to be the first satellite developed ISSL and demonstrate the ultra-small satellite bus system on orbit. In this small satellite project, many unique systems and project management has been taken to overcome the short of resources and troubles. Also world wide cooperation and information dispatch has been an important topic.

Authors: ['V. Pletser', 'O. Minster', 'S. Kremer', 'C. Kirschhock', 'J. Martens', 'P. Jacobs', "F. Freud'Homme", 'L. Vautmans', 'R. Kassel', 'R. Bosch']
Title: European microgravity facilities for zeolite experiments on the international space station
Publication: IAC 2002 congress proceedings, 53rd  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  10–19 October 2002, Houston, United States
Abstract:
Synthetic zeolites are complex porous silicates. Zeolite catalysis and related zeolite-based technologies have a growing impact on the economics and sustainability of products and processes in a growing number of industrial sectors, including environmental protection and nanotechnology.
A Sounding Rocket microgravity experiment led to significant insight in the physical aggregation patterns of zeolitic nanoscopic particles and the occurrence of self-organisation phenomena when undisturbed by convection.
The opportunity of performing longer microgravity duration experiments on zeolite structures was recently offered in the frame of a Taxi-Flight to the International Space Station (ISS) in November 2002 organized by Belgium and the European Space Agency (ESA). Two facilities are currently under development for this flight. One of them will use the Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG) in the US Lab. Destiny to achieve thermal induced selforganization of different types of Zeosil nanoslabs by heating and cooling. The other facility will be flown on the ISS Russian segment and will allow to form Zeogrids at ambient temperature.
On the other hand, ESA is studying the possibility of developing a dedicated insert for zeolite experiments to be used with the optical and diagnostic platform of the Protein Crystallisation Diagnostic Facility (PCDF), that will fly integrated in the European Drawer Rack on the Columbus Laboratory starting in 2004. This paper presents the approach followed by ESA to prepare and support zeolite investigations in microgravity and will present the design concept of these facilities.

Title: IRIS : Towards a fast and reliable stage weight prediction method
Publication: IAC 2002 congress proceedings, 53rd  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  10–19 October 2002, Houston, United States
Abstract:
The knowledge of the structural mass fraction of a given stage, which affects the performance of a rocket, is essential for the analysis of new or upgraded launchers or stages, whose need is increased by the quick evolution of the space programs and by the necessity of their adaptation to the market needs. The availability of this highly scattered variable is of primary importance at the early steps of the preliminary design studies.
At the start of the staging and performance studies, the lack of frozen weight data leads to rely on rough estimates, generally derived from printed source. The present empirical approach allows thus to get approximated values, inducing some result inaccuracy as well as difficulties of performance ranking for a multiple option analysis.
This forms a classical harsh fact of the preliminary design system studies, insufficiently discussed to date. It appears therefore highly desirable to have, for all the evaluation activities, a reliable, fast and easy- to-use weight or mass fraction prediction method. Additionally, the latter should allow for a pre selection of the alternative preliminary configurations, making possible a global system approach.
For that purpose, an attempt at modeling has been undertaken, whose objective was the determination of a parametric formulation of the mass fraction, to be expressed from a limited number of parameters available at the early steps of the project. It is based on the innovative use of a statistical method applicable to a variable as a function of several independent parameters.
A database of several conventional stages, operated with either solid or liquid propellants, has been elaborated, in conjunction with an evolving set of geometrical, physical and functional parameters likely to contribute to the description of the mass fraction and presumably known at the early steps of the preliminary design. Polynomial expressions of the mass fraction have been made up, associated to a confidence level. The outcome highlights the real possibility of a parametric formulation of the mass fraction for conventional stages on the basis of a limited number of descriptive parameters and with a high degree of accuracy, lower than 10%. The formulas have been later on tested on existing or preliminary stages not included in the initial database, for validation purposes. Their mass faction is assessed with a comparable accuracy, with a current limitation for 'small' stages. The polynomial generation method in use allows also for a search of the influence of some of the parameters.

Title: ISRU in the context of future European human Mars exploration
Publication: IAC 2002 congress proceedings, 53rd  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  10–19 October 2002, Houston, United States
Abstract: ISRU or In-Situ Resource Utilisation is the use of Martian resources to manufacture, typically, life support consumables (e.g. water, oxygen, breathing buffer gases), and propellant for a return journey to Earth. ESA through its GSTP and Aurora programmes has been investigating the system level design of a number of mission elements as potential European contributions to an international human Mars exploration mission intended for the 2020-2030 timeframe. One of these is an ISRU plant, a small chemical factory to convert feedstock brought from Earth (hydrogen), and Martian atmospheric gases (C02 and trace quantities of nitrogen and argon) into methane and oxygen propellant for Earth return and life support consumables, in advance of the arrival of astronauts. This paper will review and quantify the baseline chemical reactions essential for ISRU, including C02 collection and purification, Sabatier reduction of C02 with hydrogen to methane and water, and electrolysis of water in the context of the latest requirements. In addition, the paper will explore the options for compressing, cooling and storing gaseous products, methods for extracting buffer gases (such as nitrogen), and chemistries for producing additional oxygen. The paper will be written from the viewpoint of what European industry might be able to offer to a future set of Martian ISRU requirements, but in the context of an international human Mars mission. In addition, this paper will detail the selected reaction chemistries for each required subsystem, giving (where possible) mass, power and volume estimates. These will be drawn together, justified and presented as a system level design for an ISRU plant. Finally, a technology roadmap for ISRU development will be covered, suggesting near term (2002-2006), medium term (2006-2015) and long term (2015-2030) priorities which could enable a European ISRU capability to be qualified for initial human Mars exploration.

Title: Immobilization induces a very rapid increase in osteoclast activity
Publication: IAC 2002 congress proceedings, 53rd  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  10–19 October 2002, Houston, United States
Abstract: We studied in a randomized, strictly controlled cross-over design the effects of 6 days 6° head- down tilt bed rest (HDT) in 8 male healthy subjects in our metabolic ward. The study consisted of two periods (phases) of 11 days each in order to allow for the test subjects being their own controls. Both study phases were identical with respect to environmental conditions, study protocol and diet. Two days before arriving in the metabolic ward the subjects started with a diet. The diet was continued in the metabolic ward. The metabolic ward period (11 days) was divided into 3 parts: 4 ambulatory days, 6 days either HDT or control and 1 recovery day. Continuous urine collection started on the first day in the metabolic ward to analyze calcium excretion and bone resorption markers. On the 2nd ambulatory day in the metabolic ward and on the 5th day in HDT or control blood was drawn to analyze serum calcium, parathyroid hormone, and bone formation markers. Urinary calcium excretion was as early as the first day in immobilization increased (p < 0.01). CTX- and NTX-excretion stayed unchanged the first 24 hours in HDT compared to the control. But, already on the 2nd day of immobilization both bone resorption markers significantly increased. We conclude from these results - pronounced rise of bone resorption markers - that already 24 hours of immobilization induce a significant rise in osteoclast activity in healthy subjects. Thus, it appears possible to use short-term bed rest studies as a first step for the development of countermeasures to immobilization.

Title: Interoperability trends in Extravehicular Activity (EVA) space operations in the 21st century
Publication: IAC 2002 congress proceedings, 53rd  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  10–19 October 2002, Houston, United States
Abstract:
No other space operations in the 21st century more comprehensively embody the challenges and dependencies of interoperability than EVA. This discipline is already functioning at an unparalleled level of interagency, inter-organizational and international cooperation. This trend will only increase as space programs endeavor to expand in the face of shrinking budgets.
Among the topics examined in this paper are hardware-oriented issues. Differences in design standards among various space participants dictate differences in the EVA tools that must be manufactured, flown and maintained on-orbit. Presently only two types of functional space suits exist in the world. However, three versions of functional airlocks are in operation. Of the three airlocks, only the International Space Station (ISS) Joint Airlock can accommodate both types of suits. Due to functional differences in the suits, completely different operating protocols are required for each. Should additional space suit or airlock designs become available, the complexity will increase. The lessons learned as a result of designing and operating within such a system are explored.
This paper also examines the non-hardware challenges presented by interoperability for a discipline that is as uniquely dependent upon the individual as EVA. Operation of space suits (essentially single-person spacecrafts) by persons whose native language is not that of the suits’ designers is explored. The intricacies of shared mission planning, shared control and shared execution of joint EVA’s are explained. For example, once ISS is fully functional, the potential exists for two crewmembers of different nationality to be wearing suits manufactured and controlled by a third nation, while operating within an airlock manufactured and controlled by a fourth nation, in an effort to perform tasks upon hardware belonging to a fifth nation. Everything from training issues, to procedures development and writing, to real-time operations is addressed.
Finally, this paper looks to the management challenges presented by interoperability in general. With budgets being reduced among all space-faring nations, the need to expand cooperation in the highly expensive field of human space operations is only going to intensify. The question facing management is not if the trend toward interoperation will continue, but how to best facilitate its doing so. Real-world EVA interoperability experience throughout the Shuttle/Mir and ISS Programs is discussed to illustrate the challenges and illuminate the potential pitfalls present for any technical discipline facing this trend of 21st century space operations.

Title: Low-cost cold-gas RCS for the sloshsat FLEVO small satellite
Publication: IAC 2002 congress proceedings, 53rd  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  10–19 October 2002, Houston, United States
Abstract: A low-cost cold-gas Reaction Control System (RCS) has been designed and developed for liquid-slosh experiments in the ESA- sponsored Sloshsat FLEVO small satellite. Four spherical carbon/epoxy-wound stainless steel tanks of a “leak before burst” design store 1.6 kg of the gaseous nitrogen propellant at 473 bars corresponding to 20°C. Each tank is equipped with an accessories assembly, that includes a pyrovalve of a “self seal” design and a filter. The cold-gas propellant is supplied to twelve especially developed 0.8-N thrusters at a steady regulated pressure. Before reaching the thrusters the gas passes through a surge damper, a two- stage pressure regulating assembly and a latch valve. For safety and redundancy, two relief valves are mounted downstream of the regulators. A breadboard test system, that completely simulates the pneumatic nature of the SLOSHAT RCS, was used for ground test evaluation of the RCS performance in various modes of operation (continuous and pulses of various duty cycles) and for development experiments. Thruster startup and shut-down time periods were less than 5 ms. Delivered specific impulse of 70 s in vacuum was demonstrated. The RCS successfully passed the required qualification and acceptance tests.

Title: Mars sample return : Architecture and mission design
Publication: IAC 2002 congress proceedings, 53rd  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  10–19 October 2002, Houston, United States
Abstract:
Mars Sample Return (MSR) architecture and mission engineering, led by Boeing for JPL, is presented. The study sought credible data to support planning a 2011 mission to return 500g of scientifically selected samples.
Phase 1 compared diverse architecture options to accomplish the mission. 17 theme-based architectures were conceived, quantified, measured, and scored. Two primary and three secondary architectures were recommended.
Phase 2 developed engineering detail for a simple architecture specified by JPL: dual mission to two landing sites; short-range, radioisotope-powered sampling rovers; Mars orbit rendezvous; and electric return propulsion with Shuttle rendezvous. The design comprises nine system elements. Solutions for sample handling and breaking the back contamination chain are detailed. Total mission duration is five years.
Technology tailoring, rather than technology creation, is required. Mission development cost, including margins and wraps, is $2.8B. The study concluded that many schemes can feasibly accomplish Mars sample return, depending on program objectives adopted.

Title: Radiation effects and hardening techniques for spacecraft microelectronics
Publication: IAC 2002 congress proceedings, 53rd  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  10–19 October 2002, Houston, United States
Abstract: Natural radiation from the Van Allen belts, solar activity and cosmic rays found outside of the protection of the earth’s atmosphere can produce deleterious effects on microelectronics used in space systems. Historically, civil space agencies and the commercial satellite industry have been able to utilize components produced in special fabrication process foundries that were developed during the 1970s and 1980s under sponsorship of the Departments of Defense (DoD) and Energy (DoE) to harden components against radiation effects. In the post-cold war world the DoD and DoE push to continue to advance the rad-hard processes has waned. Generally the available rad-hard components lag 2+ technology node generations behind state-of-the-art commercial technologies. As a result space craft designers face a large performance gap when trying to utilize available rad-hard components. Compounding the performance gap problems, rad-hard components are also becoming increasingly harder to get. Faced with the economic pitfalls associated with low demand versus the ever increasing investment required for integrated circuit manufacturing equipment most sources of rad-hard parts have simply exited this market in recent years, leaving only two domestic US suppliers of digital rad-hard components. This paper summarizes the radiation induced mechanisms that can cause digital microelectronics to fail in space, techniques that can be applied to mitigate these failure mechanisms, and ground based testing used to validate radiation hardness/tolerance. The radiation hardening techniques can be broken down into two classes, Hardness By Process (HBP) and Hardness By Design (HBD). Fortunately many HBD techniques can be applied to commercial fabrication processes providing space craft designers with radiation tolerant Application Specific Integrated Circuits (ASICs) that can bridge the performance gap between the special HBP foundries and the commercial state-of-the-art performance.

Title: Selected precepts in lunar architecture
Publication: IAC 2002 congress proceedings, 53rd  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  10–19 October 2002, Houston, United States
Abstract:
The 1997 NASA Habitats and Surface Construction Roadmap defined three classes of lunar and planetary architechue, ranging from habitats built entirely on Earth to habitats built on the extraterrestrial surface. The definitions are: Class 1 - Pre-integrated, landed complete; Class 2 - Pre-fabricated, assembled, deployed or inflated on the surface; Class 3 - In-Situ Resource Construction.
The extreme environmental conditions on the Moon shape and constrain Lunar Architecture in far-reaching ways. These environmental threats and stressors include vacuum, .18 G partial gravity, radiation, micrometeoroid impacts, the 28-day diurnal cycle, extreme thermal cycling, and pervasive dust. Also, the unique instance of the landing zone poses a human-made potential environmental hazard. The design and development of lunar construction technologies and habitats must respond effectively to these threats. For this reason, developing Lunar Architechue will be challenging and complex.
Although it is reasonable to characterize the individual elements of a lunar base as Class 1,2, or 3, in actuahty, none of them on the Moon (or Mars) would be purely of one class. To explicate this "hybrid" character of surface construction, this paper presents three further units of analysis in architectural design research: taxonomy, typology and morphology.

Title: University satellite consortium and space education in Japan centered on micro-nano satellites
Publication: IAC 2002 congress proceedings, 53rd  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  10–19 October 2002, Houston, United States
Abstract:
This paper reviews the current status of space engineering education in Japan especially centered on micro satellites and discusses how to foster such activities. Hands-on training using micro satellites provides unique opportunity of space education to university level students, by giving them a chance to experience the whole space project cycle from mission creation, satellite design, fabrication, test, launch, operation till analysis of the results. Project management and team working are other important skills that can be trained in these projects. Micro satellites are not only useful for education but also are promising as a new player in space development or space business.
The importance of micro satellites as a tool for space engineering education will be discussed first, followed by the description of its importance as a new player in space development. Then the history of the related activities in Japan will be reviewed, starting with Satellite Design Contest to current real satellite projects and "UMSEC," a university community to support students' activities of developing satellites and rockets. Finally, we will propose several actions which should be pursued by building some international university community.

Title: Uses of computed tomography in the NASA materials science program
Publication: IAC 2002 congress proceedings, 53rd  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  10–19 October 2002, Houston, United States
Abstract:
Computed tomography (CT) has proved to be of inestimable value in enabling investigators to appraise samples as varied as the Mechanics of Granular Materials (MGM) to electronic materials to space grown materials such as meteorites. The system at Kennedy Space Center (KSC), because of its convenient geographical location, is ideal for examining samples prior to launch and immediately after returning to Earth. It also has the advantage of the choice of fluxes, including the use of x- rays and a radioisotope of cobalt isotope, the latter being basically monochromatic. The measured
absorption permits a reasonable measurement of density to be made from which chemical composition can be determined. Due to the current dearth of long duration space grown materials, the CT instrument has been used (1) to characterize materials prior to flight, (2) to determine thermal expansion values, and (3) to examine meteorites, examples of long duration space grown materials. Examples of determination of composition of solid solutions, including mercury cadmium telluride and germanium-silicon alloys will be shown. Other important parameters which have been measured include the variation of density with temperature for materials to be used in future flight experiments. This involves the fabrication of a single zone furnace incorporating a heat pipe,
and the installation of the unit on to the CT instrument. As a test material, lead has been heated to 900°C, and incrementally cooled to establish thermal equilibrium while CT readings and digital radiographs (to measure length changes) have been taken. The precision of length measurement, and the exact location and definition of the bottom of a rounded sample limits the precision of the length measurement. Nevertheless, once the sample has solidified and filled the fused silica tube, reasonable reading can be obtained. Most critical is the density change in the solid, through the melting point and at higher temperatures in the liquid state. These data are needed for engineering purposes to aid in the design of containment ampoules and cartridges, and for the investigator to perform fluid flow calculations. A sample of a lead-antimony has been partly measured; this alloy will be used by Professor Poirier in a planned flight experiment. Finally, three-dimensional results will be shown of the structure of a two-phase metallic meteorite of metal and sulfide, in which the iron-nickel phase has coarsened during slow cooling over hundreds of millions of years.

Title: 2001 : Building for space travel - The history of space exploration in an art museum context
Publication: IAC 2001 congress proceedings, 52nd  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  1–5 October 2001, Toulouse, France
Abstract:
“Ars sine scientia nihil est,” or “Art without science is nothing.” So said the medieval French Master Mason Jean Mignot, referring to the ‘science’ of geometry that acted as the foundation for good proportions in architecture. Although attitudes in recent centuries have tended to compartmentalize the arts and sciences, two experiences at The Art Institute of Chicago have shown that the fine arts and science and technology all still co-exist within aerospace subjects. The first instance of this investigation was the 1996 exhibition, book, and series of public programs entitled Building for Air Travel. Architecture and Design for Commercial Aviation. This examined the role that architects, industrial designers, and graphic designers have played in creating airports, aircraft factories, airliner interiors and airline corporate identity over the past eight decades.
Our current exhibition and public interpretive project 2001: Building for Space Travel is a sequel to that very successful traveling exhibition on commercial aviation. 2001: Building for Space Travel examines the roles that architects and designers have played in the shaping of structures, interior spaces and corporate identity for space exploration, in reality as well as science fiction. The epic film 2001. A Space Odyssey is used as a focal point in the overall interpretation since even leading aerospace figures such as Wernher von Braun encouraged his designers and engineers to use that film as a source of inspiration to make space travel an everyday occurrence for all. Our project examines the role that design arts professionals have played in the history of space travel within three categories that are extensions of life and design activity on earth: our image .of the cosmos, before and after space travel; conflict in space; and exploration of the wilderness.
This paper will summarize the themes, installation, and public programs of 2001:Building for Space Travel at The Art Institute of Chicago in comparison with other activities within that museum’s Department of Architecture related to the history of aerospace technology, from exhibitions to archival collections. In so doing, it will present unique circumstances where a fine arts museum has endorsed and successfully implemented a series of programs related to aerospace design and technology.

Title: An attempt to operationally deploy the "lessons learned"
Publication: IAC 2001 congress proceedings, 52nd  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  1–5 October 2001, Toulouse, France
Abstract:
Lessons Learned are considered by Alcatel Space industries, to be a strong lever for improving competitiveness and reducing risks within the company.
Backed by significant Management commitment, an operational Lessons Learned system has been implemented.
The Lessons Learned system completes the core quality management system, by offering new projects straightforward access to the key issues of previous projects.
Simplicity was the key design driver throughout system development.
Based on a conventional model, i.e.
® collection of facts and events,
• definition of the Lessons Learned,
® use of the Lessons Learned,
® feedback on use of the Lessons Learned, the system relies more on the people involved, than on an automatic expert system.
A documentary database tool is nonetheless used.
Process design was started up in March 2000, we’ve been testing the procedure and initial data on some operational projects since September 2000; implementation and deployment was started in February 2001.

Title: Coverage robustness to orbital parameter drifts : An additional criterion to design a constellation
Publication: IAC 2001 congress proceedings, 52nd  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  1–5 October 2001, Toulouse, France
Abstract:
Up to now, coverage optimizations of satellite
constellations were only assuming nominal satellite
trajectories, without any orbital disturbances. These
assumptions are good at crudely discriminating
between many candidate constellation patterns. But
in the final steps of the selection, we often have to
deal with a whole bunch of patterns exhibiting similar
coverage characteristics. In this case, additional
optimization criteria are welcomed to drive the
selection of the best constellation pattern. Among
many potential criteria, the coverage robustness to
orbital parameter drifts can be considered
advantageously because in real life, satellites are not
following perfect orbital trajectories. A good
coverage robustness will usually mean fewer station
keeping maneuvers and a better fuel consumption
that can then be translated into a longer satellite
lifetime. Some numerical results are presented to
support these assertions.

Title: Development of a small capacity Li ion battery for space
Publication: IAC 2001 congress proceedings, 52nd  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  1–5 October 2001, Toulouse, France
Abstract:
For a few years, there has been a general trend to design smaller and smaller spacecrafts, in order to meet low cost goals or to insure redundancy. Reduced scale spacecrafts such as microsatelllites, automatic probes, small planetary stations and vehicles present specific requirements in terms of energy storage, in parallel with demand for low cost or OTS components.
SAFT answer to this request by developing a lithium ion battery, based on existing cells, slightly modified to meet space environment requirements. This paper describes SAFT development plan for a new, reliable and low cost small capacity battery for space. It also includes a description of the cell itself, battery assembly, electronics concept and first tests results, such as Beginning Of Life data and preliminary cycles.

Title: Heat exchanger configurations for aerospace pre-coolers
Publication: IAC 2001 congress proceedings, 52nd  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  1–5 October 2001, Toulouse, France
Abstract:
Most air-breathing engine cycles for future launch vehicles which are designed for speeds close to the momentum drag limit of around Mach 6 require a pre-cooler heat exchanger to cool the air collected by the intake before any further processing (compression, separation) can be undertaken. The mass and volume of these heat exchangers are a critical part of the viability of the engine cycle for use in a future launcher. It has been found that the configuration of the heat exchanger is an important factor in achieving the required performances.
There are three main factors of importance:
1. The first factor is the tube geometry which determines the compactness and mass. Here it can be shown that simple fine tubes offer the most mass effective solution.
2. The second factor is the tube flow pattern that determines the pressure drop across the heat exchanger. Here the use of fractal patterns can be used to minimise the pressure losses.
3. The third factor is the overall flow configuration. Here both pure cross flow and pure counter flow configurations present disadvantages.
A hybrid pseudo-counter flow configuration is presented and described which resolves these difficulties. It will be shown that this configuration has a powerful level of flexibility allowing independent optimisation of both the internal and external fluid paths. This adapts the design to the best needs of any air-breathing engine cycle which can include both cryogenic fuelled aircraft and combined cycle rocket engine based launchers. The SKYLON pre-cooler is used to illustrate the configuration solutions combined.

Title: Lightweight chambers for thrust assemblies
Publication: IAC 2001 congress proceedings, 52nd  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  1–5 October 2001, Toulouse, France
Abstract: New materials and fabrication techniques have been successfully used to create actively cooled thrust chambers that weigh less, and potentially operate hotter, than conventional designs. Results could improve the performance and payload capacity of many vehicles, including new Reusable Launch Vehicle (RLV) concepts. Polymer Matrix Composite (PMC) and Metal Matrix Composite (MMC) materials replaced traditional metal alloys for structural jackets and manifolds. Ceramic Matrix Composite (CMC) materials and an advanced copper alloy (GRCop-84) were used for chamber liners to significantly increase operating temperatures. Several small chambers were fabricated and tested with promising results to demonstrate that designs over 50% lighter are feasible. New fabrication techniques were demonstrated, including an advanced casting technique and a low cost vacuum plasma spray process. Based on the favorable results for the MMC, PMC and GRCop-84 materials, similar concepts were applied to larger chamber designs. These larger units are currently being fabricated for testing in 2001. Hot-fire testing on the larger units will directly compare performance results between a conventional chamber design and these “lightweight” alternatives. The technology developed and demonstrated by this effort could benefit new RLV programs, as well as other existing and future engine designs.

Title: Prediction and validation of the structural random vibration and internal acoustic environment induced by the launch acoustic load
Publication: IAC 2001 congress proceedings, 52nd  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  1–5 October 2001, Toulouse, France
Abstract:
During the Launch phase, the structures withstand an heavy acoustic excitation mainly generated by the engines and the aerodynamic forces over the whole of the vehicle. The acoustic excitation generates a random vibration environment that has to be assessed to specify the secondary structures design loads and qualification environment of the mounted equipment. The target of the present work is to verify the reliability of the simulation techniques based on Finite Element Method (FEM) and the statistical Energy Analysis (SEA) principles; these tools have been used for the derivation of spacecraft Random Vibration Environment (RVE). The starting point is a collection of test data measured on a reference Acoustic Test Launch configuration. Then, mathematical models representing the reference test configuration have been developed and validated; after validation these models shall be upgraded to represent actual spacecraft launch configurations. Similarity of structural layout was a condition for the modelling baseline development.
The prediction of the RVE responses had to be performed by combining different analysis methods in order to cover the large frequency band of a the typical launch acoustic environment (20 Hz - 2kHz). This combined approach has been applied to the Multi-Purpose Pressurised Logistic Module (MPLM)) project.
The large amount of data measured throughout the MPLM primary structure, the secondary structure, and the mechanical interfaces of the equipment units, allowed a complete validation of the analysis tools. Various analysis cases were performed and the results correlated with the test data. During the correlation activity, the computed structural Power Spectral Density (PSD) levels have been compared to the experimental data acquired by accelerometers mounted on the test item.
Besides, the computed Internal Sound Pressure Levels (SPL) have been correlated to the pressure signals measured by the MPLM internal microphones.
From this experience it was confirmed that the hybrid approach using FEM & SEA techniques is well suited to define the preliminary spacecraft vibration environment induced by the Acoustic loads in the broadband frequency. The validated analysis procedures can be typically applied in a pre-test phase to drive the set up and also to design a low cost test configuration.
Moreover, the availability of the MPLM test database, combined with small dedicated characterisation tests (e.g. material attenuation factors measurements) and validated analysis tools enables to design similar spacecraft structures without the need of complex and expensive qualification tests at system levels. For example, this approach is currently used for the Columbus Orbital Facility, node 2 and node 3 ISS modules.
The so assessed RVE is actually used as input for the Design Loads and Qualification Test Level definition of secondary structures and equipment units.
Based on this verification approach, potential design problems can be identified at an early status to avoid, in principle, late expensive modifications.

Title: Project GALILEO from Ganymede back to Io
Publication: IAC 2001 congress proceedings, 52nd  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  1–5 October 2001, Toulouse, France
Abstract:
Galileo has now completed two years of the Galileo Millennium Mission and the spacecraft continues to gather new and exciting observations of the Jupiter system. In late December 2000, Galileo teamed with Cassini in the first ever collaboration between two missions to simultaneously study an outer planet and its surrounding environment. The unique opportunity of having two very capable spacecraft perform complementary observations is yielding new insights into the interactions of the solar wind with the magnetosphere, the atmospheric dynamics of Jupiter, the rings, and the tenuous atmospheres of Ganymede and lo. While Galileo provided high-resolution remote sensing observations during its Ganymede 29 encounter, Cassini acquired large-scale contextual views. Both spacecraft observed magnetospheric bow shock crossings and the same high velocity dust stream originating from the vicinity of lo. Following the successful lo encounters in late 1999, the Galileo mission was specifically designed to reduce radiation damage by keeping the spacecraft outside the intense radiation environment, close to Jupiter with the goal of being operational when Cassini flew by en route to Saturn. Following Ganymede 29, the focus of the mission shifted back to lo as the spacecraft performed a gravity assist at Callisto to set up lo flyby geometries enabling definitive observations of that moon’s magnetic field.
For a 14-week period around the Ganymede 29 perijove passage, Galileo collected continuous fields and particles data providing a complete slice from the solar wind through the magnetosphere and back out again. Collection of this data set required a new level of sequence design complexity to integrate real-time and recorded data acquisition with concurrent data playback. Significant engineering issues and future plans are described. Each passage close to Jupiter brings new
challenges to spacecraft operations as the cumulative radiation dosage approaches three-and-a-half times the design limits. Engineering data on spacecraft and instrument performance in this harsh environment is very useful to designers of future missions to Jupiter and its moons.
Science results which continue to change our fundamental understanding of the Jupiter system, particularly the Jovian magnetosphere and magnetic fields of the satellites, are also presented.

Title: Status of the DELFT aerospace re-entry test vehicle
Publication: IAC 2001 congress proceedings, 52nd  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  1–5 October 2001, Toulouse, France
Abstract:
The DART (Delft Aerospace Re-entry Test) project entails the development, building and repeated flights of a small, reusable, low cost, re-entry testbed, for the purpose of fundamental studies of selected topics concerning re-entry.
The main mission goals are the collection of aerothermodynamic data in a real re-entry flight and the design and validation of a hot metallic load-carrying external structure for the vehicle. The emphasis of the aerothermodynamic measurements is on high-quality measurements in a clean, unpolluted boundary layer. Subjects of interest are shock wave-boundary layer interaction, laminar-to-turbulent transition and catalicity of materials. The use of metallic materials allows for this clean boundary layer, obtaining which would not be possible with use of ablative materials.
While the metallic material, PM1000, is able to withstand temperatures up to some 1250°C, aerodynamic heating is such that this temperature will be exceeded without cooling. For this cooling, two distinct methods are used. For the thermally highest loaded nose region, a direct water cooling method is used; for the lower-temperature main body, a new, patented cooling method is used based on improved radiation cooling.
The vehicle is a simple axisymmetric sphere-cone-flare configuration, and will fly a fully ballistic trajectory. This, in combination with the low cost flight opportunity of the Russian Yolna launcher, leads to a project that is substantially cheaper than all current competing proposals.
The DART project is led by Delft Aerospace, in co-operation with Fokker Space, NLR and ESA-ESTEC in the Netherlands and with IT AM and SRC Makeyev in Russia.

Title: Thermal and ECLSS performance during the first MPLM mission
Publication: IAC 2001 congress proceedings, 52nd  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  1–5 October 2001, Toulouse, France
Abstract:
The MPLM (Multi Purpose Logistics Module) is a cooperative project between NASA, ASI (with ESA involvement for the Environmental Control Life Support procurement) and was designed, developed, produced, integrated and delivered by Alenia Spazio (Turin plant). The MPLM is one of the Elements constituting the ISS (International Space Station) and, with respect to the other Elements, it is not permanently attached to the ISS, but transported by the Orbiter from/to the Earth, since its primary use is to re-supply and return cargoes.
The MPLM capability to support the logistic flights is guaranteed during several mission phases (ground, Orbiter transportation, on-orbit docked to the Station).
The MPLM design includes an Environmental Control System (ECS), made up of two sections: the Environmental Control and Life Support System (ECLSS), essentially devoted to providing a comfortable environment for the crew; and the Internal Thermal Control System (ITCS), formed by its active and passive sections, for heat collection and transportation from payloads and subsystems and to protect the MPLM from the external environment.
During the first MPLM flight, the Alenia Spazio ECS team supported the NASA Mission Control Center (Houston) with an on site team providing 24 hours a day mission coverage. This support included the possibility to run Thermal Mathematical Models in real time, while another ECS team was present in the Turin plant to guarantee additional support. In particular, one of the most critical aspects during a MPLM mission is to maintain the air pressure below the MPLM Positive Pressure Relief Valves actuating limit. At the same time, also the minimum temperature needs to be controlled to avoid condensation within the pressurized module. Furthermore, the air pressure, during the reentry in atmosphere, must be higher than the MPLM Negative Pressure Relief Valve actuating limit.
All these aspects are pursued by managing the MPLM shell heaters switching on/off cycles following dedicated crew manual commands included in the flight plan. During the mission the ECS team has the task to monitor the telemetry data (mainly MPLM air pressure and temperature) and to determine if the Module thermal behavior is in accordance with the predicted one. In case of discrepancies, proper heater operation adjustments must be considered.
In addition the real time support includes the resolution of some problems caused by ECS components malfunctions.

Title: DEVELOPMENT AND EVALUATION OF THE MARS PATHFINDER INFLATABLE AIRBAG LANDING SYSTEM
Publication: IAC 1998 congress proceedings, 49th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  28 September–2 October 1998, Melbourne, Australia
Abstract:
The entry, descent, and landing system of the Mars Pathfinder spacecraft includes a unique subsystem of airbags for impact attenuation. The airbag geometric configuration and associated landing dynamic analysis was performed by the Jet Propulsion Laboratory and Sandia National Laboratories [1,2]. ILC Dover performed detailed design and fabrication of subscale and full-scale prototypes and flight airbag systems.
This paper presents key steps in the development effort that produced the airbag system, including materials selection, patterning, fabrication issues, component design, and packaging/deployment.
