These steps outline many elements common to the development of engineered softgoods products for aerospace applications.

Title: DEVELOPMENT AND UTILIZATION OF THE APM LOGISTICS SIMULATION MODEL (LSM) FOR RESUPPLY DEMAND AND SPARE ANALYSIS SUPPORT
Publication: IAC 1998 congress proceedings, 49th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  28 September–2 October 1998, Melbourne, Australia
Abstract:
The Attached Pressurised Module (APM) constitutes one element of the European contribution to the International Space Station (ISS) programme. The APM, whose operative life will be 10 years, is presently scheduled to be launched and docked to the Space Station in early 2003. The APM project is developed according to the European Space Agency (ESA) requirements.
The Columbus Logistics Simulation Model (COL LSM) has been developed in support of the APM design. The COL LSM satisfies the logistics needs for a statistic tool to analyze support needs of the APM module during the E phase and to compare the results against the design requirements and constraints. To meet this result, the COL LSM provides reports and graphics related to maintenance, parts transportation and storage, Logistics Availability, resupply demand. These projections are derived from a collection of statistics rolled-up from Montecarlo simulations. In addition, the COL LSM capability to release outputs at equipment level offers a valid support to the Spares Assessment and Recommendation process through the performance of a sensitivity analysis aiming to optimize the operational availability of the equipment. The COL LSM constitutes, together with the Columbus Logistics Support Analysis (COL LSA) Support Record System database, an integrated software platform to support the development of the logistics analyses. The COL LSA database, through an interface report, imports in the COL LSM the pre- processed data set necessary to perform the logistics calculations.
The COL LSM allows an easy handling of the COL LSA data to enable the creation of equipment hierarchical structures that, together with the logistics scenarios and models created within the COL LSM, can properly simulate the system behavior.

Title: Design and Development of Observation and Scientific Windows for Manned and Planetary Modules
Publication: IAC 1998 congress proceedings, 49th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  28 September–2 October 1998, Melbourne, Australia
Abstract: Initial design concepts for scientific windows in manned and planetary modules must precede the design of the modules themselves. This must begin with a list of prioritized requirements for ail possible uses. Windows are just one of several configurations for general purpose “ports” in module outer walls, and they create “facilities within a facility”. Their service lifetimes over 10-25 years of continuous use over extremely broad spectral ranges of 0.1 to 100 microns mandate change-out capability. Window or pane replacement can be equally useful in remedying contamination/micrometeoroid surface damage effects as well as providing very broad spectral utility. Also, provisions for a clean, dry, gas stream across the inner working surface is required to eliminate fogging caused by cabin humidity and near-by operators’ breath. For habitation modules placed on planetary surfaces as opposed to orbiting modules, the effects of local terrain as sources of blockage and scattering, as well as those associated with the configuration of the station complex, itself, require careful evaluation. These and other design considerations about contamination Control during design, fabrication, testing, and use, as well as the avoidance of optical and infrared radiometric scattering both externally and internally, and access to power, command and data links for window-mounted instrumentation during operational use, are covered in this paper.

Title: ENVISAT RA-2 Advanced Radar Altimeter: Instrument Design and Pre-Launch Performance Assessment Review
Publication: IAC 1998 congress proceedings, 49th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  28 September–2 October 1998, Melbourne, Australia
Abstract:
RA-2 is a second generation spaceborne radar altimeter designed and developed by ALENIA AEROSPAZIO (ALS) in the frame of the European Space Agency (ESA) ENVISAT programme. The project, started at beginning of 1990, reached its completion in October 1998 with the delivery of the Instrument Flight Model to Daimler- Benz Aerospace, Dornier (the mission prime contractor of ENVISAT) for its integration on the platform.
RA-2 only partly resembles in its characteristics those of ERS-1 / ERS-2 first generation Radar Altimeters, designed by ALS. Principal innovative features of the RA-2 are: dual frequency operation (Ku and S band) for ionospheric bias correction of the range measurements, enhanced precision range measurements over oceans, capability of including in the instrument telemetry data down linked to ground In-phase and Quadrature samples of individual Ku band radar echoes, resolution adaptivity and robust tracking algorithms to allow range measurements and radar echoes collection not only over open oceans but also at land-ocean boundaries, ice and land regions with the real objective of continuous global Earth topography mapping.
Aim of this paper is to provide an overview of the instrument key design characteristic-, and to present instrument pre-launch performance results derived from the evaluation of the test results gathered during the instrument integration and characterisation campaign of the Flight Model (FM).

Title: Experience of Development of the Liquid Rocket Engine with Fuel-Rich Preburner Cycle
Publication: IAC 1998 congress proceedings, 49th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  28 September–2 October 1998, Melbourne, Australia
Abstract:
One of the basic trends of improvement of power-mass and dimensional characteristics of main liquid rocket engines (LRE) is, in the last years, application of staged combustion power cycle employing feel-rich prebumer.
In some cases the launcher stage layout causes necessity to use an immovable engine for the thrust vector control. In these cases the preference may be given to the high-power feel-rich gas injected into the thrust chamber nozzle downstream of the nozzle throat.
As is generally known, the feel-rich prebumer gas of NTO+UDMH propellants possesses high power characteristics. This allows to utilize it for the engine thrust vector control. Just that very factor has predetermined creation of the engine with optimal power-mass characteristics.
The task of the feel complete gasification requires solution of a number of problems. Elaboration of such an engine has been performed at Yuzhnoye State Design Office.
The engine is designed for a missile second stage. Employment of this engine has allowed to increase considerably ballistic characteristics of the latter. The report presents general characteristics of the engine, its schematic, as well as data on development of its basic components: combustion chamber, turbopump, prebumer.

Title: FEDSAT - AUSTRALIA'S ENTRY INTO THE SATELLITE BUSINESS
Publication: IAC 1998 congress proceedings, 49th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  28 September–2 October 1998, Melbourne, Australia
Abstract: The stage is set for Australia to launch itself into the satellite business. The implications of the FedSat mission to Australia are potentially far reaching. This talk outlines the involvement of Australia in space since the days of Blue Streak until the present time. With the launch of FedSat, we will have begun the very necessary process of building up a satellite design, fabrication, test and control infrastructure in Australia. There are precedents throughout the South East Asian region, that reflect the growing culture of satellite technology. With this as background, the ultimate focus of Australia's space industry is addressed.

Title: HAZARDS TO SPACEFLIGHT
Publication: IAC 1998 congress proceedings, 49th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  28 September–2 October 1998, Melbourne, Australia
Abstract:
This is a critical time in the history of human space activities as there is increasing interest in the use of space for terrestrial applications and in the expansion of the space frontier. The hazards resulting from human activity in space, coupled with the intrinsic hazards of the space environment, represent a growing threat for the expansion of the human presence in space.
Radiation represents a primary concern either for manned or unmanned missions. The effects on spacecraft, such as charging and electrical equipment failures can jeopardize mission success. Shielding and Space Weather Forecasting are two mitigation methods that can minimize the radiation effects on spacecraft.
Only 5% of objects orbiting the Earth are operational spacecraft. Detection and data collection methods are developed to know the distribution of debris and to have a statistical sampling of particle fluxes. The ways to mitigate are to protect spacecraft against collisions and to minimize the population of debris.
As for crewed spaceflight, space is a foreign and hostile environment for humans due to radiation, vacuum and microgravity. Moreover, numerous psychological stressors are at work in this environment, which can lead to the development of social and psychological problems.
Because of the difficulty of quantifying space hazards, S.W.O.T. (Strength, Weakness, Opportunity, Threat) analysis is a flexible technique allowing decisionmakers to analyze these four factors to recommend and to mitigate hazards.
Finally, legal and policy instruments are required to facilitate and allow the definition and enforcement of appropriate mitigation measures.

Authors: ['A.M. Baker', 'J. Keravala', 'J. MacFarlane', 'R. Newlands', 'R. Osborne', 'D. Sadler', 'R. Smith']
Title: HYBRID MOTOR DEVELOPMENTS WITHIN THE UK AMATEUR ROCKETRY FIELD
Publication: IAC 1998 congress proceedings, 49th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  28 September–2 October 1998, Melbourne, Australia
Abstract:
Aspirespace is a UK organisation whose vision is to inspire and excite people about science and technology, using space as a medium. A key goal for realising this is the development of a series of evolutionary, recoverable rocket vehicles. Aspirespace is committed to the development of hybrid rocket motors to power these vehicles, and has recently tested a small nitrous oxide/polyethylene hybrid, the H2. This paper covers the design process which created the H2, the test programme and equipment developed by Aspirespace to verify motor simulations and outlines Aspirespace hybrid rocket motor applications.
The H2 was fabricated for a component cost of under £500, with an approximate firing cost below UK£15 per 1000Ns of total impulse, a cost reduction factor of >12x compared to an equivalent impulse solid rocket motor. Total design impulse was between 670 and 1600Ns, depending on the oxidiser tank used and based on a predicted Isp of 220s. Ignition was successful at the 1st attempt. Initial tests indicated a performance within 3% of Isp and 14% of total impulse predictions. The testing programme is on schedule to obtain sufficient data for the design of a flight optimised hybrid motor capable of propelling a research vehicle to 6000m+ apogee.

Title: Innovations for Competitiveness: European Views on “Better-Faster- Cheaper”
Publication: IAC 1998 congress proceedings, 49th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  28 September–2 October 1998, Melbourne, Australia

Title: NUMERICAL STUDY ON INTERNAL FLOW FIELD OF SRM WITH FINOCYL GRAIN AND SUBMERGED NOZZLE
Publication: IAC 1998 congress proceedings, 49th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  28 September–2 October 1998, Melbourne, Australia
Abstract: Internal flow field of SRM is quite complicate and plays an important role in research and design of SRM. In this paper, numerical simulation is carried out for the 3-D aft flow field in combustion chamber of SRM with finocyl grain and submerged nozzle, and for the 3-D transonic flow in the nozzle, the effects of submergence ratio on the flow structure of aft flow field in SRM are also studied. AF method is used to solve 3-D thin-layer N-S equations, dissipations, local time step, residue smoothing, stability factor and decomposition of computational domain are introduced to get fairly good stability and adaptability. The results show that there is a recircular zone in the back-wall domain of submerged nozzle, and the 3-D flow characteristic is significant. There exists a distinct interface between recircular zone and main flow region, a stagnation point zone near the back wall of submerged nozzle makes the thermal environment worse. The submergence ratio does effect on the flow pattern in the aft domain in combustion chamber. These results provide useful basis for SRM design.

Title: OPTIMISED STORABLE PROPELLANT UPPER-STAGE FOR ARIANE 5-EVOLUTION LAUNCHER
Publication: IAC 1998 congress proceedings, 49th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  28 September–2 October 1998, Melbourne, Australia
Abstract:
The GTO commercial satcom launch market
surveys show a continuous trend toward larger
size and larger mass for payload. The
European launcher industry, in co-ordination
with ESA and CNES agencies, has then looked
those last months to the most appropriate way
to answer this market tendency, with the goal
to improve the Ariane 5 launcher via a new
upper-stage, while maintaining its cost
competitiveness, its reliability and increasing its
flexibility for other type of missions.
This lead to the pre-development study of a
performance optimised storable propellant
upper-stage using a new turbo-pump engine
together with the capability of performing flights
with long ballistic phases and multiple ignitions.
After a short recall of the main launcher
requirements, this paper presents the design
analysis and optimisation process which has
been applied for the stage architecture concept
and for its propulsion system preliminary
design. It puts in evidence the principal design
constraints and shows the architecture choice
evolution together with the selection of the
propulsion system main features.
The major characteristics of the new turbopump
80-100 kN thrust class engine are
presented as well, in order to allow the
discussion of the main propulsion functional
characteritics, and the summary of the tradeoffs
applied for maximizing GTO performance,
together with controlling of the development
risks. The impacts on stage design and functional
characteristics due to mission profile with long
ballistic phases are also put in evidence.
A short review of the programmatic aspects
finalise the presentation of this new upperstage
pre-project.

Title: Problems of Modern Constructions of Orbital Complexes Solar Batteries : Resource, Prediction, Calculation and Experimental Development
Publication: IAC 1998 congress proceedings, 49th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  28 September–2 October 1998, Melbourne, Australia
Abstract: The problems of prediction of a resource, calculation and experimental development of constructions of solar batteries on the honeycombed foundation of modem orbital complexes with a long exploitation period (up to 5 - 10 years) are considered. The new, theoretically- experimental approach to assigning scientifically justified regimes of accelerated tests of such constructions permitting to replace prolonged tests by short-term tests, equivalent to them. The approach is based on separation of mechanisms quasistatic and fatigue of processes of a damage accumulation in materials of the constructive elements of the battery. In a basis of the given approach puts the following statements: a) the damage in an arbitrary point of a considered body is determined only by level by operating stress and time of their operation; b) the ratio of a fatigue component in a common damage of a material in a considered point to its quasistatic component is magnitude invariant in relation to spent tests not dependent from selected regimes of tests. For a realization of the given approach it is necessary to have of curve prolonged strength, and also curve fatigues for want of symmetric cycle of a loading, obtained from the tests patterns for fixed values of temperatures appropriate to a range of temperatures under conditions exploitation and tests. The definition of the stress-strained state and choice of optimum parameters of a construction of the battery is carried out with use of the volumetric finite elements, by a solution of a three-dimensional boundary value problem of theimoviscoelastoplasticity and with use of the classical theory of the plates also. The common methodology of assigning of regimes of accelerated tests of a construction of the solar batteries with reference to space vehicles such as "Microsputnik" is considered.

Title: Robotics Sidewall Logistics Carrier Concept for the International Space Station
Publication: IAC 1998 congress proceedings, 49th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  28 September–2 October 1998, Melbourne, Australia
Abstract:
Many of the International Space Station (ISS) external payloads and assembly orbital replacement units cargo items will be launched within the Orbiter bay. These hardware elements are typically planned for Extra-Vehicular Activity (EVA) sidewall, Orbiter direct (keel and trunions), EXPRESS Pallet, Unpressurized Logistics Carrier (ULC), Spacelab Pallet (SLP) or extended Duration Orbiter (EDO) Pallet type launch configurations. These cargo items require either EVA or cross bay structures. Transferring or deploying cargo via the ISS and Space Shuttle robotics reduces the requirement for astronauts to conduct EVA operations. ISS fine robotics, requiring the Special Purpose Dexterous Manipulator (SPDM), are currently not planned for operation within the Orbiter Bay, due to safety constraints. Large arm robotics; e.g., Shuttle Remote Manipulator System (SRMS) and Space Station Remote Manipulator System (SSRMS), are currently planned for Extra Vehicular Robotics (EVR) operations within the Orbiter bay. A system providing the capability to manifest smaller EVR type payload/ORU items, to the ISS, on the Orbiter sidewall would enhance the resupply and return capability of the Space Shuttle to the ISS.
The Robotics - Sidewall Logistics Carrier (R-SLC) concept is a design solution for putting small payloads on orbit while meeting the requirement to transfer experiment and logistics equipment between the Space Shuttle and the International Space Station by robotics rather than EVA. The concept, design, and fabrication were conducted by students and faculty at the Naval Postgraduate School (NPS) and Boeing.
Through maximizing off-the-shelf technology, the R-SLC concept provides a lightweight, standalone means to carry small payloads aloft in the Shuttle cargo bay. This hardware will be fully Remote Manipulator System (RMS) compatible for on-orbit removal and retrieval operations. EVA operations will only be required where system power failures or robotics malfunctions occur.

Authors: ['K. Isozaki', 'K. Yonemoto', 'O. Kitayama', 'A. Miyahara', 'H. Watanabe', 'S. Okaya', 'M. Ibusuki']
Title: Status Report on Space Tour Vehicle “Kankoh-maru” of Japanese Rocket Society
Publication: IAC 1998 congress proceedings, 49th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  28 September–2 October 1998, Melbourne, Australia
Abstract:
Since 1993 the Transportation Research Committee of the Japanese Rocket Society (JRS) has been conducting a conceptual design study of a vertical takeoff and landing, fully reusable Single-Stage-to-Orbit (SSTO) rocket space tour vehicle for low Earth orbit operation. The vehicle is now called “Kankoh- maru” after the first modern western style steam-ship introduced to Japan in the Edo- era about 140 years ago.
The JRS Study Program is now in its third phase, studying design requirements and standards for technical certification of space tour vehicles. The committee has first reviewed the existing Japanese aviation regulations applied to passenger aircraft and helicopters approved by the civil aviation bureau of the Japanese Ministry of Transportation. The surveyed issues are flight characteristics, strength, structure, propulsion, equipment and operation.
There are many issues to be reconsidered and added for an orbital vehicle operated with rocket propulsion. The takeoff and landing procedure is one of the critical items that is very different from that of aircraft and helicopters in the matter of abort capability. The vehicle design must also take the specific environmental conditions into account, such as orbital temperature, vacuum, meteoroid, space radiation, cryogenic temperature of propellants and aerodynamic heating during reenty, in order to protect passengers and ground safety.
The safety standards for the new concept of “ sp ace worthiness” will play an important role for manufacturers supplying commercial space tour vehicles. This activity of the JRS is unique and is expected to promote space commercialization.

Title: TECHNICAL APPROACH FOR ON-BOARD LIGHT-WEIGHT REMOTE SENSOR DESIGN
Publication: IAC 1998 congress proceedings, 49th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  28 September–2 October 1998, Melbourne, Australia
Abstract: The significance of on-board lightweight remote sensor designing is briefly described, with emphasis on the main technical approach for light-weighting design of high-resolution remote sensor . Along with the emerging of small-earth observation satellite, there is a demand for high- resolution visible remote sensor with long focal-length optical system, if we follow the conventional design, the size and weight will increase sharply, so it is necessary to seek the light-weight design approach. The main means of light-weight are using TDICCD with catadioptric or reflect optical system with small relative-aperture and grand field of view, reducing the weight of mirror by using light-weight structure, and using carbon-fabric composite material, and using micro-electronic technique and high rate image compression technical.

Title: THE X-33 PROGRAM , PROVING SING LE STAGE TO ORBIT
Publication: IAC 1998 congress proceedings, 49th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  28 September–2 October 1998, Melbourne, Australia
Abstract:
The X-33, NASA’s flagship for reusable space plane technology demonstration, is on course to permit a crucial decision for the nation by the end of this decade. Lockheed Martin Skunk Works, NASA’s partner in this effort, has led a dedicated and talented industry and government team that have met and solved numerous challenges within the first 26 months. This program began by accepting the mandate that included two unprecedented and highly challenging goals: 1) demonstrate single stage to orbit technologies in flight and ground demonstration in less than 42 months and 2) demonstrate a new government and industry management relationship working together with industry in the lead.
During 1997, critical design reviews were conducted and these elements went into fabrication and test. The flight liquid oxygen tank was the first major element to complete final assembly. This tank was delivered to the Skunk Works assembly area in early February 1998. The liquid hydrogen tanks are currently in final assembly and testing and will be delivered to vehicle assembly in the next few months.
Another new technology element of the X-33, the aerospike engine is an engine concept that has never been flown, but has been extensively ground tested. While the aerospike engine will be flown for the first time on the X-33, it is a marriage of both heritage and advanced technology components. The aerodynamic shape of the X-33 and the follow on single stage to orbit is referred to as a lifting body. The lifting body shape has been studied and even flight tested over the past several decades, however this particular incarnation of the shape will be the first ever subjected to hypersonic flight conditions.
X-33 space plane flight tests are to be conducted in an unprecedented manner: takeoff from the Edwards Air Force Base in California to two landing sites in Utah and Montana. Since this is the first overflight of populated areas of the US by a rocket powered space plane, NASA decided to prepare an Environmental Impact Statement (EIS). In October 1997, the final EIS was released within one year and is precedent setting for an EIS, particularly for a program of this complexity. With this milestone achieved, construction of the prototype spaceport proceeded and is nearing completion. It will be completed by October 1998.
Major X-33 flight hardware has been tested, delivered, and assembly of the vehicle is well underway in anticipation of its flight test program commencing in the summer of 1999. The decision to proceed with a Single Stage To Orbit as a commercial venture is expected in the fall of 1999.

Title: The Iridium Satellite Constellation: A Positive Force for Public Awareness of Space Activities
Publication: IAC 1998 congress proceedings, 49th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  28 September–2 October 1998, Melbourne, Australia
Abstract: A new generation of communications satellites orbiting the earth is presenting amateur astronomers and the general public with an exciting new experience — the ability to view objects that at times will be brighter than the brightest star or planet in the sky! Named the Iridium satellite constellation, this collection of artificial satellites circles the earth fourteen times daily. Each one is physically about the size of an automobile. Originally planned as a way for persons with portable telephones to communicate anywhere in the world using space-based technology, an unexpected feature of the design has caused the visual appearance of these spacecraft to reflect the light of the sun like a giant mirror. While one might argue that the relative sameness of the night sky is rarely punctuated by anything dramatic, the Iridium satellites are about to change that view.

Title: The Road from the NASA Access-to-Space Study to a Reusable Launch Vehicle
Publication: IAC 1998 congress proceedings, 49th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  28 September–2 October 1998, Melbourne, Australia
Abstract:
NASA has established a goal of providing low-cost
reliable access to space. While this goal has been around
for many years, it received a major impetus when the
U.S Congress mandated the Access-to-Space study in
1993. This study concluded that a rocket powered single-
stage-to-orbit vehicle offered the best opportunity for
low-cost reliable space transportation by the first decade
of the new millennium. This required a focused technology
development program before such a vehicle could
be built. NASA recognized that no commercial entity
would commit to the development of a single-stage-toorbit
vehicle without the U.S. Government’s participation.
To this end, NASA entered into a cooperative
agreement with industry to mature the required technologies.
This effort includes the development of an experimental
subscale-vehicle known as the X-33, an extensive
ground-based program to provide the required additional
technology development, and conceptual through preliminary
design of an operational reusable launch vehicle.
Following this effort, a decision will be made whether or
not to proceed with the detailed design and fabrication
of an operational vehicle.

Title: Design, Analyses, and Fabrication Procedure of AiVlTEC Cell, Test Assembly, and Radioisotope Power System for Outer-Planet Missions
Publication: IAC 1997 congress proceedings, 48th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  6–10 October 1997, Turin, Italy
Abstract:
This paper describes the results of OSC's DOE- sponsored AMTEC (Alkali Metal Thermal to Electric Conversion) generator studies. The paper was prepared in response to an invitation from the International Astronautic Federation for the presentation of a one-hour keynote lecture on our AMTEC studies at the Space Nuclear Power and Propulsion Systems session of the 48th International Astronautical Congress. The paper covers a broad range of topics, which explains its unusual length.
After presenting the background of those studies and the operational principles of the AMTEC converters, it describes a novel methodology for the coupled solution of the interdependent thermal, electrical, and fluid flow differential and integral equations governing their performance, and the application of that procedure to OSC's recommended cell design.
As explained in the paper, that design was the result of parametric analyses of 35 cell design variations to determine the individual effects of 27 design parameters and various operating parameters on the cell's power output, efficiency, and critical temperatures. The analysis revealed a method of substantially improving the cell’s performance by enhancing the internal reflectivity of the cell wall, and identified a specific cell wall composition and coating to achieve that goal. The paper presents a set of OSC-recommended cell design parameters for the ultimate long-service flight generators, as well as a set of parameters for an interim cell design for planned short-term ground tests. The primary difference between them is that the ultimate design employs refractory metal components to enhance compatibility with high-temperature sodium vapor, while the
interim design is based on stainless steel, nickel, and Haynes-25, which are expected to be adequate for initial short-term tests, but not for long-duration missions at high operating temperatures. The paper also presents a detailed fabrication sequence for the recommended interim cell design, which is being implemented by AMPS, Inc., for a DOE-sponsored technology development program.
It then describes the extension of that analytical procedure to a variety of OSC-designed radioisotope- heated generators employing the recommended cell design, with particular attention to the thermal insulation between the outside of the 16 cells and the inside of the generator housing. The studies found that the performance of the generator is optimized by employing a hybrid insulation system, in which the space between the cells is filled with fibrous Min-K insulation, and the generator walls are lined with tapered (i.e., graded-length) multifoil insulation.
The paper then examines the performance of the OSC generator designs for various fuel loadings, output voltages, and mission phases, and assesses their ability to meet the stipulated temperature constraints and power demands of the Europa Orbiter and Pluto Express missions under consideration by NASA.
Finally, it presents an OSC-recommended design and fabrication procedure of an electrically heated 4- cell test assembly with hybrid insulation, to simulate the prototypic 16-cell generator. That test assembly will be analyzed by OSC, built by AMPS, and tested by the Air Force Phillips Laboratory (AFPL), to check the validity of the analytical predictions. The reason for basing the recommended test assembly on the interim rather than the ultimate refractory metal cell design is to avoid the delays required to develop the new technology for the latter.

Title: Development of a 15m class modular mesh deployable antenna
Publication: IAC 1997 congress proceedings, 48th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  6–10 October 1997, Turin, Italy
Abstract: We propose a modular concept and a cable-mesh deployable antenna structure as means to constructa 15m class antenna reflector. The level of our technology has advanced to a new stage. This involves optimizing the design given the system requirements, and then fabricating engineering models and verifying their performance. An integrated design environment has been constructed to facilitate the design of extremely large but very light antenna structure. Several design criteria can be optimized simultaneously by using newly developed design and analysis tools. A newly developed analysis tool, SPADE, can analyzenon-linearstructural responses, flexible body dynamics, and thermal deformation. In addition, SPADE can aid in the design of truss members, cables, and mesh elements. Design inputs are the size of each module, properties of structural members, and truss topology. They are optimized against the total weight, eigen frequencies, thermal deformation and stowed size. Under present design considerations, we conclude that a total weight of less than 132 kg and eigen frequencies of more than 0.8 Hz can be achieved for an 18m x 16m antenna reflector. The reflector consists of 14 modules, each 4.8m in diameter. Three of the 14 modules were fabricated as engineering models which were able to verify the design method and analytically obtain the reflector’s structural/mechanical characteristics.

Title: FAST AUTONOMOUS OPTOELECTRONIC ANALYSER OF SPATIAL FREQUENCIES SPECTRUM OF REMOTELY SENSED IMAGES WITH INCOHERENT LIGHT SOURCE
Publication: IAC 1997 congress proceedings, 48th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  6–10 October 1997, Turin, Italy
Abstract:
Spatial frequencies spectrum contains essential information on the image texture, which can be used for real time remotely sensed image selection. Optoelectronic spatial spectrum analyser utilises the lens feature to perform instantly 2D Fourier transform of an image, which gives a possibility for fast operation.
In the paper the questions of incoherent light source usage in the optoelectronic Fourier spectrum analyser are considered. Usage of incoherent light source makes it possible to provide an optimal spatial filtering of the spectrum, reduce a sensitivity to phase distortions and obtain a compact and rugged design of the device, suitable for onboard installation.
Special algorithm of spectrum image digitising is developed to enlarge a range of spatial frequencies to be processed and maximise the photosensitivity.
The algorithms have been developed to detect the anomalies of wave pattern on the ocean surface and artificial structures presence on the remotely sensed images on base of analysis of spatial frequencies spectrum, obtained in incoherent optical system.
The results of experimental testing of proposed algorithms are also given.

Authors: ['M. Shimizu', 'K. Itoh', 'H. Sato', 'T. Fujii', 'T. Igarashi', 'K. Okamoto']
Title: Fabrication and Tests of Single Crystal Mo Solar Thermal Thruster
Publication: IAC 1997 congress proceedings, 48th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  6–10 October 1997, Turin, Italy
Abstract:
One potentially attractive propulsion concept offering significant payload gains for orbit transfer from LEO to higher Orbits, station keeping and attitude control of spacecraft is thermal propulsion using light gas (typically hydrogen) as propellant and various kinds of heat energy. Solar Thermal Propulsion (STP) is a typical thermal propulsion with high Isp (500 - 1,000 s), appropriate thrust magnitude range (1 - 10 N) and possibly much less space pollution than chemical propulsion systems.
One of the most important investigation items of STP is a thruster (solar-receiver/propellant-injector) made of refractory metal such as rhenium, tungsten and molybdenum or advanced high temperature ceramics because of the high operating temperature (1,000 - 2,500 K) involved.
In the previous paper, preliminary design, fabrication and experimental results are presented, using 20 mm diameter thrusters made of single crystal molybdenum which NRIM had patented. This is a perfect (non-defect) material, namely no brittleness due to recrystallization during high operating temperature condition. The carbon sheet gasket was applied at the first phase, which is unsuitable to high temperature hydrogen, and nitrogen working gas max. temperature within the thruster chamber reached higher than 1,850 K (namely, the Isp is over 700 s for hydrogen gas) at 0.2 MPa of the chamber pressure, using the small solar concentrator of 1.6 m in diameter of half paraboloid (by cutting-in-half, the paraboloidal shape precision was rather deteriorated) and 0,65 m of the focal length.
This paper presents, using the 1.6 m dia. full and precise paraboloidal concentrator newly installed, higher propellant temperature test results of single crystal Mo thruster with super high temperature brazing alloy of Mo/Ru which can seal hydrogen gas, instead of the carbon sheet gasket. Tire target temperature is over 2,250 K, whichi is over 800 s of Isp for hydrogen propellant gas. In addition, in order to prevent the thruster cavity wall and Mo/Ru from vaporizing under the condition of high temperature over 2,500K and high vacuum, tungsten CYD- coating was performed on the cavity wall.

Title: Optimal Shape Design of Air Intakes for Air Collection Engines (ACE)
Publication: IAC 1997 congress proceedings, 48th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  6–10 October 1997, Turin, Italy
Abstract: The success of Air Collection Engines (ACE) depends on the efficient integration of the many sub-systems involved. This paper describes the tools developed to design a supersonic air intake of the mixed extemal/intemal compression type that will feed the engine or the air liquefaction plant or both, during the different phases of the mission. One design procedure aims at finding the shape of minimum total pressure losses. An alternative strategy aims at designing intakes which attain prescribed Mach number and flow deviation at the throat. Two design points are selected and their off-design behaviour is predicted by space- and time-marching CED models. The CFD analyses eventually provide the performance charts of the air intakes.

Title: Space Art and Education
Publication: IAC 1997 congress proceedings, 48th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  6–10 October 1997, Turin, Italy
Abstract:
Space Art has been a growing activity in Europe and in the USA since the end of the 70'ies. With space exploration, space programmes and activities have constantly become a source of inspiration and ideas, particularly suitable for art.
Through ARSAT, a non-profit- making organisation created in 1983 and composed of international members, the development of space art is a new element in the way space applications and space technology are presented to the public. Starting with Earth observation satellites, the artists exploit the remote sensing images as a support to their artistic message. This paper will present two projects: Signature Terre, which consisted of a 380,000 sq.m design on the ground, photographed by Spot 1 on 6 October 1989 and the future Constellation Europe project using the European Space Agency’s ERS satellite for a European signature of the 14 ESA Members States.
In the field of Manned Spaceflight, the artists propose unusual concepts of orbital structures and experiments which, for some of them, received the scientific and technical validation from space experts. The unusual approach, from the art point of view, combines common sense and aesthetics, which, in general, are immediately perceived and understood by the general public.
The paper discusses ways and means to incorporate space art and its artists in the loop of Space and Education structures.

Title: Strategies for the Exploration of Mars
Publication: IAC 1997 congress proceedings, 48th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  6–10 October 1997, Turin, Italy
Abstract:
At the ten-week 1997 summer session of the International Space University held at Rice University in Houston, USA, students executed design projects with the object of practicing international teamwork and developing ideas that can be useful in planning and contributing to future space programs. They were asked to adopt a viewpoint unconstrained by existing national policies or international agreements, and to make their own best estimates of likely future trends, available technologies, and mission goals.
One of the 1997 projects dealt with strategies for the future exploration of Mars. Beginning with an extensive survey and review of existing world plans, the students went on to consider robotic missions with respect to main scientific objectives, technology demonstrations, and precursor exploration activities related to future human missions to Mars.
In parallel with those investigations, the team considered the potential opportunities and obstacles inherent to the preparatory phases of manned Mars missions, evaluating political, social, technical and managerial factors, as well as opportunities for pooling those international efforts that will influence effective and timely mission implementation. This paper presents a summary of the results of the ISU 97 Mars design project.

Title: System Description and Flight Operations of the Beppo-SAX Satellite
Publication: IAC 1997 congress proceedings, 48th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  6–10 October 1997, Turin, Italy
Abstract:
The operational characteristics of Beppo-SAX (Satellite for Astronomy in X-ray) have been explicitly defined to continuously and reliably execute the planned observations of scientific mission lasting for at least two years of. Consequently, the satellite design has been conceived to support the flight operations by means of a decentralised intelligent architecture making extensive use of on-board software functions. This resulting structure is, in particular, capable to autonomously perform the on-board resource management, the anomalies detection and recovery, the execution of scientific and attitude plans and, above all, the coordination of the scheduled actions with the current satellite status.
After outlining the main system features, the paper presents the first flight results, acquired during satellite commissioning, when the Satellite System Team directly participated in the mission control at the Operations Control Centre (OCC). The system functionalities and performances were successfully tested during the commissioning phase, where a few problems, due to unexpected anomaly occurrences, had to be solved by the team in charge, also by means of the Beppo-SAX Software Maintenance Facility (SMF). At the end of the commissioning, the activities continued during the full scientific mission as on-call support from Alenia Aerospazio premises, providing operations consultancy, trouble shooting, trend analysis, and software upgrading. The problems encountered, the solutions adopted, and the experience gained in the Beppo-SAX flight check-out and mission support are also described in the article.

Title: VIBRATION AND JITTER CONTROL IN SPACECRAFTS
Publication: IAC 1997 congress proceedings, 48th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  6–10 October 1997, Turin, Italy
Abstract: Smart structures are structures with built-in sensors/actuators that can actively change their geometry and/or physical properties to adapt to the working environment. This paper presents a smart structure design with built-in piezoelectric sensor/actuator and controller for (1) dither excitation (2) vibration suppression and (3) shape control on space system applications. A smart structure specimen, an aluminum beam with surface bonded piezoelectric sensor/actuator, is fabricated, analyzed, and tested. Three control circuits driven by 9VDC battery have also been developed. It is shown experimentally that the smart structure of integrated sensor, actuator, and controller is effective both in vibration control and jitter control.

Authors: ['Y. Kogo', 'H. Hatta', 'N. Tanagusha', 'T. Sato', 'T. Mizutani', 'H. Ohnabe']
Title: Advanced Carbon-Carbon Composites for Tip Turbine Structure of ATREX Engine
Publication: IAC 1996 congress proceedings, 47th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  7–11 October 1996, Beijing, China
Abstract: A feasibility study was carried out to apply a carbon/carbon (C/C) composite to a turbine disk of Air-Turbo-Ram-Jet engine. The C/C composite has not been successfully applied to such a primary structure subjected to dynamic load. The optimum design of the turbine disk made of C/C composites were explored in two kinds of structure, i.e., monolithic and joined. The monolithic structure was assumed to be composed of three-dimensionally reinforced (3D) fabrics and the joined structure divided into three components. Through the discussion, the joined structure was shown to be superior to the monolithic structure. It is due to the reason that in the joined structure the optimum arrangement of reinforcing fiber can be easily made obeying the stress distribution in the turbine disk.

Title: Distributed Task Constellation Design Optimization: An Operations Research Approach To Earth Observing System Configuration Design
Publication: IAC 1996 congress proceedings, 47th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  7–11 October 1996, Beijing, China
Abstract:
The NASA Earth Observing System (EOS) is an ambitious 15-year program to monitor key global indices of the planet's biosphere. Conceived well before the end of the Cold War, the EOS program has experienced an excruciating series of draconian budget cuts and redesigns. Clearly, there is a strong need for an algorithmic design tool that would enable EOS system architects to design to cost while achieving maximum performance with managed risk.
This paper presents the results of a multi-year effort to prototype an entirely new approach for performing the configuration design of constellations such as the Earth Observing System. Furthermore, the configuration solution identified is not merely a feasible design, but is the globally optimal EOS constellation for ensuring the reliable collection of the most important measurements on a performance per cost basis. By taking a systems-oriented approach and formulating the EOS configuration design process as an operations research problem, the configuration subproblems of instrument selection, payload definition, and spacecraft scaling/launch vehicle selection were addressed.
The EOS mission goal is comprised of many key measurement tasks that are distributed amongst a constellation of dissimilar remote sensing spacecraft. The configuration decision process of such a
distributed task constellation (DTC) defies the "traditional" numerical modeling methods, due to their failure to efficiently handle high permutation situations such as for the EOS configuration design. This design challenge of choosing from a wide breadth of feasible, but non-optimal, configurations must first be addressed to identify die most cost effective and robust EOS configurations.
After the enthusiastic response at IAF '95 for the previous papers1 on the DTC process, it is a great pleasure to now present the results of this work. The EOS mixed integer programming formulation involved over 1,000 variables in over 1,000 constraint equations solved for global optima, thus prototyping a unique process for optimizing DTC design, and providing an EOS constellation configuration design sensitivity analysis.

Title: Electrohydraulic non-reaction vibration generator for test of objects in satellite on an orbit
Publication: IAC 1996 congress proceedings, 47th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  7–11 October 1996, Beijing, China
Abstract:
Development of space engineering in regard to building the spacecraft of different purpose and delivery means of different equipment from orbit to earth surface had caused a formation of new scientific and technological trends of works: space materials science and biotechnology, space biology and medicine. An objective of these trends is a use of space factors, in first turn, of weightlessness as technological factor in making the different unique matters, materials and bioproducts.
Up to the present a great experimental and scientific data in regard to space materials science and biotechnology is accumulated, relying on which a proceed to a stage of experimental and industrial production of number of matters with unique characteristics in space is possible.
The Yuzhnoye State Design Office investigations in this trend have showed in principle a feasibility of building the space technological means using both long - term orbital flights and dash ballistic - curve flights. There is not a critical necessity in explanation of economic and technical feasibility to realize as more as possible a wide range of space technologies in ballistic - curve flights.

Title: GLOBAL DESIGN OF SATELLITE CONSTELLATIONS : A MULTI-CRITERIA PERFORMANCE COMPARISON OF CLASSICAL WALKER PATTERNS AND NEW DESIGN PATTERNS
Publication: IAC 1996 congress proceedings, 47th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  7–11 October 1996, Beijing, China
Abstract:
Basically, the problem of designing a
multisatellite constellation exhibits a lot of
parameters with many possible
combinations : total number of satellites,
orbital parameters of each individual satellite,
number of orbital planes, number of satellites
in each plane, spacings between satellites of
each plane, spacings between orbital planes,
relative phasings between consecutive orbital
planes.
Hopefully, some authors have theoretically
solved this complex problem under
simplified assumptions : the permanent (or
continuous) coverage by a single and
multiple satellites of the whole earth and
zonal areas has been entirely solved from a
pure geometrical point of view. These
solutions exhibit strong symmetry properties
(e.g. : Walker, Ballard, Rider, Draim
constellations) : altitude and inclination are
identical, orbital planes and satellites are
regularly spaced, etc...
The problem with such constellations is their
oversimplified and restricted geometrical
assumption. In fact, the evaluation function
which is used implicitely only takes into
account the point-to-point visibility between
users and satellites and does not deal with
very important constraints and considerations
that become mandatory when designing a
real satellite system (e.g. : robustness to
satellite failures, total system cost, common
view between satellites and ground stations,
service availability and satellite reliability,
Launch and Early Operations Phase,
production constraints, etc...).
An original and global methodology relying
on a powerful optimisation tool based on
Genetic Algorithms has been developed at
ALCATEL ESPACE. In this approach,
symmetrical constellations can be used as
initial conditions of the optimization process
together with specific evaluation functions. A
multi-criteria performance analysis is
conducted and presented here in a parametric
way in order to identify and evaluate the
main sensitive parameters. Quantitative
results are given for three examples in the
fields of navigation, telecommunication and
multimedia satellite systems. In particular, a
new design pattern with very efficient
properties in terms of robustness to satellite
failures is presented and compared to
classical Walker patterns.

Title: NEW ENTRY IN THE COMMERCIAL LAUNCH VEHICLE MARKET
Publication: IAC 1996 congress proceedings, 47th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  7–11 October 1996, Beijing, China
Abstract:
Rockwell International is now actively involved in the marketing and sale of the Cyclone launch vehicle. This paper summarizes the capabilities of this vehicle, describes launch operations and defines the Cyclone role within the spectrum of potential commercial launch opportunities.
A brief history of the Cyclone launch vehicle is presented, portraying its evolution and launch record. The Cyclone performance and operational characteristics are summarized, with special attention given to the integration approach, operational cycle, and time requirements for payload integration through completion of launch. Of particular interest is the relatively short time span needed to integrate and launch Cyclone payloads, with on-pad launch time typically less than 24 hours and sequential launches possible in less than 1 1/2 days.
An overview of the commercial satellite market is provided tracing historical trends andfuture market projections. These diverse and expanding commercial satellite systems are financially dependent upon successful orbital insertion of large numbers of satellites in a relatively short timeframe. This paper illustrates how the Cyclone launch vehicle is a viable solution to the commercial success of
these systems.______________________________

The Cyclone launch vehicle is one of the world’s most reliable space launchers with an impressive 97.9% success rate. This vehicle has been in operation for the past 30 years with over 200 launches to date. More than 20 Cyclone missions have involved multi- manifested payloads, all of them successfully launched. Both the two-stage Cyclone-2 and the three-stage Cyclone-3 are available for commercial launches to LEO at very cost effective prices. The expected lead time from contract to launch is only 18-24 months.
Two operational launch sites are currently available for commercial Cyclone launches:
• Plesetsk Spaceport in northern Russia
- primarily Cyclone-3 launches
• Baikonur Cosmodrome in Kazakhstan
- primarily Cyclone-2 launches
With the Cyclone, a high performance LEO satellite launch vehicle for a variety of missions with a multi-manifested satellite approach is now available to the commercial satellite market. Yuzhnoye has considerable experience in the design and development of multiple satellite launch dispensers and other vehicle modifications. Its design team is now completing the launch dispenser system for the Globalstar system where 12 satellites will be deployed from each Zenit-2 launch vehicle. Like the Cyclone, the Zenit is also designed and produced in Ukraine by Yuzhnoye and Yuzhmash.
The team of Rockwell International’s Satellite Delivery Systems, the Yuzhnoye Design Office and the Yuzhmash Production Association are committed to the future expansion of the Cyclone launch vehicle into the worldwide commercial satellite market. Our joint experience base in launch vehicle design, production, payload integration and launch operations is the key element in this future marketing partnership.

Title: OPTIMAL SEMI-ANALYTICAL GUIDANCE FOR REENTRY FLIGHT
Publication: IAC 1996 congress proceedings, 47th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  7–11 October 1996, Beijing, China
Abstract: The guidance problem for reentry flight of space vehicles is considered. The guidance concept is similar to that of the U.S. Space Shuttle entry guidance in that a reference drag acceleration profile is tracked. But in this paper the reference drag profile is parameterized and optimized as piecewise linear functions of the energy. Analytical expressions for accurate range prediction and the performance index, the accumulated heat load, are obtained, which enables fast design of constrained optimal trajectories for both off-line studies and possible on-board application. A property of the optimal drag profile is studied to ensure that the obtained trajectory is fly- able. A nonlinear control law is derived for trajectory tracking, which guarantees globally asymptotically stable tracking of the reference drag profile. Numerical results for a conceptual single-stage, reusable launch vehicle are provided to demonstrate the optimal design of drag profiles and the performance of the trajectory control law.

Authors: ['D. Sabath', 'M. Krischke', 'W. Kast', 'M. Kowalczyk', 'M. Kruijff', 'E. Van Der Heide']
Title: Results of the rarabolic flight tests on the RAPUNZEL deployer
Publication: IAC 1996 congress proceedings, 47th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  7–11 October 1996, Beijing, China
Abstract:
The tether assisted re-entry of small payloads is a highly interesting tool for space transportation especially for the return of small payloads from space station ISSA. The small tether mission RAPUNZEL was initiated in 1991 by the Institute of Astronautics, TU München and the Kayser-Threde Company to design a low cost and feasible tether experiment for the verification of the tether assisted re-entry. Together with the Samara State Aerospace University, Russia a mission concept on a Russian Resurs or Photon capsule was developed. Based on this mission a déployer has been designed, mainly based on technology of the textile industry, which insures high reliability at low cost. Recently a similar configuration is being discussed for the ESA-TSE mission.
The mam work during the recent time was the development and test of the breadboard model of the déployer system. After successfully completing initially ground tests with the déployer, further tests during the ESA Parabolic Flight campaign in November 1995 were conducted. After a short introduction of the overall mission scenario, the planned configuration in orbit, this paper will present the results of the microgravity test campaign onboard the KC-135 aircraft and compare them to ground test. The déployer showed a good performance during all tests including ejection of the endmass, deployment, and braking. Problems that occurred during the tests will be discussed and solutions for the detected flaws and the results of the redesign now in progress will be presented. These verifications have shown the feasibility of the concept and will lay the base for the planned development of the flight model of the déployer.

Title: SMALL AND MEDIUM LAUNCH VEHICLES TO EXTEND THE ARIANE 5 TRANSPORTATION SERVICE
Publication: IAC 1996 congress proceedings, 47th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  7–11 October 1996, Beijing, China
Abstract:
The heavy launch vehicle ARIANE 5 has been optimized for dual GTO launch and for heavy man-rated payloads in LEO. The present trend of commercial satellites being always to mass increase, the ARIANE 5 Evolutions in the near futur will increase its GTO performance and also in LEO up to 18 or 20 tons.
Therefore, ARIANE 5 is not well suited for small payloads in LEO or MEO, due to the launch cost associated with high payload mass capability. For payloads between 500 kg and 4 tons in LEO or MEO other launch vehicles could be better transportation systems, if multiple payload launches are not possible (in this case ARIANE 5 remains a good candidate).
Since some years AEROSPATIALE is studying, under CNES contract or under its own funding, various "ARIANE Complementary Launch Vehicles", A.C.L.V. (L.C.A., lanceurs complémentaires ARIANE, in french) having the capability to meet the need of the commercial LEO and MEO market as well as some particular governmental and scientific missions.
With other european and french industrials, AEROSPATIALE try to propose some new type of industry/government partnership to design develop and to operate these new launch vehicles.
This paper will provide some details on the concept, based on maximum use of existing hardware, facilities and know how, to reduce the corresponding development cost and to propose a competitive transportation system in addition to ARIANE 5 to the future LEO and MEO market.

Title: SOURCES OF “LITTLE” SPACE
Publication: IAC 1996 congress proceedings, 47th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  7–11 October 1996, Beijing, China
Abstract:
In late 1958, in Yuzhnoye Design Office, a group of enthusiasts headed by professor V.M. Kovtunehko, concurrently with the work on military hardware, began the development of a two-stage launcher on the basis of military rocket R-12 (SS-4) that had the range of 2000 km.
That laid the basis of the development of space trend and actually, without knowing about it, the basis of conversion in the Design Office. The future showed that the idea of developing the launch vehicle for spacecraft on the basis of military rocket, that was passing successfully flight tests at that time, would turn out to be extremely fruitful. For the use of R-12 as the first stage small modifications were required, but the second stage on which the engine was installed burning liquid oxygen and unsymmetric dimethylhydrasine had to be developed and built anew. The use of modules of the same diameter that were on the first stage allowed to considerably reduce the period and cost of manufacturing the second stage due to the use of existing process equipment and completing elements and to perform onground operations and launch on the existing equipment of launching complexes.

Title: SPACEBORNE RADAR INTERFEROMETRY AND THE MITIGATION OF NATURAL DISASTERS
Publication: IAC 1996 congress proceedings, 47th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  7–11 October 1996, Beijing, China
Abstract:
Spaceborne radar data can be used in many ways for natural hazard reduction. The most conventional use of radar data is the recognition of flooded areas by the dark signature of still water i a radar image associated with the all- weather capability of the instrument. We could switch to risk-mapping in this field by using the high precision digital terrain models produced by radar interferometry on relatively flat areas. The proved accuracy (=lm) of the models is unmatched by other space borne techniques.
The dense spatial sampling (100 pixels/km^) provided by radar interferometry in the detection of displacements associated with its accuracy (=3-10 mm) makes it an important tool for assessing most natural hazards. This tool, which requires the analysis of two radar images acquired at different times, could be used as a cheap warning signal in the case of volcanoes as we demonstrated in the case of Mount ETNA (Sicily), where changes in the
volcano shape were observed, which took place between the two image acquisitions. Existing radar systems can already provide the data required for a global monitoring of all potentially hazardous volcanoes. Radar interferometry can also contribute to the understanding of earthquakes, especially in poorly equipped areas, since it does not require ground instrumentation. It is equally well suited to monitor man-made activities which may result in natural disasters, such as mining and water pumping. Several examples will be shown in order to substantiate the use of this technique.
The technique is currently limited by the contribution of the propagation in the atmosphere and the change of the soil in long periods of time which may spoil the interference patterns. However, current spaceborne radars proved capable of delivering the information most of the time, although they were not designed for this purpose. Our experience could help design better systems in the future. Current system limitations should not prevent us to use radar interferometry in an operational way now.

Title: SPACECRAFT MANUFACTURING IMPLICATIONS FOR VOLUME PRODUCTION SATELLITES
Publication: IAC 1996 congress proceedings, 47th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  7–11 October 1996, Beijing, China
Abstract:
To date, practically all spacecraft development programmes have followed a trend of ever increasing size, complexity, mass and cost. Today's missions may typically result in a spacecraft which has a mass at launch of the order of 10000 kg and a cost of around $150 million. Over the past ten years the emergence of the 'small satellite', with a mass of less than 1000 kg, has in part, reversed this trend, albeit whilst in many cases, employing the same design and manufacturing approach used for their conventional counterparts.
Both conventional and small satellites have design and manufacture implications resulting from the conflicting low production quantities and high reliability requirements. Even series satellites tend to undergo significant redesign work for particular mission requirements resulting in the retention of high costs. Attempts to lower costs to date have centred on the use of modularity and 'off-the-shelf designs, which have had some success, particularly in the arena of small satellites.
Proposals for new spacecraft applications, such as global mobile communications, require the use of satellite constellations. The size of a constellation is dependant upon its application, however present concepts range from 20 to 850 satellites [1], Many of these proposals suggest the use of existing spacecraft development methods. However, other methods, not currently associated with spacecraft design, may lead to significant cost reductions, whilst maintaining a sufficiently high level of reliability and redundancy. Two programmes which have already tried to adopt some of these methods are Iridium [2] and Globalstar [2], which will borrow ideas from the automobile industry in the manufacture of the 72 and 56 satellites (including in-orbit spares) required for the respective constellations.
This paper will outline some of these new methods, describing factors which will be of primary importance in the future development of constellation satellites if an entirely new low cost approach is to be developed. These include the impact and importance that computer aided engineering will have across the manufacturing activities, embracing design, production, simulation and test, as well as integration and testing procedures, component classification and even configuration control.

Title: THE NEXT GENERATION OF HIGH POWER SATELLITES
Publication: IAC 1996 congress proceedings, 47th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  7–11 October 1996, Beijing, China
Abstract:
The next generation of broadcast satellites
will be larger and more capable than the
current generation. This continues a trend
that has existed since the first broadcast
satellites were put into service. The next
generation will be able to generate ten to
fifteen kilowatts of power that will energize
a payload capable of providing viable
direct-to-user services in any populated area
of the world visible from any point on the
geosynchronous arc. The ability to provide
a service this comprehensive will allow the
satellite manufacturer to produce a more
standardized spacecraft design that will
vary primarily in its coverage capability
from customer to customer.
This paper will discuss the generic
conceptual design of such a satellite. A
general description of the various
subsystems will be presented. Those areas
of the necessary technologies which need to
be further developed in order to efficiently
build such a satellite design will be defined and discussed. The potential problem areas
associated with the design will be summarized.

Title: Testing a Light Weight Ablator for Planetary Entry
Publication: IAC 1996 congress proceedings, 47th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  7–11 October 1996, Beijing, China
Abstract:
Stringent requirements made it necessary to develop new materials for the application in future reentry and planetary entry missions. Besides further progress in ceramic matrix composite technology this need implies the evolutionary improvement of ablative thermal protection systems.
Dasa Domier developed a light weight ablator material (Do 31-family) which is among the candidate heat shield materials for the European Manned Space Transportation Program (MSTP) and for Mars Entry Probes. The main design driving requirements for the heat shield of the Mars Entry Probe are low mass, high resistance to thermal loads and resistance against dust erosion during penetration of the Martian atmosphere. A subscale test model of such a heat shield, a demonstrator, has been designed, analyzed and fabricated. The Do 31-F ablator consists of porous phenolic resin reinforced with ceramic short fibers. The ablator material is filled in a phenolic honeycomb which is bonded to the substructure. The specially manufactured ablator material has a low density of about 0.6 g/cm3.
In this paper, firstly material properties of the Do 31-F ablator are presented which have been obtained in the MSTP ablator evaluation programme. In the heat shield development programme for Mars entry probes thermal shock
tests and arc jet tests both on specimens and on the subscale test model have been performed which are reported in the following. Additionally, test results of dust erosion simulation are presented carried out by an accelerator with particle velocities up to 7 km/s.

Title: Vibration Suppression of Graphite Composite Smart Structure by Digital Signal Processing Controller
Publication: IAC 1996 congress proceedings, 47th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  7–11 October 1996, Beijing, China
Abstract: The stringent design requirement of spacecraft systems has created the need for smart structures—structures with built-in piezoelectric sensor/actuator that can actively change their physical geometry and/or property. This paper presents the vibration suppression of a smart structure by using digital signal processing (DSP) controller. A graphite fiber composite laminated beam embedded with a pair of piezoelectric sensor and actuator is designed, fabricated and tested for its effectiveness in vibration control. Analysis and experiment show that the embedded piezoelectric sensor and actuator can be applied successfully to vibration measurement and to vibration suppression, respectively. The DSP controller enables one to minimize the structural vibration of high frequency modes in real-time.

Title: ASTRONOMIA PARA LA FAMILIA: A PROGRAM FOR NASA EDUCATION OUTREACH RELYING ON PARENTAL INVOLVEMENT HANDS-ON ACTIVITIES AND APPROPRIATE USE OF THE WORLD WIDE WEB
Publication: IAC 1995 congress proceedings, 46th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  2–6 October 1995, Oslo, Norway
Abstract:
We describe the bilingual Astronomia Para La Familia/Family Astronomy Project, which is a bilingual (Spanish-English) education outreach project of UC Berkeley’s Center for EUV Astrophysics. The project develops and operates weekend astronomy and space science workshops for 7-8 grade students and their parents of Hispanic background. The project is patterned on the successful Family Science and Family Math programs from UC Berkeley’s Lawrence Hall of Science. Family Astronomy has been designed and implemented in collaboration with the East Bay Consortium (a non-profit organization that develops education programs involving students and teachers of the Oakland Unified School District) and with the Association of Mexican Professionals of Silicon Valley. The collaboration also involves Professor Emily van Zee from the University of Maryland’s College of Education and a graduate student from the UC Berkeley School of Education to help guide the design and assess the effectiveness of the program. The workshops will be pilot-tested in fall of 1995 during weekend activities for 7-8 grade students and their families as part of East Bay Consortium programs. This project investigates methods by which collaboration among teachers, other professional educators, scientists, and families can help increase (a) middle-school students’ and their parents’ interest in science as well as (b) parental involvement in the science education of their children. The study focuses on collaborative science activities enhanced by images and data accessible through World Wide Web technology carried out in an informal and supportive setting.
The workshops focus on hands-on activities requiring child and parent participation that demonstrate explicit concepts in astronomy and space science. Such activities include observations of astronomical objects using the naked eye and measuring instruments constructed during the workshops, such as a simple astrolobe. The program includes a visit to the satellite operations center for the NASA Extreme Ultraviolet Explorer Satellite at the University of California, Berkeley, and involves workshop participants in using the Internet to access astronomy and space science data on the World Wide Web. All the project materials, activities, and methods are being documented on the CEA Education World Wide Web pages (URL: http://www.cea.berkeley.edu/Education). The CEA’s Science Information Infrastructure NASA-funded project disseminates the materials to collaborating science museums such as the Exploratorium and Lawrence Hall of Science.

Title: Aerodynamic Controllability of a Selected Re-entry Test Vehicle
Publication: IAC 1995 congress proceedings, 46th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  2–6 October 1995, Oslo, Norway
Abstract:
A small and low-cost re-entry vehicle can be a good means for testing new heat-resistant materials and qualifying newly developed subsystems in a realistic flight environment, to complement ground tests and numerical experiments. Ballistic re-entry vehicles, however, will encounter high heat loads, which modern heat-resisting materials find difficult to withstand. One way to lower the encountered heat flux is to aerody- namically control the vehicle. In this paper, we discuss the aerodynamic design and the controllability of a moderate L/D re-entry vehicle with a triangular cross-section and a blunt nose, with 3 flaps at the base for aerodynamic control.
The aerodynamic design is done using analytical expressions for both the aerodynamic properties and the trajectory. The resulting design is verified by numerical trajectory integration. Furthermore, a sensitivity analysis is performed using 6-d.o.f. guided and controlled simulations to check the controllability of the test vehicle. For this analysis Taguchi’s orthogonal arrays are used. The advantage of using these arrays is that they reduce the required number of simulations to be studied. We showed that it was no problem to fly a nominal trajectory. The vehicle is sensitive, however, to errors in the location of the centre of mass, and exhibits a strong interaction between roll and yaw.

Title: Department of Electrical Engineering
Publication: IAC 1995 congress proceedings, 46th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  2–6 October 1995, Oslo, Norway
Abstract: Design of a Ka-band (20-GHz) GEO satellite shaped offset reflector antenna for producing a contoured beam to cover the Taiwan region is presented. The design of this shaped reflector antenna is for the future GEO satellite communication or DBS applications to serve the Taiwan region. The geometric optics (GO) method and aperture phase optimization procedures are employed for reflector surface shaping. The physical optics (PO) method is used to accurately calculate the far-field radiation pattern. The simulation results show that the designed shaped reflector produces a Taiwan region converge beam and effectively reduce the antenna gain level in the nearby region of mainland China.

Authors: ['Geoffrey A. Landis', 'Phillip Jenkins', 'Joseph Flatico', 'Larry Oberle', 'Mike Krasowski', 'Steven Stevenson']
Title: Development of a Mars Dust Characterization Instrument
Publication: IAC 1995 congress proceedings, 46th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  2–6 October 1995, Oslo, Norway
Abstract:
The atmosphere of Mars has a considerable load of suspended dust. Over time, this dust is deposits out of the atmosphere. The mechanism and the temporal and geographical variation of this deposition are not well characterized. Measurements of settling rates and dust properties are of considerable scientific interest. Atmospheric dust affects the atmospheric solar absorption and thus the heat balance of Mars, as well as serving as nucléation sites for water and C02 frost, while settled dust causes albedo changes across the surface; knowledge of dust properties is also of engineering interest to design of mechanisms, solar arrays, and radiators.
Two instruments have been designed and fabricated to measure the dust accumulation during the course of the Mars Pathfinder rover mission: the solar-cell coverglass transmission experiment to measures the change in optical opacity of a transparent coverglass as dust settles on the surface, and the quartz crystal monitor measurement of accumulated dust loading, which measures the mass of dust deposited by measuring the changes in resonant frequency of an oscillating quartz ciystal as dust settles on the surface.
An additional instrument, a CCD microscope to image individual dust particles is under development for flight on a future mission.

Title: EVALUTION MODEL OF SAFETY LEVEL OF SPACE-ROCKET SYSTEMS
Publication: IAC 1995 congress proceedings, 46th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  2–6 October 1995, Oslo, Norway
Abstract:
The report presents a model for determination of (he safety level of a rockct-spacc system. The model has its origin in the concept considering an accident as an abnormal event taking place due to occurrence of certain kinds of failures designated the emergency ones. The latter are transformed into an accident through an emergency situation which is a fast-developing abnormal process. To provide the required level of safety, the rocket-space systems are equipped with issued safeguard systems consisting of diagnostical and executive portions.
As a major safely index, the probability of freedom from accidents is adopted.
In methodical respect, there have been derived expression for determination of the major safety index, for ascertaining the probability of accident prevention in case of occurrence of emergency failures, and for evaluation of degradation of probability of the main system failure-free operation, caused by the false actuation’s of the safeguard system.

Title: LIQUID DROPLET RADIATOR FOR HIGH POWER SPACE SYSTEM
Publication: IAC 1995 congress proceedings, 46th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  2–6 October 1995, Oslo, Norway
Abstract:
Expansion of space study and development range depends on the solution of spacecraft power supply problem. But application of powerful sources is mainly limited by the absence of efficient design of radiator for releasing the excess heat, allowing to release maximum heat flow at minimum dimensions. Preliminary estimations show that the heat release system mass (for the installation with electric power supply of over 500 kW) is a substantial part (about 50%) of the whole power supply set mass and is the main limiting factor.
Solution of this problem might be found while developing a principally new radiator construction having the movable surface that creates a possibility to reduce the radiator mass substantially (down to 2 - 3 times) at the insignificant complication of technology. 
The concept of liquid-droplet radiator is of the most interest. In this case heat is released into the space by plane layer, consisting of a large number of small droplets of the liquid coolant, moving from generator to collector. Practical realization of this concept depends on the solution of two problems. First of all, generation of a large number of small uniform droplets of 100-300 um in diameter with the velocity of 5-10 m/s in the form of a plane layer with angular divergence of separate small jets of less than 10 mrad at a distance of some tens of meters. The second problem, not less complex, is the droplet flow collection at minimum coolant losses. As the problems of mathematical modeling for the processes of radiation heat and mass transfer within the plane droplet layer under vacuum conditions are discussed already in scientific publications in details, experimental study of
nonodispersed generation and
droplet flow collection isunder great attention.

Title: LOW-EARTH ORBIT SATELLITE CONSTELLATIONS PROVIDING REGIONAL COMMUNICATION SERVICES
Publication: IAC 1995 congress proceedings, 46th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  2–6 October 1995, Oslo, Norway
Abstract:
Following the present trend towards small satellites, the implementation of multiple-satellite based systems (constellations) becomes possible.
