The big amount of these projects is devoted to a global coverage. Worldwide communication is certainly the field where the intrinsic characteristics of satellite-based systems , i.e. the absence of ground equipments, becomes more evident.
Nevertheless, also a restricted, regional market could be interested in such a solution, if a covered area exceeds some tens of degrees in longitude and latitude.
But, first of all, LEO are easier than GEO with respect to the launch possibilities, either in terms of rocket and launch site avalaibility. Still, good visibility conditions from high latitudes are difficult or impossible to meet with GEO platforms. Then, primary and absolute advantage of low altitude systems dwells in the better quality of service, in terms of delay time.
This paper deals with the possible orbital design for such a kind of programs, which differ in some remarkable way from the global coverage ones. Intermediate step in design is represented by zonal coverage, where all longitudes have to be served. Then, the additional constraint in longitude is added to the one in latitude, defining the regional coverage problem. Other possibility is represented by multiple regional services, where one constellation offers the coverage to Europe, North America and Far East.

Title: NEW APPROACH TO LOW COST SPACECRAFT: GLOBALSTAR, M-BUS AND OTHER ALENIA SPAZIO ADVANCED CONCEPTS
Publication: IAC 1995 congress proceedings, 46th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  2–6 October 1995, Oslo, Norway
Abstract:
The satellite market is increasingly demanding and manufacturers must compete with high performance products within limited budgets and tight delivery schedules. A new approach is therefore required from the concept design to the verification phase and the launch base activities. For many years, ALENIA Spazio has been improving the competitiveness of its products by in-house studies and participation in programmes such as GLOBALSTAR and CESAR/M-BUS. In GLOBALSTAR, ALENIA Spazio is responsible for integrating and testing 56 flight model satellites - the space constellation - together with developing and producing 112 on-board telecommunication antennae, to be done in under two years with a production rate of 3 satellites per month, far above the usual.
This paper highlights ALENIA Spazio’s views on new approaches to reduce satellite costs and delivery times; it also describes the activities and expected results concerning the design trends and system level activities for innovative spacecraft. Information will also be provided on a multi-mission, multi-purpose spacecraft that ALENIA Spazio has proposed to meet the requirements of small missions and limited resources, allowing scientists low cost access to space. This M-BUS is decoupled from the payload to the maximum extent, but is designed for small launcher fairings such as the planned Italian improved SCOUT, PEGASUS XL and LOCKHEED LLV. The advantage of the modular design is the ability to meet the requirements of the scientific missions as well as remote sensing oriented to Earth observation. The paper will introduce some improvements currently under study to support the CESAR programme, under company and Italian Space Agency funding. Other spacecraft configurations will be proposed to cope with
different mission constraints and applicable to different launchers. The paper also analyses new approaches for cost, mass and production scale reduction.

Title: STUDENT COMPETITION ON SATELLITE DESIGN: ACHIEVEMENTS AND LESSONS LEARNED
Publication: IAC 1995 congress proceedings, 46th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  2–6 October 1995, Oslo, Norway
Abstract:
Both enthusiasm and incompetence to space access among students are recognized in Japanese universities. It is widely accepted that space access needs a large amount of fund and extreme hi-tech, which are made available only by space agencies and large companies. Unfortunately it is true in many cases, but it is not so if the mission is limited to certain kind, educational purposes, for instance. Short-life single mission spacecraft can be build, launched and operated by relatively small group of students and instructors with modest fund which may be within reach of educational organizations. "Satellite Design Contest" was planed and conducted to foster this concept by academic societies, independent of government involvement. Its purposes are to evoke free way of thinking in realizing what one wants to do in space, and to make introduction into educational field a realistic goal and motive. It is further aiming at creating environment toward actual launches of student build satellites, as have been done in Europe, US and other part of Asia.
There is a general trend in Japan that young people walk out of science and engineering field into more service oriented jobs. This was accelerated during past decade while economic boom prevailed nation wide. There are exceptions. Microelectronics, intelligent machines and space are examples. These fields are quite popular among students, and only the very best join into laboratories dealing with these technologies. Maintenance and development of science and engineering capability in general would be best realized by widening and deepening education level in these fields. Space engineering is supported by a vast number of students who want to major this field, but has a small capacity both in education and industry among noted field. This is quite a contrast with electronics and mechanical engineering fields, for instance, which seem to have unlimited demand of resource in industry and uncountable education facilities established in almost every universities. Perhaps, 50% or more of students in engineering field have interest in space, and 20~30% wish to major space engineering if chances are given. In reality, capacity is only 4% in case of Kyushu University engineering divisions, and this includes aeronautics. Averaging over all universities in Japan, the capacity is less than 1%, while demand remains similar. It is therefore concluded that space education is not capable enough to absorb potential energy of young people, and wasting and spoiling much of it, partially creating a reason to walk out of science and engineering. Activities that provide chances of access to space to the young people, in wide area of science and engineering, would be beneficial both for the society and the youths.

Title: SYSTEM DESIGN FOR INTERNATIONAL SPACE MISSIONS
Publication: IAC 1995 congress proceedings, 46th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  2–6 October 1995, Oslo, Norway
Abstract:
Due to the increased costs in the execution of complex missions, many space agencies are cooperating in international missions.
Die benefit of this multi-national co-operation in joint projects is that it provides a solid basis for future collaboration, particularly for more complex projects such as the contribution to the International Space Station.
However, it is important to take this international character into account when planning and designing new missions. The system design for such missions is outlined in the paper, along with an explanation of the ideas developed in this field by the German Aerospace Research Establishment (DLR) and the Russian Mission Control Centre (ZUP).
The overall system design, based on jouit longterm experience and on current mission analysis techniques, includes all major components and the relevant interfaces for the exchange of all mission data: video, voice, telemetry and telecommand.
Of particular interest in this area is the opportunity provided to both German and European experimenters for the execution of Telescience missions, whereby scientists can directly interact with their experiments, on-board MIR.
This development is in line with the current trend to increase the support to the end-user either in the mission control center or at remote user centers.
Through the joint development of flight-operations plans and procedures, invaluable experience has been and will continue to be acquired. This unique collaboration will place both parties in an ideal position to support future projects both at European and International Idvel. •

Title: TOW-PHASE THERMAL CONTROL SYSTEM FOR INTERNATIONAL SPACE STATION ALPHA RUSSIAN PORION
Publication: IAC 1995 congress proceedings, 46th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  2–6 October 1995, Oslo, Norway
Abstract: International Space Station ALPHA (ISSA) will present the assembly of many modules with total heat load a few tens of kilowatts. Collection, transport and rejection of low-potential heat will be provided by central two-phase thermal control system (TPS). The collaborative research by RSC“ENERGIA” and KhAI in developing of the Multipurpose Space Platform and MIR-2 Station showed that under high heat loads and long heat transport distances two-phase thermal control system has the advantages over single-phase one in mass and in ability to satisfy users requirements. The experts in USA, Western Europe, Russia and Ukraine arrived at a similar conclusion about TPS concept of design, which is being used now for ISSA. This concept is commonly referred to as a thermal bus concept, when single-phase thermal control systems of the individual modules are connected with central TPS through interface evaporative heat exchangers. Thermal bus concept provides stable thermal regime at any number of attached modules and at variations in heat loads. Such a concept is now being considered as a basic one for ISSA Russian Portion. The paper contains the concept of ISSA TPS design, principal scheme and basic parameters of ISSA TPS, current status of experimental (ground and flight), and mathematical modelling, description of the problems and plans for future.

Title: VEGA: A NEW LOW COST APPROACH FOR A LIGHTSAT LAUNCHER
Publication: IAC 1995 congress proceedings, 46th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  2–6 October 1995, Oslo, Norway
Abstract:
The modular Vega Launcher Family is being developed for dedicated and multiple launches of lightsats. The concept of Vega most powerful version, the Vega MK3", is based on a three stage design which utilizes solid rocket motors (SRM) for each stage to achieve a low cost family of reliable launch vehicles.
Nominal Vega MK3" payload delivery capability is around 600 Kg to a 700 Km circular, polar orbit. The useful payload accommodation volume is approximately 11 nA The Vega design is based on the well-known and reliable architecture where the three main stages are stacked one on top of another. The SRM cases are fabricated using composite materials based on filament winding technology. The first two stages are equipped with thrust vector control (TVC) systems and the needed electric and pyrotechnic units. The vehicle equipment bay (VEB) is located directly above the third stage and includes the Vega guidance, navigation and control system (GNC), hydrazine attitude control (ACS) system and the telemetry and safety systems. A payload fairing, with an outer 2.4 m diameter, is mounted around and above the VEB.
The Vega launch vehicle family is based on a design- to-cost process, where the cost is the primary driver. Performance is traded with the cost requirements to provide a cost effective launch solution.
The paper describes the general history of the small launcher development in Italy which has led to the current Vega family concept. The current Vega configurations are described with emphasis on the launcher design-to-cost philosophy, performance and safety and operations scenarios.

Title: AUTOMATED TRANSFER VEHICLE STATUS AND EVOLUTIONS
Publication: IAC 1994 congress proceedings, 45th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  9–14 October 1994, Jerusalem, Israel
Abstract:
The conceptual idea of an Automated Transfer Vehicle (ATV) contributing to the logistics servicing of a LEO space station arose in Europe in the mid-eighties. ATV is required to be launched by Ariane 5, automated and autonomous when ouside space station vicinity. ATV has also to cope with a full design/operation compatibility with the on-orbit manned infrastructure. Furthermore, a design goal for ATV is to make it simple to develop, build and operate together with a low recurring and operation cost.
Concepts for ATV have been studied in parallel since 1987 by two industrial teams led respectively by Aerospatiale and DASA on successive ESA contracts. These progressive study steps have led to build a good technical basis (Phase A like) showing nevertheless two main options for ATV concepts respectively AEROSPATIALE and DASA-MMS ones.
The last ATV study step, run from November 93 to June 94, in parallel by Aerospatiale and DASA-MMS aimed at implementing last changes in the LEO infrastructure and some new ESA requirements and guidelines. It aimed also at looking at commonalities between ATV and Crew Transportation Vehicle, the newly introduced element of European Manned Spaceflight Programme.
This paper aims at presenting shortly the present study status on ATV. It presents also the main results of the last study mentioned previously, underlining associated ATV concepts. It concludes on trends or open areas that may afreet in the friture ATV concept and its potential roles within the emerging LEO Manned Infrastructure.

Title: DITHER EXCITATION AND VIBRATION SUPPRESSION OF SPACECRAFT WITH SMART STRUCTURES
Publication: IAC 1994 congress proceedings, 45th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  9–14 October 1994, Jerusalem, Israel
Abstract: The stringent design requirement of spacecraft systems has created the need for smart structures—structures with built-in piezoelectric sensor/actuator and control circuit that can actively change their physical geometry and/or properly. This paper presents a smart structure design for dither excitation and vibration suppression in spacecraft systems. Two smart structure specimens—an aluminum beam with surface bonded piezoelectric materials and a glass fiber composite laminated beam with embedded piezoelectric sensor/actuator—are designed, fabricated, and tested for their effectiveness in vibration control. A circuit is also developed to provide the efficient control input to actuator and reliable signal output from sensor. Analysis and experiment show that the smart structure design can be applied on-board spacecraft for jitter control in attitude system and stictibn prevention in deployment mechanism system.

Title: Development and Use of the Galileo and Ulysses Power Sources
Publication: IAC 1994 congress proceedings, 45th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  9–14 October 1994, Jerusalem, Israel
Abstract: The Galileo mission to Jupiter and the Ulysses mission to explore the polar regions of the Sun required a new power source: the general-purpose heat source radioisotope thermoelectric generator (GPHS-RTG), the most powerful RTG yet flown. Four flight-qualified GPHS-RTGs were fabricated with one that is being used on Ulysses, two that are being used on Galileo and one that was a common spare (and is now available for the Cassini mission to Saturn). In addition, an Engineering Unit and a Qualification Unit were fabricated to qualify the design for space through rigorous ground tests. This paper summarizes the ground testing and performance predictions showing that the GPHS-RTGs have met and will continue to meet or exceed the performance requirements of the ongoing Galileo and Ulysses missions.

Title: IRIDIUM DEBRIS MITIGATION PRACTICES AN UPDATE
Publication: IAC 1994 congress proceedings, 45th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  9–14 October 1994, Jerusalem, Israel
Abstract: The Iridium TM Program represents the most exciting prospect in space operations in the world today. However, it also represents one of the biggest engineering challenges as well as one of the best commercial opportunities ever. This paper will update the conununity on the progress on the trend setting approach Motorola has taken in orbital debris mitigation. It will delineate the attributes of a comprehensive program being implemented during the design phase and to be continued through the operations phase. The challenges are being met head-on and Motorola is aggressively seizing the opportunity to set new standards in debris mitigation.

Title: Low Earth Orbit mobile communication satellite systems: a tw o-year history since WARC-92
Publication: IAC 1994 congress proceedings, 45th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  9–14 October 1994, Jerusalem, Israel
Abstract:
Mobile communication satellite systems have regularly made the headlines of space industry publications in the 1990s. This paper adopts a new perspective—how the systems evolve over time—to describe the main technical features of the two main types:
- big-LEO systems with voice capabilities: Iridium, Globalstar, Odyssey, Inmarsat P21,
- little-LEO non-voice systems: Orbcomm, Starsys.
This approach reveals the considerable changes, even upheavals, that have affected the design of system components. The apparent stability in the designs is due to outside observers gradually and perhaps unquestioningly perceiving the changes. People’s capacity to forget, compounded by the attraction of innovation, may also have a lot to do with it.
We present the likely causes of these changes: regulatory environment, market forces, financial arrangements , being at the early design stage, etc. We also analyze the effects of these forces on the systems, and deduce the general trends.

Title: ON THE DESIGN OF A WASH WASTEWATER TREATMENT UNIT FOR INTERPLANETARY MANNED SPACESHIPS
Publication: IAC 1994 congress proceedings, 45th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  9–14 October 1994, Jerusalem, Israel
Abstract: The paper offers a procedure for designing a reverse osmosis unit made up of a microfilter, reverse osmosis module, and a polishing adsorbent bed, for water recovery from shower, handwash, and clotheswash wastewaters aboard space stations and interplanetary spaceships. The procedure is based on the original theoretical models developed for microfiltration with pore clogging, plug-flow microfiltration with compressible cake formation, crossflow microfiltration, reverse osmosis desalination, and on several experimental techniques, which allow efficient, not time-consuming, determination of design parameters. The models make it possible to predict not only the throughput of microfilters, the permeate flow rate and solute rejection of RO apparatuses for various operating conditions by using the results of a single experiment alone, but also get information on the structure of the microfilters and the properties of the wastewaters to be processed. The models may find application in other areas of life support system design and water treatment.

Title: OPERATION OF LOW-THRUST NUCLEAR-POWERED PROPULSION SYSTEMS FROM DEEP GRAVITATIPONAL ENERGY WELLS
Publication: IAC 1994 congress proceedings, 45th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  9–14 October 1994, Jerusalem, Israel
Abstract:
Part 1. Advanced space propulsion systems based upon the application of nuclear energy in rocket-style engines are capable of providing specific impulses (exhaust velocities) up to three orders of magnitude greater than those possible with the most powerful chemical rocket engines. However, most nuclear engines, as presently conceivable, would be, to some extent, limited in specific propulsive power (thrust power per unit engine mass) so that high exhaust velocity could only be achieved at the expense of corresponding reduction in thrust and acceleration. Nuclear-electric propulsion (NEP), which is seen by many to be the most likely candidate to power future spacecraft to the outermost Solar planets and beyond, would be severely constrained in this respect. Such constraint would result in a situation in which acceleration would be so low that a spacecraft employing such a propulsion system would take many years to reach full velocity, even in "flat" space. In practice, the spacecraft, almost certainly, would be assembled and stocked in LEO and would have to start its mission by climbing out of the deep energy well created by the gravitational fields of Earth and Sun. If it did so under its own power, significant degradation of its dynamic performance could result. Specific power limitation might be eliminated or, at least, greatly reduced by the adoption of an explosive propulsion system of the ORION type. Such a system, designated MEDUSA, has been described in recent literature. Relatively high accelerations would be possible by this means, but the dispersion of all the fission products from the explosions, into the surrounding space, would necessitate starting such a system from a remote station, far above LEO and this might largely offset any advantage over NEP deriving from the much greater specific power and thrust of the explosion system.
Part 2. In a power-limited or acceleration-limited flight the thrust acceleration on the gravitational acceleration local ratio, say, V determines how much the spacecraft undergoes strong Gravity Losses (GL), in terms of speed decrease, and a longer Transfer Time (TT) compared with the corresponding impulsive-based ideal mission. In the second part of this paper we present the v-dependent GL and TT penalty curves for Rocket Propulsion sample missions to the near heliopause and Sun's gravitational lens zone. The computations have been performed by existing large codes that are based on a full implementation of the non-linear programming approach to the optimal flight design. The Cowell method of Special Perturbations in Celestial Mechanics, including the J2 for Earth and the correct treatment of the high-energy rocket propulsion system, is used for a spacecraft moving in the Earth-Moon-Sun system. The numerical integrators consist of the Burlish-Stoer, 5th and 8th-order variable-step Runge-Kutta methods, depending on trajectory arc. The impact, which cannot be neglected, of the mentioned curves on both spacecraft mass and technology is pointed out. In particular, the central role of the specific power in advanced rocket engine is confirmed, especially when a scientific mission to a very distant target is planned. The considerations are based on extensive quantitative results.

Title: PORTS AND WINDOWS ON MANNED SPACECRAFT AND ON LUNAR AND PLANETARY HABITATION MODULES
Publication: IAC 1994 congress proceedings, 45th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  9–14 October 1994, Jerusalem, Israel
Abstract: A design concept is presented for ports for manned spacecraft and surface modules that can have a broad variety of uses covering a wide range of exploratory, research, technological and operational disciplines. The design also incorporates modularity and flexibility that permits reconfiguration in-situ using only Intravehicular Activity (I VA); Extravehicular Activity (EVA) is never required. The use of such ports as interchangeable windows to support work in the observational sciences and transmission technologies is examined, and for a variety of airlock applications, as well as for accommodating base plates for such diverse uses as external mechanical manipulators, additional module solar cell power or radiating surface area, ion engines, phased array transceivers, etc. Five essential design features are identified that must be fabricated and integrated into spacecraft or surface modules initially. All other developments and modifications can be provided later, permitting reductions in initial costs and even promoting later cost sharing with users, while preserving and significantly extending these ports’ usefulness over many decades.

Title: PROPELLANT CHARACTERISATION AND DESIGN OF A HYBRID ROCKET ENGINE
Publication: IAC 1994 congress proceedings, 45th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  9–14 October 1994, Jerusalem, Israel
Abstract: This paper describes development work on hybrid rocket systems for future university space projects. These rockets need to be manufactured with the facilities of a typical university workshop. This objective required the characterisation of suitable propellants. Polyethylene and polymethyl-methacrylate with gaseous oxygen were selected for their good performance, non-toxic exhaust products, easy availability and economy. The work determined the empirical relationship between combustion port area and burning rate of the solid fuel. It proved important to discriminate between changes in burning rate as opposed to effects caused by changing injector efficiency as the fuel surface regressed as well as varying oxygen flow rate. Two polymeric fuels were examined to determine if the observed trends in burning rate and regression characteristics are particular to a given fuel or more generally applicable. Average burning rates were determined by weighing. The experimental work was used to design a test hybrid rocket engine with 80 N thrust. This will be used to extend the research.

Title: Rhesus
Publication: IAC 1994 congress proceedings, 45th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  9–14 October 1994, Jerusalem, Israel
Abstract:
In the framework of the NASA/CNES RHESUS scientific experiment, dedicaded to study the biomedical and biological effects of the microgravity environment using the RHESUS monkey as a human susbstitute, MATRA MARCONI SPACE has developed a very sophisticated Life Support System designed for up to 20 day's SPACELAB Mission.
The RHESUS Life Support System has been developed both to ensure full animal comfort and to provide automated life support to minimize crew interactions ; these are limited to Feeder and Urine cassette changes and monkey contingency operations using a Glove Box. Accommodation of a monkey in a manned mission has induced very stringent safety requirements, particularly for biocontainment and odour control.
The animal is installed on a rackable seat allowing animal introduction in the SPACELAB just before launch. Monitoring is ensured by environmental sensors (humidity, temperature, sound, light level) and by two video cameras positionned inside the monkey compartment.
Many interactions using long duration missions simulations have been performed by animal specialists from CERMA to validate the Animal Interfaces.
Physiological data are acquired and processed by the RHESUS Measurement System (NASA) which will
condition signals from implanted and external animal sensors.
The animal is fed by an automatic pellet dispenser. This is achieved by the animal playing with a joystick and gaining an onboard NASA Psychomotor test, with a limitation of 900 pellets per day. The Feeder cassette capacity is 3 000 pellets and will be changed every three days by the astronaut. Water is delivered ad libitum by lixit suction. Monkey ventilation is achieved by a controlled air flow which also collects debris and faeces in the Waste Management System. The function of this equipment is to crush and store the waste material during the 20 day mission and then allow onground datation and analyses.
The Urine Collection System (UCS) is of prime interest for scientists since it allows very precise on-ground analyses obtained from in-flight mixing, sampling and urine storage of five 30 ml samples per day in the SPACELAB Freezer. The UCS distribution to each sample is ensured by a camshaft. The UCS contains many monitoring devices to guarantee animal safety, ensures two levels of containment for urine and copes with pressurized system maximum design pressure safety requirements.
All functions are performed automatically by a microcomputer linked via a serial interface to the overall RHESUS experiment Flight Data System (NASA).
The RHESUS Life Support has been delivered in MARCH 1994 to CNES/NASA after successful qualification tests.

Authors: ['R.F. Malina', 'S. Bowyer', 'D. Werthimer', 'C. Donnelly', 'D. Ng', 'J. Cobb']
Title: THE BERKELEY SETI PROGRAM: RECENT RESULTS FROM SERENDIP HI AND DESIGN STATUS OF THE NEXT GENERATION SERENDIP IV SYSTEM
Publication: IAC 1994 congress proceedings, 45th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  9–14 October 1994, Jerusalem, Israel
Abstract: We discuss factors that contribute to the highly cost- effective SERENDIP IV system. This machine will analyze 160 million channels simultaneously every 1.7 s with 0.6 Hz frequency resolution. This is a factor of 16 larger than any existing SETI system. Contributing to the success of this device is an innovative system design based on a modular architecture that combines multiple high-speed, general-purpose processors with highly specialized digital signal-processing electronics. This machine carries out 200 billion operations per second (a rate equivalent to that of hundreds of Cray supercomputers). We also report results from our ongoing search for narrow-band radio signals of extraterrestrial origin. We are currently conducting the world’s most encompassing SETI search using the SERENDIP III system on the 305-m NAIC Radio Telescope in Are- cibo, Puerto Rico. SERENDIP HI has logged over 8000 hr of quality observing time and processed 70 trillion spectral bins in 2.75 yr of observation. We have searched over 90% of the Arecibo-visible sky at least once and have examined over 65% of the sky at least three times. We have detected over 400 candidate signals which were seen twice at the same celestial coordinates and frequencies or that exhibited the characteristic point-source beam pattern of the Arecibo telescope. Unfortunately, this is about the number expected from Poisson processes.

Title: THE ODYSSEY™ SATELLITES IN MEO ORBIT
Publication: IAC 1994 congress proceedings, 45th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  9–14 October 1994, Jerusalem, Israel
Abstract: This paper describes the design of the satellites in the Odyssey™ system proposed for world-wide communications from personal, portable handsets. The Odyssey™ system space segment constellation is medium earth orbit (MEO) based. The orbits are circular at 10,354 kilometers and are inclined 50 degrees. The communication payload is a simple frequency translating (bent-pipe) repeater supporting 37 mobile communication beams that form a 40 degree coverage pattern on the earth. Each satellite incorporates several features not previously employed in MEO orbits. A directed coverage approach provides system communications availability at high latitudes by continuously repositioning the beams by maneuvering the satellite as it passes over the coverage region. The electrical power subsystem features a gallium arsenide solar array and a battery clamped architecture that controls the primary bus voltage by the battery voltage. Secondary voltages are provided by miniature converters embedded in each of the electronic components. The satellite contains a dual mode integral propulsion subsystem that uses hydrazine and nitrogen tetroxide during main engine, high thrust burns for orbital insertion. Monopropellant hydrazine thrusters provide attitude control during main engine burns and provide thrust for orbit maintenance maneuvers.

Title: THE UNKNOWN PAGES OF BIOGRAPHY
Publication: IAC 1994 congress proceedings, 45th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  9–14 October 1994, Jerusalem, Israel
Abstract:
The authors attempt to trace creative development (1954-1971) of Michael K. Yangel, the Chief Designer of space-rocket systems. His name is closely connected with the history of formation of Yuzhnoye Design Office that has been named after Yangel. At the same time, this is the history of space rocketry development in Ukraine.
High rate of development and perfection of the developed systems are characteristic of the activity of Chief Designer and the Design Office headed by him. Within the unprecedented term in propulsion history, not only the creative collective with its style of work was f irmed, but also the new principal trend was chosen in designing rocket complexes which use storable propellants and the independent inertial control system. How and why this became possible, what the role of Chief Designer was- these and other questions connected with Yangel's activity are analyzed by the authors.
The paper highlights main stages of the space-rocket complexes development, from SS-4 to SS-9, and traces continuity and updating of further projects up to SS-18.
Great attention is given to development of launch-vehicles and spacecraft of the Cosmos, Intercosmos, Meteor series.
The authors analyze the development of load-bearing structural arrangement, the use of new materials, the improvement of technological processes.
Against this background, the authors attempt to find the key to explain the phenomena of Yangel as an ideologist, organizer and the manager of large-scale technical projects from the viewpoint of philosophy and pioneer decision-making, the role of engineering intuition and prediction of rocketry trends.

Title: Teledesic Global Wireless Broadband Network System Architecture, Technologies and Design Features
Publication: IAC 1994 congress proceedings, 45th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  9–14 October 1994, Jerusalem, Israel
Abstract:
This paper will address the technical aspects and unique features of the new Teledesic
space segment architecture, technologies and design approaches. The paper's introduction will summarize and categorize all the current "Little'1 and "Big" communications LEO's and briefly extrapolate the current technology and economic trends that drive us inevitably to higher frequency bands and much larger constellations (> 1000 satellites). The capabilities of the extremely high- performance and high-power Teledesic LEO satellites will be described (e.g., many kWs, 100's of MIPS, 1000 mps, 1000's of beams, etc.). Many of the subsystem components, materials and processes developed for space exploration and national defense have application directly or indirectly in Teledesic's space segment. The Teledesic satellites are a new class of small satellites, which demonstrates the important commercial benefits of using technology developed for other purposes by U.S. National Laboratories (such as JPL and LLNL). After describing the space segment, the paper will address constellation operations and debris mitigation. The new Teledesic satellite manufacturing, integration and test approaches will also be addressed which use modern high volume production techniques and result in surprisingly low space segment costs. Finally, the paper will discuss the impact of the development of such satellite systems. The volume of advanced components and services such as launch services, required to construct and replace such large LEO constellations is sufficient to propel certain industries to world market leadership positions, and enable a revolution in the price and performance of LEO and GSO commercial communications satellite systems that will affect us all.

Title: A PLURIDISCIPLINARY APPROACH for human communication in future space missions
Publication: IAC 1993 congress proceedings, 44th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  16–22 October 1993, Graz, Austria
Abstract:
The proposed contribution presents the details of pluridisciplinary and cross-cultural researches (purpose, methodology and planned steps) on the human reliability in complex systems . Specialists in psychology, sociology, physiology and ethology have started to work together on the improvement of the man-machine interactions.
During future manned space flights, the astronauts will have to accomplish long-time missions, linked to the Earth only by way of electronic media (video, phone, electronic mail, virtual tools, ...), therefore the understanding and the control of communications, between the station and the ground, and inside the station become crucial, especially for the anticipation of most of the eventual troubles.
The complementary trends in this pluridisciplinary approach intend to design a new work organization in the concerned control centers implying adapted responsibility share, human protocols, procedures and infonnation handling.
French and Russian engineers and researchers have began to collaborate, bringing together theoretical and practical knowledge, with intend to specify and design this new work organization for control of such future manned space crafts.

Title: AEROSHELL CONCEPTS TRADE-OFF FOR MARS LANDERS
Publication: IAC 1993 congress proceedings, 44th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  16–22 October 1993, Graz, Austria
Abstract:
One option for ESA's potential participation in the future exploration of Mars is the deployment of a network of small surface stations for performing extended geophysical, chemical and meteorological measurements. An assessment study, performed by ESA, gave an overall mission description and a typical entry scenario.
A broad trade-off was performed on candidate surface station aeroshells. Three configurations were investigated with different separation scenarii between aeroshell and surface stations. That led to several candidate architectures, which were studied considering three main kinds of aerobraking decelerator concepts : rigid, deployable or composed of stretched fabrics.
For each combination of solutions, detailed investigation on suitable materials was performed, taking into account three thermal protection technologies :
. cold structure thermally protected by appropriate heatshield materials,
. hot structure (thermostructure), where the structural and thermal functions are met by the same components, but which requires additional thermal insulation in some specific areas,
. semi-hot structure (heat sink thermal protection), based on materials with large specific heat capacity. This solution needs additional thermal insulation.
This paper presents the aeroshell thermal protection system alternatives investigated and summarizes the results of the major trade studies undertaken. The ranking and the selection of the best suited solutions reflect several design drivers, the most important of which are low mass, cost and risk aspects.
Finally, two reference configurations were selected for further study on analytical design verification and manufacturing aspect investigation.
Both thermostructural analysis and buckling assessment were performed. The expected margins are given for all the TPS elements and emphasis was put on a clear definition of the TPS interface specifications. A preliminary validation file was drawn for both concepts and the main results are presented in this paper.

Title: Application o f RITA to the Geostationary Satellite Artemis
Publication: IAC 1993 congress proceedings, 44th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  16–22 October 1993, Graz, Austria
Abstract:
Ion Propulsion is baseline to be used for orbit control of the geostationary communiction satellite Artemis, which is in development in Europe under ESA/ESTEC responsibility with Alenia Spazio as the main contractor. An Ion Propulsion Package (IPP) will be installed on the satellite, consisting of 2 RITA's (RF Ion Thruster Assembly) as developed by DASA in Germany and 2 EITA's (Electronbombardement Ion Thruster Assembly) as developed by Matra Marconi Space in England. The IPP will perform N/S stationkeeping during the 10 years of satellite mission time.
RITA has been flown as an experiment on the European Retrievable Carrier EURECA. It has been successfully operated during 130 cycles and 240 hours of thrust at thrust levels between 6 and 10 mN. After retrieval of EURECA by the Space Shuttle RITA will be investigated to complete the results of this experiment.
For the application on Artemis the RITA design as for EURECA will be used with improvements, which became evident during ground testing and during operation in space.
The development of the hardware for Artemis has finished its Breadboard Phase in 1991. Now the Engineering Qualification Models are under development and will be qualified in early 1994. Flight Model fabrication will start after that and will take about 18 months. The launch of Artemis is planned for 1996.

Title: Design of constellations of satellites
Publication: IAC 1993 congress proceedings, 44th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  16–22 October 1993, Graz, Austria
Abstract: This paper describes possible ways for determining Walker delta-pattern constellation characteristics when global visibility is required. First the algorithm used to compute the worst seen point on Earth is exposed. Then, using this algorithm to compute the critical point, the different orbital parameters are considered in their turn, and ways to determine them are discussed. Concerning altitude, a simpie law is given, that may be used to compute the minimum number of satelites required. Finally, other possible constraints that could be taken into account are exposed, including directions to optimize the results with constellations that do not have Walker properties.

Authors: ['H. Haid', 'M. Von Bradke', 'H. Schneider', 'R. Pleger', 'K. Maile']
Title: From Plasma Channel to Real Reentry Testing
Publication: IAC 1993 congress proceedings, 44th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  16–22 October 1993, Graz, Austria
Abstract:
In November 1992 we had the opportunity to test successfully for the first time in Europe two fiber reinforced ceramic specimens under the severe conditions during atmospheric reentry of a Russian FOTON capsule. The project was financed by DARA, coordinated by Kayser- Threde (Munich) and successfully conducted by the Russian KB FOTON.
The specimens were mechanically embedded into the ablative heat shield of the capsule. The C/C-SiC specimens were fabricated by use of a liquid phase siliconizing process developed within the DLR Institute of Structures and Design. As such CMC materials are designed for high temperature applications in hot structures and thermal protection systems (TPS) of space reentry vehicles, material and structural component testing becomes an essential aspect in vehicle development and use.

Title: Intersatellite optical crosslink testbed for 300/650 MBPS
Publication: IAC 1993 congress proceedings, 44th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  16–22 October 1993, Graz, Austria
Abstract:
This paper describes the design, fabrication, and preliminary testing of a high datarate intersatellite laser crosslink testbed being built at The MITRE Corporation in 1993 on IR&D funding. Wideband laser drivers and optical receivers for signals at datarates of 300 Mbps and 650 Mbps have been designed and built, and are being integrated into a laboratory testbed for system level testing. This testbed includes laser wavelength division multiplexing of three colors, representative of that required for a flight implementation. The optical crosslink testbed has input/output interfaces with RF signals from uplink/downlink hardware simulators, described in a companion paper.1
The design of this optical crosslink is unique, in that it is based on direct analog modulation of the crosslink lasers with the wideband signal waveform from an incoming RF link (i.e., an uplink or space crosslink). Nearly all of the optical crosslink designs proposed to date have been for digitally modulated laser links, typically for applications where a wideband digital data stream originates at a sensing or imaging satellite and needs to be crosslinked to a destination satellite. The motivation for the analog modulation scheme in this paper is driven by end-to-end applications that include satellite uplinks, crosslinks, and downlinks, to avoid the requirement for processing satellites to detect, demodulate, regenerate, and remodulate multiple FDM channels of data at each of the two (or more) satellite crosslink nodes. This is particularly important for wideband channels that represent a composite of many different signals and modulation formats. The datarates, frequencies, interfaces, and requirements chosen for this testbed were based on the NASA TDRSS satellite and an upgrade being considered for a TDRSS-to- TDRSS crosslink capability. More generally, these datarates and the resulting testbed implementation are representative of an arbitrary RF-modulated wideband optical crosslink.
The optical crosslink testbed described in this paper is a hardware proof-of-concept that addresses a flight-like laboratory implementation of a bent-pipe optical crosslink to facilitate evaluation of its performance. The goals of this project include demonstrating the maturity and performance of optical crosslink technology representative of that required for flight hardware. To this end, the design is based on a wavelength plan suitable for flight implementation, to permit validation of channel- to-channel isolation, as well as receiver sensitivity, system linearity, and other key parameters. The preliminary results to date are very encouraging. We have found the laser/driver design to be quite linear, permitting testing with the lasers operating at full power (no back-off) and 95% modulation depth, with in-band intermods at least -40 dBc, and out-of- band harmonics and spurs typically greater than -55 dBc.

Title: SPACE STATION FREEDOM MOBILE SERVICING SYSTEM FROM ENGINEERING MODELS TO FLIGHT HARDWARE
Publication: IAC 1993 congress proceedings, 44th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  16–22 October 1993, Graz, Austria
Abstract:
The redesign activity of Space Station initiated in 1993 by the U.S.A. has caused a significant perturbation to the Canadian program which entered the flight-hardware manufacturing phase in support of the assembly of the Station which was planned to commence in 1996.
The Canadian Space Agency and its industrial team, led by SPAR Aerospace, have concluded a key series of Design Reviews of the Mobile Servicing System, Canada’s contribution to Space Station Freedom. Following successful completion in December 1992 of the Critical Design Review of the Space Station Remote Manipulator System, the team has embarked on manufacture and test of flight hardware. The Preliminary Design Review of the Special Purpose Dextrous Manipulator, held in February 1993, confirmed the design of an optimized, lower-cost SPDM. The Canadian team contributed an essential component to the Space Station Man-Tended Capability CDR.
The development of MSS ground control, diagnostic and training facilities is an equally important element of the Canadian Space Station Program. The MSS Ground Segment will include core facilities to be housed in the Canadian Space Agency’s new Headquarters building at St. Hubert, Québec, together with related engineering support provided by the industrial team.
Canada’s contribution to the assembly of Space Station Freedom is now expected to begin at a very early stage of the process, as CSA works with NASA’s Space Shuttle Program to develop the Canadian Space Vision System for use in guidance and control of the Shuttle Remote Manipulator System in Space Station assembly.
Potential users of Space Station Freedom
continue to prepare for the operations and utilization phase by undertaking microgravity experiments in a variety of facilities. Strategic technology programs, aimed at enhancing the capability of Canada’s industrial and university sectors to support future growth and evolution of the Mobile Servicing System, are starting to provide concrete spinoff benefits. The recent award to CSA’s prime contractor of a licence to use and commercialize the government’s MSS technology represents a significant step towards maximizing commercialization and economic benefit of all areas of the program.

L’activité de transition de la Station spatiale que les États-Unis ont débuté en 1993 a causé une perturbation significative au programme canadien. Ce dernier était à la phase de production du matériel d’envoi qui devait être utilisé pour l’assemblage de la station débutant en 1996.
L’Agence spatiale canadienne et son équipe industrielle ont terminé, sous la direction de SPAR Aérospatiale, une série cruciale d'examens de la conception du système d’entretien mobile (SEM), qui représente la contribution du Canada à la station spatiale Freedom. Après avoir achevé avec succès, en décembre 1992, l’examen critique de la conception du télémanipulateur de la station spatiale, l’équipe s’est lancée dans la fabrication et la mise à l’essai de matériel informatique de vol. L’examen préliminaire de la conception du manipulateur agile spécialisé (MAS), qui a eu lieu en février 1993, est venu confirmer qu’on avait conçu à faible coût un MAS aux capacités optimales. L’équipe canadienne a joué un rôle essentiel dans l’examen critique de la conception de la station spatiale, dans sa version visitée.
La mise sur pied d’installations de commande au sol du SEM, de diagnostic et de formation en la matière est un élément tout aussi important du programme canadien de la station spatiale. Le secteur sol du SEM comprendra des installations centrales qui trouveront place au nouvel édifice qui sert de siège à l’Agence spatiale canadienne à Saint-Hubert, au Québec, en même temps que le soutien technique connexe fourni par l’équipe industrielle.
Le rôle joué par le Canada dans l’assemblage de la station spatiale Freedom devrait maintenant commencer à un stade très précoce du processus, car l’ASC travaille avec le programme de la navette spatiale de la NASA à mettre au point le système canadien de vision spatiale qui servira à guider et à commander le télémanipulateur de la navette dans l’assemblage de la station spatiale.
Les éventuels utilisateurs de la station spatiale Freedom continuent à se préparer à la phase des opérations et de l’utilisation en entreprenant des expériences de microgravité dans toutes sortes d’installations. Des programmes technologiques stratégiques, destinés à améliorer le potentiel des secteurs industriel et universitaire du Canada afin de concourir à la croissance future et à révolution du système d’entretien mobile, commencent à porter fruit concrètement, par ricochet. La licence que s’est vu décerner dernièrement le maître d’oeuvre de l’ASC pour utiliser et commercialiser la technologie gouvernementale du SEM représente un pas de géant vers la maximisation de la commercialisation et des avantages économiques de tous les secteurs du programme.

Title: SPACE TOURISM FOR EUROPE - A CASE STUDY
Publication: IAC 1993 congress proceedings, 44th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  16–22 October 1993, Graz, Austria
Abstract: This paper discusses the long-range perspectives for commercial passenger transportation into Low Earth Orbit (LEO): a European Space Tourism Initiative. Southern Spain is introduced as a potential location for ‘Spaceport Europe’ from which commercial space trips would be conducted. Based on a market model for a thirty-year time span (2020 to 2050), three different market growth scenarios are developed (no growth; low growth; high growth). These concepts introduce a launch vehicle design which comprises the best features of current European launch vehicle projects (eg SÀNGER, STS-2000) that promise a significant reduction in recurring costs. Technological variables of the transportation system and the infrastructure as well as transportation demand trends have been used as input for an integrated operations and cost model. Computer simulation of passenger transport within the given time span produced cost trends which promise specific transportation costs of as low as $60,000 (1990 values) per seat. Admittedly, such cost figures require very high passenger numbers that might be beyond any real demand.

Title: THE APOLLO’S CUP RACE TO THE MOON - A COMPUTER-BASED SIMULATION SYSTEM FOR COOPERATIVE LEARNING GROUPS
Publication: IAC 1993 congress proceedings, 44th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  16–22 October 1993, Graz, Austria
Abstract: The Apollo's Cup Race to the Moon is a classroom simulation for middle-grade cooperative learning teams. The simulation uses three program modules: Inform, Design, and Race. The Inform module contains information and other resources related to solar sailing. Design provides the tools to design a solar sailer. Race incorporates a mathematical module for calculating solar sailer trajectory and displays the simulated race. Resources and materials provided in the programs address diverse learning style preferences and varying abilities among students. The goal of the simulation is to provide an authentic problem solving experience that promotes scientific and mathematical understanding and interest in space science. Field testing of the simulation will be conducted in local middle schools in the spring.

Title: THE SMALLSAT REVOLUTION.... BACK TO THE FUTURE ?
Publication: IAC 1993 congress proceedings, 44th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  16–22 October 1993, Graz, Austria
Abstract:
In engineering, as in the sciences, mathematics and the arts, evolutionary processes ultimately lead to the sophistication of simplicity. The smallsat revolution is producing a return to sensible scales of size, mass, and cost. Space missions have evolved from modest flight research to complex, space-based laboratory and operational systems. A continual growth in vehicle mass was enabled by increasing launch capabilities; more significant, however, was the explosive growth in “capability density,” provided by the solid state technology revolution and focused advancements in space technologies. Interestingly, the evolution of space systems parallels that of computer systems, i.e., from mainframes, to desktop minicomputers, to today’s advanced laptop microcomputers.
Until recently, many space program plans assumed continuing growth in vehicle size and collateral lift capability; this yielded excessive system complexity, extended design and development cycles, and unrealistic unit flight cost and risk. At the same time, a market pull by other segments of government, commercial and university users spurred the development of a new class of space systems... smallsats. Smallsats began with simple, short lifetime scientific experiments and technology demonstrations. A small launch vehicle industry emerged to serve a new generation of highly capable smallsats, and networked systems of smallsats. New technologies and lessons learned in small satellite development and operations are leading to new design approaches, including highly modular, multi-mission spacecraft. Small satellites can now support long-life, complex operational missions such as commercial communications, earth observations, and military surveillance.
The growth in satellite technologies is not over. Unabated trends augur systems built with nanocircuit electronic devices, micro- and perhaps nano-scale mechanical devices, optical and photonics breakthroughs, mechanical and electromechanical devices, sensor cooling, vehicle navigation and control and ultra-lightweight materials, structures and power storage systems. Technology advances will also be achieved through “spin-in” from non-space, commercial fields. The design, fabrication and operation of this new genre of spacecraft will change. As with computers, modular plug-in elements could be employed in standardized model runs. Technological change, at an evermore rapid rate, will be incorporated without complete system redesign. End-to-end design, build and fly schedules will be substantially compressed. Clustered/distributed systems on orbit will be maintained and/or upgraded by replacing relatively inexpensive smallsats.
What may look like a return to Sputnik and Explorer class spacecraft is, in reality, the beginning of a new generation of highly capable space vehicles and mission systems.

Authors: ['Ulf J. Lindqwister', 'Stephen M. Lichtenfels', 'Edgar S. Davis', 'Harold L. Theiss']
Title: The GPS Topex/Poseidon Precise Orbit Determination Experiment: Implications for Design of GPS Global Networks
Publication: IAC 1993 congress proceedings, 44th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  16–22 October 1993, Graz, Austria
Abstract: Topex/Poseidon, a cooperative satellite mission between United States and France, aims to determine global ocean circulation patterns and to study their influence on world climate through precise measurements of sea surface height above the geoid with an on-board altimeter. To achieve the mission science aims, a goal of 13-cm orbit altitude accuracy was set. Topex/Poseidon includes a Global Positioning System (GPS) precise orbit determination (POD) system that has now demonstrated altitude accuracy better than 5 cm. The GPS POD system includes an on-board GPS receiver and a 6-station GPS global tracking network. This paper reviews early GPS results and discusses multi-mission capabilities available from a future enhanced global GPS network, which would provide ground-based geodetic and atmospheric calibrations needed for NASA deep space missions while also supplying tracking data for future low Earth orbiters. Benefits of the enhanced global GPS network include lower operations costs for deep space tracking and many scientific and societal benefits from the low Earth orbiter missions, including improved understanding of ocean circulation, ocean-weather interactions, the El Nino effect, the Earth thermal balance, and weather forecasting.

Title: Thermocapillary Convection in a Three Layer System, a BDPU Experiment for IML2 Mission
Publication: IAC 1993 congress proceedings, 44th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  16–22 October 1993, Graz, Austria
Abstract:
Thermocapillary convection in multi-layer systems has gained a great interest since it can be notably related to the crystal growth in encapsulated floating zone. Therefore several microgravity experiments on this particular topic have been recently selected for space flight and sounding rockets.
Pure thermocapillary instability (thermal gradient perpendicular to the interfaces) in a symmetrical configuration will be studied during the IML 2 mission (June 1994) in the multi-user facility BDPU. The preparation of this microgravity experiment is reported including the selection of the fluids and tracers, the surface tension measurements, the container design, the filling procedure and parabolic flight experiments on the mechanical stability of such a system.
Original features of the Marangoni-Bénard instability in three-layer systems with respect to single or two-layer systems are also reported. For the pure Marangoni effect, when the thermal diffusivities of the fluids are the same, an oscillatory regime is described and its stability far from the critical point is demonstrated in contradistinction with the two-layer system.
For the specific system, Fluorinert FC70 - silicone Oil 50 cS - air, the selection of pattern depending on the relative influence of both mechanisms of instability and on the relative height of the layers has been experimentally observed using infrared thermography and compared with linear stability analysis and numerical simulation.

Authors: ['Jerry R. Newsom', 'Peiman G. Maghami', 'W. Keith Belvin']
Title: Validated technology for the reduction of spacecraft vibrations Controls-Structures Integration (CSI)
Publication: IAC 1993 congress proceedings, 44th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  16–22 October 1993, Graz, Austria
Abstract: The NASA Langley Research Center has constructed several testbeds to assess the viability of flexible structure control. These testbeds have been fruitful in assessing controlled structures on a system level. It is found, however, that simply adding sensors, actuators, and a control system to an existing structure (i.e. space platform) is not the preferred methodology for improving pointing performance. When the structure is designed without regard to pointing control, significant design freedom is lost. The preferred design procedure is to simultaneously design the structure and the control system, hence, the name controls-structures integration. By designing the structure and control system simultaneously, much higher efficiency can be achieved. In this study, an 18 m long truss structure with several appendages was enhanced through integrated controls and structures design. The design was fabricated and tested for validation of the methodology. Test results collaborated predictions and showed a 60 percent reduction in control energy for the enhanced test article.

Authors: ['P. Ngo', 'K. Krishen', 'D. Arndt', 'G. Raffoul', 'V. Karasack', 'K. Bhasin', 'R. Leonard']
Title: A HIGH TEMPERATURE SUPERCONDUCTIVITY COMMUNICATIONS FLIGHT EXPERIMENT
Publication: IAC 1992 congress proceedings, 43rd  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  28 August–5 September 1992, Washington, United States
Abstract:
A high temperature superconductivity (HTSC) flight experiment from the payload bay of the Space Shuttle Orbiter to the Advanced Communications Technology Satellite (ACTS) is being breadboarded. This proposed experiment, a joint project between the Johnson Space Center and the Lewis Research Center, would use a Ka- band (20GHz) HTSC phased array antenna and front-end electronics (low noise amplifier) to received a downlink communications signal from the ACTS. A conventional receiver demodulates the encoded telemetry signal which is then turned around and transmitted back to ACTS and the ground.
The HTSC phased array has nine 4x4 microstrip patch antenna subarrays which when properly phased, provide approximately 24 dB of boresight gain. An 8x8 HTSC microstrip patch array has been built and tested. A Ka-band receiver, transmitter, modem, encoder, decoder, etc., are now being built and tested. Link analyses and interface problems with the Orbiter are addressed in the paper in addition to the design, fabrication, and testing of various subsystems used in the communication link.

Title: ADVANCED TSTO VTOHL REUSABLE ROCKET LAUNCHER - STUDY STATUS
Publication: IAC 1992 congress proceedings, 43rd  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  28 August–5 September 1992, Washington, United States
Abstract:
In the framework of its effort to assess the trends of future Space Transportation Systems, AEROSPATIALE has built up a methodology to enable fair comparison between reusable all rocket and airbreathing launchers, thus allowing a rational choice for future reusable and low cost launchers.
As part of this methodology, a study devoted to an advanced TSTO, Vertical Take-Off and Horizontal Landing (VTOHL), reusable rocket launcher is performed. The selection of the present configuration was part of concepts trade-offs reported in a previous IAF paper in 1990 (IAF 90-177).
This paper presents the main results of the current investigations performed in the framework of this Advanced Manned Fully Reusable TSTO VTOHL Rocket Launcher.
As cost reduction and safety considerations require abort capabilities of the future manned launcher throughout the entire flight regime, this issue is first addressed. Since a large portion of critical failures might be attributed to the propulsion systems, the design, sizing and operations of the launcher take into account the potential failure of one or several engines of the stages during the powered flight. In that event, recovery scenarios have been investigated and it was determined when the stages could execute return-to-launch-site (RTLS), Transatlantic-Abort-Landing (TAL) or Abort- To-Orbit (ATO) abort modes. The results show that an appropriate combination of powered and gliding phases with limited relaxation on nominal constraints (loads, acceleration, ...) enables the intact stages recovery throughout the flight regime, from take-off to orbital insertion.
Emphasis has also been placed on the global optimization of the first stage to maximize the ascent powered flight capabilities of the launcher and to maximize the first stage transatlantic gliding flight range capabilities taking into account considerations on aerodynamics, thermal aspects, weight, propellants, stability and control (including separation phase). The results of a trade-off study, performed to obtain a lightweight thermostructural concept, are presented. This trade-off included hot versus thermally protected structures.
Material and design options were also explored in this trade-off.

Title: Development Status of the 260,000 Ibf Thrust Hybrid Rocket Booster
Publication: IAC 1992 congress proceedings, 43rd  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  28 August–5 September 1992, Washington, United States
Abstract:
The American Rocket Company plans to offer commercial launch services throughout the 1990s on its Aquila orbital launch vehicle. Aquila is a four-stage orbital launch vehicle capable of delivering 2,000 Ibm (907 kg) to LEO. Aquila will be propelled by the H-1800 hybrid propulsion system (260,530 Ibf -1,159 kN vacuum thrust). This paper describes the design and development of the H-1800 propulsion system. The status of the development program, including the fabrication of the first full scale development motor (DM-01) and test data from full-scale combustion port tests are discussed.

The American Rocket Company plans to offer commercial launch services throughout the 1990s on its Aquila orbital launch vehicle. The Aquila launch vehicle will be propelled by the H-1800 hybrid propulsion system, which is currently under development.
The first part of the H-1800 motor development has been completed with the successful test firings of the full scale port motor (FP-01). FP-01 has demonstrated the performance of two full scale H-1800 combustion ports. The test results from the FP motor, as well as smaller subscale motors have led to the design of the first full scale H-1800 motor (DM-01). DM-01 will be tested in the fall of 1992. This effort will lead to the flight of the HyFlyer suborbital launch vehicle in 1994 and to the flight of the Aquila launch vehicle in 1996. The first H-1800 flight on the HyFlyer vehicle will represent the introduction to the space launch industry of a new, safe, reliable and low-cost propulsion alternative to today’s conventional liquid or solid rocket propulsion.

Title: Guidelines to Increase EVA Effectiveness— Results of Aerobrake Assembly Neutral Buoyancy Testing
Publication: IAC 1992 congress proceedings, 43rd  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  28 August–5 September 1992, Washington, United States
Abstract:
Extravehicular activity (EVA) will be required for Space
Station Freedom assembly and operation and is key to the
feasibility of Space Exploration Initiative missions. Projected
extravehicular requirements for growth phases exceed
the resources allocated by Space Station Freedom Permanently
Manned Configuration requirements. This paper
provides guidelines to establish more effective extravehicular
activity systems that combine crew, telerobots, and
flight hardware. Effectiveness is increased by developing
applicable test-beds, using them to test a combination of
extravehicular activity and telerobotic systems, and focusing
results to provide recommended changes to both current
systems and future mission requirements.
We substantiate guidelines to increase EVA effectiveness
through results from aerobrake assembly neutral buoyancy
testing by McDonnell Douglas Space Systems Company
(MDSSC) Independent Research and Development (IRAD)
in April 1992. The EVA systems used in the April 1992
testing include the AX-5 8-psi suit and a shuttle style suit.
A pair of large workspace arms called the EVA and
Telerobot Positioning System (ETPS) was used to position
one of the EVA subjects and a Kraft dexterous manipulator.
Results concentrate on optimal task division between the
EVA crew member and telerobot. Guidelines are listed for
providing effective communications for joint EVA/telerobotic
operations, control for an EVA subject on the end of
a positioning telerobot, assuring safety of the EVA subject
in proximity to a telerobot, and hardware design for
simultaneous EVA and telerobot compatibility.

Title: Making Space for Australia: the Development of Australia's First Major Space Exhibition
Publication: IAC 1992 congress proceedings, 43rd  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  28 August–5 September 1992, Washington, United States
Abstract: Until the opening of Space-Beyond this World at Sydney's Powerhouse Museum in October 1988, Australia did not have an exhibition that could be considered as providing a comprehensive display of international space activities. This paper outlines the origins and development of the exhibition the production of which led to both an Australian and an international first in museum space displays. It examines the reasons for the initial exhibition proposal and the choice and development of its themes. It considers the relationship of theme, collection and design and the use of interactive and audio-visual components in enhancing the exhibition's ability to cominunicate to the visitor. The challenges of developing an exhibition without an initially defined budget or venue or an existing collection are discussed, with reference to the international co-operation and corporate sponsorship that were instrumental in the successful development of the display.

Title: Rediscovering the Potential of Solid Rocket Propulsion Systems for Low Cost Launch Vehicle and Upper Stage Applications
Publication: IAC 1992 congress proceedings, 43rd  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  28 August–5 September 1992, Washington, United States
Abstract: Solid propulsion component technologies for future space systems must not only meet current upper stage and launch vehicle performance requirements, but must have significantly lower system life cycle costs. Innovative system concepts and component technologies must be developed to meet these goals. An , in-house Phillips Laboratory, Propulsion Directorate program is working toward this goal. Thià in-house program is investigating and developing innovative technologies for all the major components in a solid rocket motor. In addition, work is being conducted to better understand the design, development and fabrication processes for conventional solid rocket motor components. Life cycle cost reduction technologies for these components are also being investigated.

Title: SP-100 SPACE REACTOR POWER SYSTEM FOR LUNAR, MARS AND ROBOTIC EXPLORATION
Publication: IAC 1992 congress proceedings, 43rd  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  28 August–5 September 1992, Washington, United States
Abstract:
The SP-100 component development began in September, 1986, based on Earth-orbital surveillance missions, Earth-orbital nuclear electrical propulsion missions, zero-gravity Earth orbital laboratory missions, and outerplanet nuclear electric propulsion exploration missions. In September, 1990, NASA established the Space Exploration Initiative (SEI), which defined the surface power systems for Lunar and Mars exploration as potential SP-100 missions. A recent NASA mission study for robotic exploration of the planets, comets and asteroids also defined SP-100 as a potential power system. The Air Force defined a future system surveillance mission as a potential application for reactor power systems. It would use the SP-100 for spacecraft power as well as for nuclear electric propulsion. As a result of the above potential applications, the SP-100 Project received functional requirements for the following three missions: (1)
Pluto Orbiter with nuclear electric propulsion, (2) Human-rated surface reactor power system for Lunar and Mars exploration, and (3) Earth surveillance with an integrated nuclear electric propulsion system. The SP-100 Project is developing the reactor power systems technology to meet these requirements so that the technical database, design tools, and specifications will be applicable for these missions.
The final step in the SP-100 program is system validation. This is presently planned to be accomplished by using the newly developed database, tools, and specifications to design, fabricate, qualify, launch, and operate an integrated reactor power system in an early demonstration mission that would also provide useful scientific data. This early demonstration mission, in parallel with the analyses and ground hardware experiments to verify mature component performance and ten-year lifetime, will validate technology readiness for Robotic, Lunar, and Mars operational missions.
The object of the SP-100 development program is to provide the engineering technical database, the analytical design tools, and the detailed process specifications necessary to design, fabricate, qualify, and use reactor power systems on future space exploration missions. The SP-100 Project is developing the database, tools, and specifications to cover a power range of 10’s to 100’s of kilowatts for missions with lifetimes of up to 20 years. The objective is being accomplished by defining potential space missions that require 10’s to 100’s of kilowatts of power. Once the missions are defined, a mission study is performed for each mission to establish the requirements for the power system. The SP-100 power system then is designed to meet the requirements for each mission. The SP-100 Generic Flight System design sets the operating parameters and configurations for all SP-100 components. The SP-100 Project maintains the power system requirements current by performing mission studies for each new potential SP-100 space mission.
The SP-100 power system design includes the following eight subsystems: (1) Reactor, (2) Reactor Instrumentation and Control (RI&C), (3) Shield, (4) Heat Transport, (5) Converter, (6) Heat Rejection, (7) Power Conditioning Control and Distribution (PCC&D), and (8) Mechanical/Structural. From the eight subsystems, the engineering technical database, the analytical design tools, and the process specifications are available for the PCC&D and Mechanical/Structural Subsystems. The database, tools, and specifications are complete for the Reactor and Shield Subsystems except for materials data from ongoing tests, and are partially complete for the RI&C, Heat Transport, Converter and Heat Rejection Subsystems. The key components for which the engineering technical database, the design tools, and the process specifications are still being developed are the thermoelectric converter, the thermoelectric electromagnetic pump, the control drive actuators, the multiplexers, the temperature and neutron flux sensors, the gas separator, and the radiator heat pipe with armor.

Authors: ['R.W. Ballard', 'N.D. Searby', 'L.S. Stone', 'R.P. Hogan', 'M. Viso', 'M. Venet']
Title: SPACELAB LIFE SCIENCES 3: BIOMEDICAL RESEARCH USING THE RHESUS RESEARCH FACILITY
Publication: IAC 1992 congress proceedings, 43rd  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  28 August–5 September 1992, Washington, United States
Abstract:
In 1985, a letter of agreement was signed between the French space agency, the Centre Nationale d'Etudes Spatiales (CNES), and the U. S. space agency, the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA), formally initiating a joint venture called the RHESUS Project. The goal of this Project, is to provide a facility to fly rhesus monkeys (Macaca mulattal to support spaceflight experiments which are applicable but not practical to carry out on human subjects. Biomedical investigations in behavior/performance, immunology/microbiology, muscle physiology, cardiopulmonary physiology, bone/calcium physiology, regulatory physiology, and neurophysiology disciplines will be performed by twenty-six investigators from the U. S. and France. The Rhesus Research Facility (RRF), hardware capable of supporting two adult rhesus monkeys in a microgravity environment, is being developed for a first flight on Spacelab Life Sciences 3 (SLS-3) in early 1996.
The primary objective for the first flight is to return healthy rhesus monkeys. The major science objectives for SLS-3 are in the behavior/performance, immunology/microbiology, and muscle physiology disciplines. The cardiopulmonary physiology, bone/calcium physiology, regulatory physiology, and neurophysiology discipline objectives will only be partially supported on SLS-3.
Individual feasibility studies have been performed by each of the discipline scientists. These studies have been progressively combined into integrated science tests. The most recent integrated test resulted in the collection of all data that will be collected for the flight except the biopotential signals. Future long duration tests will complete the science integration.
To support the science objectives, the RRF is being developed to house the two monkeys individually in identical cages known as Experiment Systems for Orbiting Primates (ESOPs). Each monkey is provided food pellets via operation of a joystick in response to the Psychomotor Test System (PTS) which includes a video display, computer, and software tasks designed to measure performance and provide environmental enrichment. Water is provided via a lixit and water distribution system. Temperature-controlled air is circulated to provide air exchange with the Spacelab cabin while maintaining biocontainment. Environmental parameters are monitored continuously in addition to physiological measurements via sensors, signal conditioners, and a comprehensive data acquisition system designed to interface with the Spacelab data management system for downlinking to the ground. Development models of this hardware have been completed and tested, culminating in the hardware Critical Design Review (CDR) and imminent fabrication of flight hardware.

Title: Space and communications in developing countries
Publication: IAC 1992 congress proceedings, 43rd  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  28 August–5 September 1992, Washington, United States
Abstract: The developments in Space technology have provided a powerful tool for rapidly spreading communication infrastructure, which is vital to the development process in developing countries. Vis-a-vis the particular needs and constraints in developing countries including limitations of terrestrial infrastructure, wide diversity in traffic pattern among urban and rural populations, lack of financial and trained human resources, urgent needs for establishing reliable communications during natural disasters and with remote/isolated locations etc., the full potential of satellite technology is not yet tapped by several countries to meet their vast and urgent needs. The paper is intended to survey the global trends in technological developments and their applications in the satellite communications that are of particular relevànte to developing countries. The response provided by international systems through their programs, the emerging aspects of the regional systems as well as the experience gained by certain developing countries through their national programs in meeting the challenge of rapidly spreading space technology applications in this area are surveyed. Through an exposition of concrete examples of configuration design and technological adaptations which were carried out in some developing countries, the relevance and opportunities of emerging global trends, technological innovations and application possibilities are discussed.

Title: A taxonomy for the evolution of human settlements on the Moon and Mars
Publication: IAC 1991 congress proceedings, 42nd  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  5–11 October 1991, Montreal, Canada
Abstract:
