The Space Exploration Initiative (SEI) has received much attention over the past five years resulting in indepth technical descriptions of several optional approaches for evolutionary surface systems for the Moon and Mars. However, those surface systems that fully encompass the goals of the SEI are too large in scope and too diverse in needed development skills to be accomphshed by NASA alone. Therefore, the technical evolutionary path must be developed within a taxonomy for partnering that promotes shared interests and shared investments. A partnering taxonomy must contain an institutional dimension as well as a time dimension. In the institutional domain, it must include options for public institutions such as states, other national laboratories, and other nations, as well as private institutions and academic institutions. In the time domain, it must include options for partnering in all phases, including pre-development, development and production, and operations.
Fortunately, a “pure” technical approach to defining the Lunar and Mars surface systems results in characteristics that naturally
promote opportunities for private industry, other national laboratories, and public institutions, both national and international, to participate with NASA. It has components that are non-aerospace related, such as civil engineering, mining, materials processing, and construction engineering, which open new opportunities for collaboration with private industry and other national laboratories. Secondly, surface systems naturally separate into somewhat autonomous zones that can be viewed as a decentralized federation or as an incorporation of profit centers, thereby facilitating cooperative ventures.
Five models of potential cooperation are proposed with varying degrees of automony. Options are suggested for how each partnering model may be integrated with the technical path of the evolution of the surface system. Some models may be best suited for international partners or other United States public institutions, others are best suited for private firms, and some are best suited as a mix of all. The five models proposed are: (1) a customer/provider relationship, which is the standard method of doing business; (2) a service provider where the Government is the sole user of the service with a guaranteed market (e.g., a utility such as supplemental power or rocket propellants); (3) a joint venture where the Government operates the facilities and agrees to provide services to another entity, but the market is non-SEI (e.g., solar-powered satellites constructed of lunar materials or 3He for fusion power); (4) a technology joint-development model, wherein a particular technology has SEI applications as well as terrestrial application, but has favorable retum-on-investment only when considered as a joint-development (e.g., automated mining or construction machines); and finally, (5) a redundancy model, wherein two or more institutions mutually agree to provide identical functional capabilities allowing reduced reliability design requirements to each and, therefore, reduced costs (e.g., emergency power or safe haven retreat).
When these models are overlaid with the technical evolutionary path of the surface systems, they demonstrate a collection of options that neatly nest within the total taxonomy for shared interests and investments by potential non-NASA partners. The taxonomy overlay demonstrates options that range from a total NASA program to one in which NASA retains only emergency, life-critical functions, and all other fonctions are shared or provided by others. As designs continue to mature, it is recommended that this taxonomy be used to communicate options and opportunities for collaboration.

Title: CNSR ROSETTA - SEPCORE : A breakthrough for earth reentry capsule
Publication: IAC 1991 congress proceedings, 42nd  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  5–11 October 1991, Montreal, Canada
Abstract:
The goal of CNSR Rosetta mission is to increase the human knowledge about the comet nucleus properties. The mission will consist, after a space flyby, in a landing on a comet nucleus, in a collection of samples and in a return to Earth with the samples stowed in a capsule performing a direct reentry. After recovery of the capsule, the samples will be analysed in scientific laboratories.
During the system definition study, the preliminary design of the Earth Return Capsule Thermal Protection Subsystem has been performed. Due to high heat flux level encountered during the reentry, a high density ablator has been selected for the heatshield This design leads to a total
mass which did not meet the mass budget requirement and jeopardized the mission.
The SEPCORE® concept has been proposed to reduce the heatshield mass. This concept requires the introduction of a thermal resistant structure. The material with high specific characteristics proposed for the aeroshell is a Ceramic Matrix Composite ( C-SiC SEPCARBINOX® ), and the insulation function is ensured by a lightweight internal multilayer material.
The application of SEPCORE® concept on the CNSR Rosetta Earth Return Capsule allows a 50 % mass saving of the Thermal Protection Subsystem which represents about 20 % of the overall capsule mass. The mass budget established with this design meet the mission requirements.

Authors: ['S. Murayama', 'H. Kobayashi', 'K. Terada', 'M. Sato', 'K. Miyoshi', 'Y. Hayasaka', 'K. Ohnishi']
Title: Development status of the liquid apogee propulsion system
Publication: IAC 1991 congress proceedings, 42nd  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  5–11 October 1991, Montreal, Canada
Abstract:
The Liquid Apogee Propulsion Syste* (LAPS) which is being developed for the Engineering Test Satellite (ETS-VI) is pressure fed. full blowdown bipropellant propulsion systea using Hydrazine (N2R4) and Nitrogen Tetroxide (NTO) as propellant. The development work has completed the critical design review on June ‘90 and Plight Model (FM) is under fabrication at present.
This paper describes the development outlook of LAPS.

Title: High-temperature thruster technology for spacecraft propulsion
Publication: IAC 1991 congress proceedings, 42nd  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  5–11 October 1991, Montreal, Canada
Abstract: A technology program has been underway since 1985 to develop high temperature oxidation-resistant thrusters for spacecraft applications. The successful development of this technology will provide the basis for the design of higher performance satellite engines with reduced plume contamination. Alternatively, this technology program will provide a material with high thermal margin to operate at conventional temperatures and provide increased life for refuelable or reusable spacecraft. The new chamber material consists of a rhenium substrate coated with iridium for oxidation protection. This material increases the operating temperature of thrusters to 2200° C, a significant increase over the 1400° C of the silicide-coated niobium chambers currently used. Stationkeeping class 22 N engines fabricated from iridium-coated rhenium have demonstrated steady state specific impulses 20 to 25 seconds higher than niobium chambers. Ir-Re apogee class 440 N engines are expected to deliver an additional 10 to 15 seconds. These improved performances are obtained by reducing or eliminating the fuel film cooling requirements in the combustion chamber while operating at the same overall mixture ratio as conventional engines. The program is attempting to envelope flight qualification requirements to reduce the potential risks and costs of flight qualification programs.

Title: Human locomotion and workload for simulated lunar and Martian environments
Publication: IAC 1991 congress proceedings, 42nd  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  5–11 October 1991, Montreal, Canada
Abstract:
Human locomotion in simulated lunar and Martian environments is investigated. A unique human-rated underwater treadmill and an adjustable ballasting harness simulate partial gravity in order to better understand how gravity determines the biomechanics and energetics of human locomotion. This study has two research aspects, biomechanics and energetics. The fundamental biomechanics measurements are continuously recorded vertical forces as exerted by subjects on the treadmill which is instrumented with a force platform. Experimental results indicate that peak vertical force and stride frequency decrease as the gravity level is reduced. Foot contact time is independent of
gravity level. Oxygen uptake measurements, VO2, constitute the energetics, or worldoad, data for this study. As theory predicts, locomotion energy requirements for lunar (1/6-g) and Martian (3/8-g) gravity levels are significandy less than at 1-g. The observed variation in workload with gravity level is nonmonotonic, however, in over half the subject population.
The hypothesis is offered that energy expenditure increases for lunar, as compared with Martian, locomotion due to the subject “wasting energy” for stability and posture control in simulated lunar gravity. Biomechanics data could influence advanced spacesuit design and planetary habitat design, while workload data will help define oxygen requirements for planetary life support systems.

Title: Launch cost reduction - How to realize ?
Publication: IAC 1991 congress proceedings, 42nd  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  5–11 October 1991, Montreal, Canada
Abstract:
Launch Cost reduction is an often cited goal for any new launch system - but what are the major criteria to make this highly desirable goal also a reality ? The first part of the paper deals with 'Lessons learned from the Space Shuttle', where very optimistic launch cost figures have been projected in 1972 which - as we know today - have proven as unrealistic. This fact is often mentioned as an argument against any future potential of launch cost reduction. However, the reasons for the Shuttle launch cost growth have be identified and can be avoided for future launch systems. The second chapter defines the elements which are comprised in the term 'launch cost'. It is proposed to use in the future a standardized definition of launch cost, in order to make cost estimations for different vehicle concepts, prepared by different companies and agencies, better comparable. The third chapter deals with the economic vehicle design optimization - replacing the performance optimization which prevailed in the past decades. Here often the vehicle complexity was increased in order to reduce the vehicle size or launch mass which, however, meant only to save some propellants - which are in fact the cheapest and most reliable items on board.
The last part of the paper identifies the vehicle design and cost trends of the future indications some realistic launch cost limits which seem to be achievable for the next generation of launch vehicles. Overly optimistic projections and goals are not really helpful, they may even be counter-productive, damaging the confidence in achieving launch cost reductions in the future.

Title: Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectrometer (MODIS) design evolution and associated development and verification of data product efforts
Publication: IAC 1991 congress proceedings, 42nd  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  5–11 October 1991, Montreal, Canada
Abstract:
The Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectrometer (MODIS) is a key observing facility to be flown on the Earth Observing System (EOS). The facility is composed of two instruments called MODIS-N (nadir) and MODIS-T (tilt). The MODIS-N is being built under contract to NASA by the Santa Barbara Research Center (SBRC). The MODIS-T is being fabricated by the Engineering Directorate at the Goddard Space Flight Center. The MODIS Science Team has defined nearly 40 biogeophysical data products for studies of the ocean and land surface and properties of the atmosphere including clouds that can be expected to be produced from the MODIS instruments shortly after the launch of EOS. The ocean, land, atmosphere, and calibration groups of the MODIS Science Team are now proceeding to plan and implement the operations and facilities involving the analysis of data from existing spacebome, airborne, and in-situ sensors required to develop and validate the algorithms that will produce the geophysical data products.
These algorithm development and validation efforts will be accomplished wherever possible within the context of existing or planned national and international experiments or programs such those in the World Climate Research Program (WCRP).

Title: Robotic vision technology for space station and satellite applications
Publication: IAC 1991 congress proceedings, 42nd  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  5–11 October 1991, Montreal, Canada
Abstract: This paper presents the robotic vision technologies newly developed for satellites and space station robotic applications at the Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence (PAMI) Lab of the University of Waterloo and at the Vision, Intelligence and Robotics Technologies Corporation (Virtek). The first part of the paper describes the use of stereo CCD camera for sensing the deformed shape of a third generation satellite. It addresses the notion of shape interpolation and error reduction. The second presents how the PAMI-Virtek Vision technologies are engineered to support the STEAR ( Space Station, Strategic Technologies in Automation and Robotics Program) sponsored by the Canadian Space Agency.

Title: Segmented rocket demonstration - Historical development prior to their use as space boosters
Publication: IAC 1991 congress proceedings, 42nd  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  5–11 October 1991, Montreal, Canada
Abstract:
In the late fifties it became obvious that the evolution of space exploration programs needed very large rocket motors. Thrust capabilities in the range of several million pounds and duration of over 60 seconds would be required. The best candidates to deliver large thrust appeared to be from solid composite rocket motors. These would be cheaper and faster to develop than corresponding liquid fueled rockets. Because extremely large size motors, loaded with solid propellants, would cause transportation problems from point of production to the launch sites, it was obvious that segmented large rocket motors would eliminate this problem. Assembly would then be performed at the launch site.
This concept was demonstrated at the Aerojet General Corporation facilities in 1957 and was further developed by a U.S. Air Force program in the following years. The demonstration of the feasibility of such an approach led ultimately to the strap-on boosters for the Titan and Shuttle used in U.S.
Space Programs . The advantages of simplified hardware fabrication, smaller production facilities including heat treatment of segments versus full-scale motors for monolithic designs, and conventional propellant manufacture and controls would give greater reliability, less rejection and thus less cost overall. Each segment could be inspected and qualified, provide interexchangeability of segments, and consequently would result in greater flexibility of application.
The program feasibility was initially demonstrated by cutting a 20-inch-diameter Regulus II booster rocket into three pieces and, by means of a lock wire design, made a three-segment rocket. Using the same propellant as in the Regulus booster and attaching the same nozzle, the motor was successfully statically fired. This program was followed with a first- stage Minuteman motor, 65 inches in diameter, which was cut in half and, after again applying a lock wire device, was loaded with propellant and successfully fired.
After these initial demon station in subscale motors, a 100-inch rocket motor program was undertaken. Segmented rocket motors with one, two, three, and five segments were fired. In all cases the joint was working without any problems. Also, fired segments were reconditioned, including the insulation and used in subsequent rocket firing. In the three-segment firing, a Titan engine was strapped onto the rocket in piggyback style in order to see the effect of vibration on the engine. Unfortunately, a nozzle failure cut this firing short by several seconds. In all cases, flight-weight hardware was used. All rockets fired successfully.
The presentation will be highlighted by a number of photographs, a discussion of materials and propellants used, and performance data, including the application of thrust vector control devices using two different liquids for injection to measure their effectiveness. 
The U.S. Air Force sponsored a 100-inch demonstration program, which led ultimately to the development and application of strap-on boosters for the Titan and Shuttle. The experience gained with handling and processing these large motors resulted in several other segmented rocket motor programs with segments of 144 and 156 inch diameters.

Title: Soviet system design for Mars program
Publication: IAC 1991 congress proceedings, 42nd  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  5–11 October 1991, Montreal, Canada
Abstract:
Due to the relative proximity to the Earth as well as to the character of geological evolution, scientific attraction and favourable counditions for the human activity. Mars seems to be the best object to be studied within the next three decades. The first manned planetary vehicle is planned to be despatched to this very planet. From this standpoint the access to qualitatively new information about Mars is urgent
The latest missions to Mars could not give the full picture of the planet. With Mars 1-4, MARINER and VIKING Spacecraft only some 15 0: of the surface of . Mars was investigated with resolution of' about 250 m. The feeble magnetic ~ field necessary to know better the composition of soil and thermal parameters of the planet of Mars is not studied yet. Detailed information about the surface parameters as well as its elementary and mineralogical composition, the nature and dynamics of the Martian atmosphere is also unavailable for us.
Multiple objectives of the planet exploration should be achieved with the realization of the integrated programme.
The programme of the planet exploration with spacecraft includes a number of sequential phases envisaging the Mars samples return to the Earth and provision of data for the future manned missions to this planet.
1st phase.
Mars exploration with the artificial satellites, balloon, small stations and penetrators (possibly a small Mars rover) aimed at locating the most promising areas for the future missions and adjusting means of the Mars rover delivery to the surface.
2nd phase.
Detailed wide-range studies of the selected Mars areas with the Mars rover and collection of soil samples with the adjustment of means for their further return to the Earth
3rd phase.
Collection and return of Mars soil samples to the Earth.

Title: Space station Freedom resource nodes
Publication: IAC 1991 congress proceedings, 42nd  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  5–11 October 1991, Montreal, Canada
Abstract: The Space Station Freedom resource nodes provide primary and backup command, control, and communication centers for the station, as well as berthing, utilities connectivity, and passage between the attached pressurized modules and the orbiter. Functional requirements and allocations for the nodes are presented, including provisions for meeting failure tolerance/redundancy management (FT/ RM) requirements. Separated redundant strings within the first node contribute to single failure tolerance for critical functions. A second control node provides an added command interface. Layouts and diagrams of the nodes are presented, including design rationale. Within each node up to four functional rack positions provide accommodation of command, control, and other equipment for the operation of the station. The design features tilt-out avionics racks and workstations, including provisions for maintenance access. A common interface pattern is defined for attaching elements.

Title: The RADARSAT synthetic aperture radar payload
Publication: IAC 1991 congress proceedings, 42nd  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  5–11 October 1991, Montreal, Canada
Abstract: The Canadian RADARSAT Remote Sensing Satellite will employ a Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) instrument with a very flexible set of operating modes that include selectable swath widths, ground incidence angle and resolution. This SAR instrument will be able to alter its beam pointing angle to anywhere within a 500 km Earth ground track, with either a wide or narrow swath, at ground incidence angles from 20 to 49 degrees. Swath widths of 50, 100, 150 and 500 km will be available as standard configurations but the antenna pattern is reconfigurable in flight to enable other swath widths to be considered. In addition, the SAR instrument will be able to alter the across-track resolution. This paper describes the many design features of the baseline design of the RADARSAT SAR payload that provide the operating flexibility. The projected performance over the mission life will be described including the breadboard model development and performance predictions.

Title: Advanced materials for space structures
Publication: IAC 1990 congress proceedings, 41st  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  6–12 October 1990, Dresden, Germany
Abstract: Potential space structures of the future will have extremely demanding goals in performance, reliability, and affordability. When compared to previous space systems, these systems will require greater accuracy/dimensional stability, longer life, greater survivability to both natural and threat environments, and producibility capability for high volume production. In order to achieve the goals in these areas, advances will be needed in materials and structural concepts. Under a program managed by the Wright Research and Development Center at Wright- Patterson AFB, Ohio, several key material areas have been selected for technology development and validation. These include tribomaterials, structural materials, and materials and techniques for dynamic control of space structures. Tribomaterials efforts involve improvements in bearings, lubricants, and similar materials to provide long life and high accuracy for moving mechanical assemblies, such as gimbals, reaction wheels, and solar array drives. Structural materials programs involve, primarily, reinforced metallic and nonmetallic composites for improvements in performance, weight reduction, and cost reduction. The third area, dynamic control of space structures, involves both active and passive damping, as well as analytical modeling capabilities, to achieve system stability necessary to meet accuracy requirements. Technologies being developed in these areas are considered generic to Space Systems. Materials are being developed either in advance or parallel to systems development in order to provide critical technologies prior to major system design decisions or to reduce systems risk, by providing alternative materials and structures for improved performance, weight reduction, or cost reduction over identified system baseline designs. In order to be cost efficient, maximum effort is extended to leveraging off materials technology development in the aircraft industry and by taking advantage of technology existing in the United Kingdom of Great Britain. Program efforts in these areas concentrate on extending the data base, addressing specific space environmental conditions, and in demonstrating generic product forms for space applications. Specific materials included in the overall program will be covered, and anticipated advantages of the materials will be presented. Product forms fabricated to date and mechanical properties will be presented. In order to qualify these materials for space applications, structural validation programs will be conducted. Potential structural validation programs such as stabilized solar arrays, light weight-stable optical benches and improved thermal radiators will be identified, along with the materials proposed for use in these applications. Anticipated payoffs for these applications will be covered.

Title: Launcher payload carrying assemblies lightweight large composite structures meet multidisciplinary requirements
Publication: IAC 1990 congress proceedings, 41st  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  6–12 October 1990, Dresden, Germany
Abstract:
The upper and payload carrying segments of launchers such as the SPELTRA of Ariane 5 have to provide sufficient stiffness and strength with a minimum mass. There are further requirements related to non structural disciplines such as thermal resistance against aerodynamic heating, external noise reduction to the payload compartment during lift off, and separation of satellites and structure in space. This set of multidisciplinary requirements is satisfied by composite sandwich shell structures with appropriate additional equipments.
This paper describes the design and essential analysis/test processes, which also cover the integrated approach for the different disciplines.
For the composite materials different fibres are selected for different components depending on either stiffness or strength requirements as design drivers.
A trade-off is made between expoxy resins and bismaleimides based on temperature resistance, outgassing, strength and stiffness properties, and impact resistance. Structural shell analyses are carried out via finite difference schemes for stiffness, stress, and buckling, while for local stresses finite element models are established. Towards noise reduction, different options are investigated: structural stiffness tailoring or application of absorber foam. Analytical approaches for structure-acoustic interaction are complemented by experiments based on scaled model tests. The separation system includes an explosive device cutting a notched separation ring. After cutting, the separation is initiated by a set of prestressed kick springs. Besides tests, explosion and cutting processes are analysed via very high frequency mathematical dynamic models while the separation process is investigated by multi-body-systems analysis.
The design, analysis, and test results show the feasibility of the design for the SPELTRA under the given requirements and mass budget. A similar system has been fully flight proven in Martin Marietta's Commercial Titan III flights .

Title: "On orbit" characterisation of communications payloads of Indian national satellite (INSAT-1C)
Publication: IAC 1989 congress proceedings, 40th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  7–13 October 1989, Malaga, Spain
Abstract:
INSAT-1C is a 3-axis stabilized
multiple payload satellite, which
has a design life of seven years.
Its payload comprises of Fixed Satellite
Service(FSS ) operating in C-band,
Broadcast Satellite Service(BSS J operating
in S-band, Data Collection Platform

with its 'Beam Centered' at Nagpur

payloads have been tested extensively

Tests conducted on the payloads

Title: A French study on air breathing launchers: STAR-H
Publication: IAC 1989 congress proceedings, 40th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  7–13 October 1989, Malaga, Spain
Abstract:
7 5 part of the French effort to assess the trends of future space transportation systems, Dassault (AMD-BA) is conducting for CNES a study on TSTO (two stages to orbit) airbreathing launchers (STAR-H), using data coming from a parallel study on hypersonic propulsion performed by SNECMA, SEP and ONERA.
During a first step, this study concentrates on a concept using a recoverable airbreathing first stage and an expendable second stage, concept already presented in the 60s, but allowing to analyse a reference vehicle within reasonable hypotheses on future technological progress.
Analyses performed deal with the main technical areas in order to identify the critical items and drive the future work on concept definition and enabling technologies. Most of the work concentrated on aerodynamics/ aerothermodynamics, structure and materials, propellant storage and management, safety aspects and trajectories.
fig. 1 - TAS 1 (1964 - 1966)
Sensitivity analyses have also been performed for the main design parameters, including propulsion characteristics. First conclusions have been derived from these analyses.
This work focused on a relatively conservative concept, shows the potential benefits of the airbreathing launchers, notably the operational flexibility, but also the very difficult technical challenges to be mastered before these launchers become operational and competitive against current launchers.

Title: Advanced facilities for crystal growth
Publication: IAC 1989 congress proceedings, 40th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  7–13 October 1989, Malaga, Spain
Abstract:
Space experiments on semiconductor crystal growth performed during the last decade clearly indicated the advantages of processing under reduced gravity. At the same time it became clear that the facility standard had to be advanced to allow an optimum use of this unique but expensive environment.
In particular the following performance features are required
- precisely adjustable and stable growth conditions
- diagnostic capabilities to get more insight into the growth process
- a very flexible process control including telescience capabilities
The new generation of european crystal growth facilities is represented by furnace like:
- the Advanced Gradient Heating Facility (AGHF)
- the Paraboloid Ellipsoid Mirror Furnace (ELLI)
- the Zone Melting Facility (ZMF)
The main design features of these facilities as well as performance test results are presented. Based on the technical status of today and the development trends of the last years, advanced facility concepts for the future are outlined.
In particular, a modular design concept for crystal growth furnaces onboard the space station is discussed.

Title: Designing space station FREEDOM for evolution
Publication: IAC 1989 congress proceedings, 40th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  7–13 October 1989, Malaga, Spain
Abstract:
This paper reviews user needs of the future both in terms of R&D users and use of Space Station Freedom to support human missions to the Moon and Mars. Space Station Freedom accommodation requirements are established and feasible configurations presented for both evolution paths.
The results of several trade studies (e.g., module pattern; customer servicing facility) also are discussed. Substantial increases in power (275kw for R&D or 175kw for Lunar/Mars initiative), crew (24 for R&D or 16 for Lunar/Mars) and lab modules (2 full labs and 3 pocket labs for R&D) are required.
The initial Space Station Freedom configuration can evolve to either a mature R&D configuration or a Lunar/Mars Transportation Node. Specific design features required to enable this evolution are still under study.
The enabling technologies for these evolution paths are primarily related to on-orbit assembly, servicing and spacecraft processing for launch. Extensive technology development and demonstration activities will be required in the early years of Space Station Freedom operations.

Authors: ['Eiji Sogame', 'Akira Konno', 'Yoshihiro Torii', 'Kenji Kishimoto', 'Keiichi Hasegawa', 'Akira Okayasu', 'Kenjiro Kalijo']
Title: LE-7 engine development status
Publication: IAC 1989 congress proceedings, 40th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  7–13 October 1989, Malaga, Spain
Abstract:
The development of LE-7, the first stage main engine of H-II launch vehicle, is now at the final stage of the prototype-I phase. Two engines were fabricated and about 40 firing tests were carried out. Accumulated duration of the tests was approximately 370 seconds.
Several technical problems, which had occurred in the breadboard model tests and the fuel turbopump tests before the prototype-I phase, were all resolved successfully. Those results were reflected in the design of the prototype-I engine.
But the development schedule was delayed for one year because of the difficulties in the prototype-I engine, especially in the high speed operation of the fuel turbopump. However, there's a good prospect concerning the development since 95% of the rated thrust was already achieved at the tests.

Authors: ['A. Schock', 'T. Hamrick', 'T. Or', 'V. Sankarankandath', 'M. Shirbachech', 'E. Skrabek']
Title: Mars rover RTG study
Publication: IAC 1989 congress proceedings, 40th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  7–13 October 1989, Malaga, Spain
Abstract:
The paper describes the design and analysis of Radioisotope Thermoelectric Generators (RTGs) for powering the Mars Rover vehicle, which is a critical element of the unmanned Mars Rover and Sample Return mission (MRSR). The RTG design study was conducted by Fairchild Space Company for the U.S. Department of Energy, in support of the Jet Propulsion Laboratory’s MRSR project.
The paper briefly describes a reference mission scenario, an illustrative Rover design and activity pattern on Mars, and its power system requirements and environmental constraints, including the RTG coohng requirements during transit to Mars. It identifies the key RTG design problem, i.e. venting the helium generated by the fuel’s alpha decay without intrusion of the Martian atmosphere into the RTG, and proposes a design approach for solving that problem. Using that approach, it describes and analyzes a variety of RTG designs, all based on the proven and safety-qualified General Purpose Heat Source module.
The first RTG option described is a very conservative baseline design, employing standard thermoelectric unicouples whose reliability and performance stability has been extensively demonstrated on previous space missions. The heat source of the 250-watt RTG consists of a stack of 18 separate modules that is supported at its ends but not along its length. The paper describes and analyzes the structure that holds the stack together during Earth launch and Mars operations, but allows it to come apart in case of an inadvertent reentry.
It then summarizes the baseline RTG’s mass breakdown, and presents a detailed description of its thermal, thermoelectric, and electrical analyses. It examines the effect of different operating conditions (beginning versus end of mission, water-cooled versus radiation-cooled, summer day versus winter night) on the RTG’s performance. Finally, the paper compares the RTGs’ specific powers for different power 1 levels (250W versus 125W), different thermoelectric element j
designs (standard versus short unicouples versus |
multicouples) and different thermoelectric figures of merit i (0.00058K-! to 0.00140K-1).
The results presented show the RTG performance achievable with current technology, and the performance improvements that would be achievable with various technology developments. It provides a basis for selecting the optimum strategy for meeting the Mars Rover design goals with minimal programmatic risk and cost.

Title: Space debris and its utilization
Publication: IAC 1989 congress proceedings, 40th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  7–13 October 1989, Malaga, Spain
Abstract: The space debris hazard is briefly described, and the sources of debris are identified. Debris may be effectively classified into three types: particles, fragments and artifacts. While it is only practicable to limit the hazard due to the third category, it is shown that collisions can generate further debris, so the future total debris population depends largely on the current artifact population. If the future hazard is to be minimised, the artifact population must be limited. A dedicated debris collection vehicle may offer the best method of achieving this and some design aspects an outline of such a vehicle are considered. It is further suggested that the mass of recovered artifacts may permit their utilisation in space tethers for momentum exchange. Other aspects and uses are considered.

Title: Advanced earth sensors for IRS satellite
Publication: IAC 1988 congress proceedings, 39th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  8–15 October 1988, Bangalore, India
Abstract:
The Indian Remote Sensing Satellite IRS-1A was launched in March 1988, carrying remote sensing payloads using Charge Coupled Devices. The satellite is a 3 axis stabilized spacecraft operating in the Polar Sun Synchronous orbit at an altitude of 904 Km. A variety of attitude sensors were used in different phases of the mission for Sun pointing, earth acquisition, attitude control and precise determination of the satellite orientation, New types of design features have been incorporated in these sensors which include earth sensors, Sun sensors, a Star sensor, magnetometer and a dry tuned gyro. The three reaction wheels in the attitude control system are controlled by the earth sensors and the dry tuned gyro. The satellite has completed over six months of its mission life and the day to day operations of the Imaging Payload are being carried out.
This paper deals in detail the functional description of the new earth sensors - (i) Conical Scanning Earth Sensor and (ii) Static Earth Sensor flown on the satellite and their inorbit performance.
The Conical Scanning Earth Sensor incorporates a brushless DC motor with an builtin optical encoder for speed control and pitch reference (Fig.l). The germanium optics accepts the energy in the 14 - 16 micron band with thermistor bolometer,as the detector. The narrow filed of view of the sensor is deflected by 45° and rotated continuously resulting in conical scan pattern. The IR detector senses the transition of space and Earth crossings and the resulting signal is processed to obtain the earth chord which is in turn used in the pitch and roll error determination-. Special features such as automatic Sun/Moon rejection, temperature compensation, thermal control of bearing are incorporated and the optics . and electronics design are optimized to achieve an overall accuracy of better than 0.08° (3 cr- ) .
The Static Earth Sensor (SES) uses the radiation balancing principle in which the radiation signals from four d-iaçrona-T-pôHnts of—-the Earth's infrared horizon are imaged and balanced. The sensor consists of four infrared telescopes mounted on a pyramid shaped base (Fig.2). The telescopes are designed for isothermal operation with double walled construction and 'use heaters in proportional control mode to ensure uniformity and stability of temperature of telescopes. To overcome the errors due to radiation gradient of Earth, special circuits are used in the sensor which measure the local radiation and normalise it by ratio technique so as to make the measurement independent of the absolute radiance. By averaging signals from all four telescopes for determination of roll and pitch errors very low noise error of + 0.02° is achieved. The sensor has a linear range of- + 2.5 and a wide acquisition range of _+ 80°.

Title: An experimental verification of the stability theory for spinning fluid-filled spacecraft
Publication: IAC 1988 congress proceedings, 39th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  8–15 October 1988, Bangalore, India
Abstract:
A large class of spacecraft employ spin stabilisation at some time or other in the course of their orbital operations. Such a stabilisation mode has the inherent advantages of passive stability and attitude "stiffness" provided the inertia ratio about the spin axis can be maintained above unity. This is generally possible with a wide range of useful spacecraft configurations.
There is a strong trend in current spacecraft, however, to carry an increasing quantity of liquid propellants.
Though not necessarily detrimental to spin stability, the presence of bulk fluids in spacecraft calls for careful design and analysis to preserve spin stability even in the face of possible fluid movement in the tanks.

Title: Application of the theory of anisotropic thin-walled beams and plates for wings made from composite material
Publication: IAC 1988 congress proceedings, 39th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  8–15 October 1988, Bangalore, India
Abstract: In considering design problems for aerospace composite structures and obtaining the integral structural characteristics such as eigenfrequencies, critical buckling loads, integral stiffness the choice of a simple one-dimensional and two-dimensional models plays an important part. These models give in some cases the possibility to find out analytical solutions and to evaluate the basic properties of the structures. The paper presents the solutions of divergence problems and static bending problems for anisotropic wings. The wings are modelled as anisotropic thin-walled beams with closed cross-section. The variational principles are used for derivation the governing equations. We pay special attention to the coupled torsion-bending effects. The influence of anisotropic tailoring on the critical devergence speed of the wing is Investigated analytically. Two-dimensional plate-like models are applied to analysis and design problems for wings of small aspect-ratio. Optimum orientation of the axes of anisotropy for the wing skin is calculated by the successive optimization method. The paper is based on the results [1-3]

Title: Communication payloads for INSAT-II
Publication: IAC 1988 congress proceedings, 39th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  8–15 October 1988, Bangalore, India
Abstract: The INSAT-II series of satellites v/ill have new features such as operation in extended C-band frequencies, high cross-polarization to enable co-location of satellites, and addition of a search and rescue 406 MHz data relay package. The paper lists the major payloads, and discusses in detail the design of the C-band FSS transponders. The major design considerations for the receiver, demux and mux filters, antennas and input/output filters are highlighted. Then the other payloads such as BSS transponder, Data Collection System (DCS) transponder. Satellite Aided Search and Rescue (SAS&R) transponder and the Very High Resolution Radiometer (VHRR) transmitter are described briefly. Major overall specifications for each of these transponders are given. Also given are the schematic block diagram of the overall communication payload,frequency plan and the primary coverage area requirement.

Authors: ['R. Gopalaswani', 'S. Gollakota', 'P. Venugopalan', 'M. Nagarathinam', 'A. Sivathanu Pillai']
Title: Concept definition and design of a single-stage-to-orbit launch vehicle-hyperplane
Publication: IAC 1988 congress proceedings, 39th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  8–15 October 1988, Bangalore, India
Abstract:
A new concept for flight to orbit is described in this paper. It involves mass addition to an ascending air-breathing, hypersonic lifting vehicle. General laws for flight to orbit with ma» addition are developed, and it is shown that payload capabilities one order of magnitude higher than even the most advanced rocket launchers is feasible.
Detailed concept definition and design studies are presented for this new hydrogen fuelled, horizontal take off, fully reusable single stage hypersonic vehicle, called'HYPBRPLANE’. The studies include results from over 5000 trajectory optimisation runs on an interactive mission analysis computer model; an analysis of various propulsion options; and design and performance optimisation of an air collection system for mass addition inflight.

Title: Current status of deployment research for a SETI space-based antenna system
Publication: IAC 1988 congress proceedings, 39th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  8–15 October 1988, Bangalore, India
Abstract: Space-based antenna systems for the search of signals from extraterrestrial intelligence were first proposed in the mid-seventies. Tentative performance specifications for systems to be built in the early part of the next century were established. Preliminary system design and mission analysis studies led to the consideration of solar-sailing transfer of principal components from the orbit of fabrication (at synchronous altitude) to the operational location (at the Sun-Earth transterrestrial libration point, at a distance of 1,500,000 km beyond Earth on the Sun-Earth line) in the eel iptic pl'ane. The principal purpose of this paper is to present the mathematical formulation of the solar-sailing transfer problem. Partial solutions of this problem involving Earth escape and close flyby of the operational location are also discussed. The relevance of these solutions to current work on the mathematically complex and numerically demanding problem of optimal control for component deployment of a SETI space-based antenna system operating in the vicinity of the Sun-Earth transterrestrial libration point is indicated.

Title: Engineering ground rules for development of a microgravity facility
Publication: IAC 1988 congress proceedings, 39th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  8–15 October 1988, Bangalore, India
Abstract:
This paper deals with the engineering guidelines and ground rules that allow turning a collection of homogeneous scientific requirements ("user requirements") into a microgravity facility capable of performing within the limits and constraints of its space carrier.
Over many years of industrial activity, payload development has shifted from the early pioneering approach to a well-organized effort.
Design modularity, adoption of standard and already qualified parts and equipment, and a greater reliance on experience-based engineering analysis are becoming standard practice in the design of multiuser, multipurpose facilities.
These have to be easier to operate, to reconfigure and to repair than ever before, despite their increased complexity due to flexibility and versatility.
The experience gained during previous flights and the broad range of flight opportunities (from parabolic flights and sounding rockets to SpaceLab) have taught us how to exploit widely varying and complex missions and operating conditions. Consequently, microgravity facility design is already underway in anticipation of the availability of the International Space Station/Columbus.
Therefore, already being faced and implemented (very often simultaneously) at an early design phase for present/future microgravity facilities are concepts such as telescience (teleoperation, data collection/reduction/transmission for ground visibility, automation), crew time savings and proficient usage, facilily-to-facility and facility-to-environmcnt interferences avoidance, resource consumption reduction, samples and consumables management and recycling, refurbishment maintenance and repair.

Title: Qualification programme of IRS fordynamic environment
Publication: IAC 1988 congress proceedings, 39th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  8–15 October 1988, Bangalore, India
Abstract: An overview of the development and execution of a comprehensive programme for qualifying IRS-1A spacecraft for dynamic environment, at system and subsystem levels, is presented. The evolution of mechanical configuration of the spacecraft, its structural design, fabrication, analysis and testing issues and the interaction of these are covered. The parallel developmental efforts in fabrication, analysis and testing which contributed to the success of the qualification programme are also highlighted.

Title: Range ambiguity suppression technique for the spaceborne synthetic aperture radar
Publication: IAC 1988 congress proceedings, 39th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  8–15 October 1988, Bangalore, India
Abstract:
The aim of any spaceborne Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) system design is to keep the range
ambiguous responses as low as possible. A higher value of range ambiguity deteriorates the SAR image quality. The wider swath requirement at
higher incidence angle ( ^ >t5°) deteriorates the range ambiguity ratio (RAR) and hence the image quality of SAR quite significantly. The requirement of minimum acceptable RAR even for very nominal swath at these incidence angles may necessitate larger antenna width, very complex weighting and
highly asymmetrical antenna elevation pattern. An alternate scheme is suggested in this paper to alleviate the criticality and complexity of the design aspects for such a requirement. Here the
chirp slope of the transmitted linear frequency modulated (LFM) pulses is reversed alternately. Hence, during the range compression significant portion of the ambiguous return is suppressed due to the mismatching with the signal reference function. The proposed method provides significant improvement in RAR and can be utilized in attaining wider swath, specifically at higher incidence angles.

Authors: ['Barbara F. Lujan', 'Ronald J. White', 'Joel I. Leonard', 'R. Srini Srinivasan']
Title: Terrestrial implications of mathematical modeling developed for Space Biomedical Research
Publication: IAC 1988 congress proceedings, 39th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  8–15 October 1988, Bangalore, India
Abstract: The history of computer modeling and systems analysis in NAS A ’ s Life Sciences Program began with the use of models describing human thermoregulation to help design cooling systems for space suits, and it continues up to the present period where artificial intelligence systems are being sought that can someday be used for medical care on a space station, lunar colony, or on a planetary voyage. This paper summarizes several related research projects supported by NASA which seek to apply computer models to space medicine and physiology. These efforts span a wide range of activities, including: mathemadcal models used for computer simulations of physiological control systems; power spectral analysis of physiological signals; pattern recognition models for detection of disease processes; and, computer-aided diagnosis programs. The present paper will concentrate on only the first of these activities and a companion paper (Paper IAF-IAA- 88-504) will focus on the others.

Title: The liquid propellant rocket project - A key space education resource
Publication: IAC 1988 congress proceedings, 39th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  8–15 October 1988, Bangalore, India
Abstract:
For many years, private experimental rocket organizations and certain educational institutions have been designing, fabricating, and launching small, high performance rockets for numerous scientific and educational purposes. Although the sophistication of the launch vehicles and payloads has at times been impressive, the propulsion systems have, with few exceptions, used solid propellants. Reasons for the dominant use of solids are many, and the challenge of liquid propulsion has kept the total number of experimental liquid flight tests in the U.S. in single figures. The use of solids, particularly Micrograin, has matured to the point that most experimental rocket propulsion systems are simply a means to an end, and are not the primary focus of a given project. However, the knowledge and skills developed in successfully prosecuting a liquid rocket project that culminates with a launch will be extremely valuable to graduate engineers entering the aerospace work force. The fulfillment of various national space goals world-wide over the next thirty years will be largely dependent on the design of effective liquid propulsion systems by the students of today. To achieve these space goals, student engineers need the practical, hands- on learning a carefully planned liquid rocket project provides.
This paper examines the important contributions a liquid propellant rocket project can make to the education process of students in college - level aerospace and astronautical engineering curriculums.
The value of this educational tool is first discussed in relation to the near term requirements of the space industry. A survey of some past liquid rocket projects is provided to give examples of the broad design spectrum available to the educator. A typical project is then described, illustrating the project scope required to meet educational objectives, as well as the educational benefits each student is expected to receive. Finally, some valuable resources that are available to support educational rocket courses are highlighted, and recommendations are made on how this significant learning program could be "sold" to colleges and universities around the world.

Title: The unified information system concept
Publication: IAC 1988 congress proceedings, 39th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  8–15 October 1988, Bangalore, India
Abstract:
Space transportation systems have become so complex and involved that information from their design, production, and operations phase activities must be highly interconnected, integrated, and appropriately presented if a cost effective and highly operable launch system is to be built.
This paper describes the Advanced Launch System (ALS) Unified Information System (Unis) which will extend from the launch vehicle to the operations, logistics, manufacturing sites, and initial sources of requirements. Recent advances in information technologies will allow for the design and implementation of such a system.
We describe the overall Unis development approach which is to utilize traditional and rapid prototyping techniques to produce both a prototype and a full-scale Unis. Unis prototype requirements and a system baseline are discussed in detail. This system baseline consists of a collection of inter-networked work groups or clusters. A Cluster consists of a network of personal workstations, conference workstations, and support hardware and software. Features of pre-prototype systems, implemented during the ALS conceptual design activity, are described. We describe our full scale implementation plan complete with data analysis, architecture development, and technology demonstration activities is also described.

Title: US space station Freedom: Orbital assembly and early mission opportunities
Publication: IAC 1988 congress proceedings, 39th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  8–15 October 1988, Bangalore, India
Abstract:
This paper describes the U.S. Space Station launch and assembly sequence and the mission support capabilities available in man-tended and permanently manned modes. Design and operational constraints, affecting launch package configurations and orbital deployment and assembly, are defined. The resulting flight configurations and associated payload accommodations are described with emphasis on the early flights through man-tended capability. The initial mission objectives will emphasize engineering data collection (structural, thermal, power, control, propulsion, etc.) to verify design and to calibrate system models and simulation tools. On-board information will be used to characterize the microgravity, electromagnetic, particulate, and other environmental features for the benefit of Space Station users. Early flight configurations will provide accommodations for attached payloads which may include experimentation in materials exposure, solar physics, and earth and stellar observations. These mission payloads, once installed and initialized by the Shuttle flight crews, will be operated by ground control from their mission specialists.
When the pressurized laboratory is added, the mission emphasis will shift to microgravity experimentation including material processing and manufacturing research, life sciences, and supporting technology research and development. These missions will be operated in a man-tended mode. Installation, real-time operation, and servicing will be performed by Shuttle flight crews during periodic visits; a combination of ground control and automatic modes will be used between Shuttle flights. As Station build-up continues, resources available for payloads will also increase. With the achievement of the permanently manned capability, continuous crew support will be available for mission activities.
This paper summarizes each step of this build-up process and the capabilities available for Station operation and payload activities versus time.

Title: Design of a new attitude measurement and control system for satellite in geosynchronous orbit using stars detection reference
Publication: IAC 1987 congress proceedings, 38th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  10–17 October 1987, Brighton, United Kingdom
Abstract:
The purpose of this paper is to describe a new concept of attitude measurement for satellite control in geosynchronous orbit applicable for various missions.
The principle is to use two-axis CCD-based star sensors as inertial detectors to get a three-axis detection and to improve pointing budgets in normal mode. The characteristics of the sensor are those of the SED12 developed by MATRA & SODERN under a CNES contract.
Two star sensors, whose field of view are 7 per 9 degrees, are placed 120° away from each other.
In these conditions, the four measurements are sensitive to roll, pitch, yaw as well as to the position in orbit. With a precise on-board orbital model, we can split the three attitude angles and provide a yaw detection. That is new and important for special applications - Inter Satellite Link, Large Satellites.
Pointing budgets are improved with respect to Earth-sensor based measurement assemblies in normal mode and remain unchanged for the station-keeping in spite of the gyroless detection and thanks to the sensor high resolution. The use of star sensors in a three-axis transfer is attractive : manoeuver flexibility and extended launch window.
No gyro information is required in operational tnodes-normal mode, station keeping. The reliability of the whole system is then increased, as no more mechanical part is in motion during the mission.
The major drawback of this system is the software complexity. The low bandwidth, typ. 1 Hz, requires particular algorithms - good state predictor, Kalman filter. Additionally, star catalogue management and possibly star pattern recognition algorithms shall be on-board processed.
Implementation of star sensors on the platform can also be difficult because of the size of their baffles. Studies have been performed for the EUROSTAR case.
Studies and tests have also been performed to ensure the radiation assessment of the optical parts and the CCD matrix during ten years lifetime in geosynchronous environment. Optical parts are not affected and the CCD matrix seems to resist to such an environment.

Title: Design of future cryogenic tanks
Publication: IAC 1987 congress proceedings, 38th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  10–17 October 1987, Brighton, United Kingdom
Abstract:
Starting from experience acquired by AEROSPATIALE on space projects such as ARIANE launcher.or future launch system (ESA contract), this paper presents the major trends for the design of reusable cryogenic tanks in future space transportation systems.
Besides general system studies on future STS, AEROSPATIALE has begun research and development activities on critical topics, such as reusable cryogenic tanks.

Title: Development of small LOX/LH2 rocket engine
Publication: IAC 1987 congress proceedings, 38th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  10–17 October 1987, Brighton, United Kingdom
Abstract:
A small liquid hydrogen (LH2) and liquid oxygen (LOX) expander cycle rocket engine tests have been successfully conducted in IHI Aioi rocket testing center in March, 1987.
The rocket engine is considered for a 1-ton class upper stage and an orbit transfer vehicle (OTV) applications. This study was continued by IHI company -fund since 1983.
The results of the tests show the validity of the design and fabrication of the small engine.
Data of the start-up characteristics, stable conditions and the performances in the some vacuum condition were also obtained.
The current engine arrangements are available for the thrust-up, power-up and high performance for the wide needs such as an upper stage engine, orbiter transfer vehicle engine and so on.

Title: Electrical current flow across the TSS: The core equipment and other related technical issues
Publication: IAC 1987 congress proceedings, 38th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  10–17 October 1987, Brighton, United Kingdom
Abstract:
This paper»Tocuses on those design aspects of the first Tethered Satellite System mission (TSS-1) which are relevant to future electrodynamic applications of the tether concept, particularly for power and thrust generation purposes. Indeed, the first mission of the Tethered Satellite System will he electrodynamic in character, because the conducting tether permits electric current to flow across the TSS.
Most Investigations will be aimed at measuring parameters describing natural and induced phenomena taking place in the ionospheric plasma. The electrical current flow across the TSS is essential for Inducing phenomena such as Alfven and EM wave radiation, charge collection and wake perturbations. The study of such induced perturbations is relevant to the understanding of the possible energy loss mechanisms associated with power generation by means of tether systems.
The TSS-l Core Equipment is a set of basic support instrumentation whose purpose is to permit, monitor and (to some extent) control the electric current flow through the tether. TSS-1 and, particularly, Core Equipment development may, therefore, he seen as an introductory but realistic exercise to gain the sort of systematic knowledge required before future power/thrust generation applications can proceed. This paper is organized as follows: section 1 contains a cursory look at the current TSS project and at the present and perspective applications of the tether concept itself; section 2 describes the TSS-1 Core Equipment while In section 3 some technical and scientific problems relevant to the
use of tether systems for power and thrust generation are examined. Section 11 eventually summarizes the experience gained from the TSS-1 project and the activities needed for technological use of electrodynamic tethers.

Title: Microgravity fluid science facilities operation
Publication: IAC 1987 congress proceedings, 38th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  10–17 October 1987, Brighton, United Kingdom
Abstract:
From a users point of view: "The various topics and different requirements covered by the Fluid Science Facilities (FSF) lead to operational needs that will eventually be auto-defined during the Facilities use itself."
This means that the FSF must be able to dynamically evolve and to suit requirements that will be defined during Facilities development and/or use, in accordance with the findings and the needs that will arise from the very same results of the experiments performed in an initial configuration. Another peculiar aspect of FSF (in comparison with other Experimental Facilities) is related to the nature of the fluid experiments. In the experiments relating to the physics of fluids, the data must be retrieved during the experiment itself. Furthermore, sometimes the controls, diagnostics, and stimuli must be applied with interactive strategies (i.e., those that depend upon the evolution of the experiment). These pecuharities differ significantly from other fields and disciplines for which experiments lead to the production of specimens that will be analyzed later, in other environments (e.g. crystals produced in space that are successively analyzed and characterized in laboratories on ground). The need of Real Time operations (experiment conduction, elaboration and analysis) motivates the interest of Tele-Science methodology, that for a FSF is much more urgent than for other areas. The limited experience with Spacelab Missions should be reviewed to identify alternate choices and operational trends that will eventually lead to an optimization of the FSF design and management to be even more user dependent and user friendly.

Title: Remote sensing the land of east and southern Africa
Publication: IAC 1987 congress proceedings, 38th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  10–17 October 1987, Brighton, United Kingdom
Abstract:
The demand for natural resources data, and for the requisite specialized services in surveying and mapping resulted in the establishment of the Regional Centre for Services in Surveying, Mapping and Remote Sensing(RCSSMRS) in Nairobi, Kenya in 1975. Since 1977 a remote sensing programme has been developed to serve some of the regional needs in training, user support and project design and implementation. This programme is now very much concerned with the application of remote sensing to crop forecasting, forest resources mapping, map revision, and other aspects of natural resources data collection and management. This paper examines training, user products and projects in which they are successfully employed.
In many applications, the satellite data are used as a substitute for a map.
This passive function can be exploited to organize existing field survey teams and use them more effectively. Mapping techniques are found to be effective for scales in the range 1:100,000 to 1 million. Large area mosaics provide valuable context for many regional features. For field assessments of crops, forest or other natural resources, the use of satellite images proved particularly valuable, both for field use and for compiling final results.

Title: Selected advanced technology studies for the US space station
Publication: IAC 1987 congress proceedings, 38th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  10–17 October 1987, Brighton, United Kingdom
Abstract:
Boeing has completed a 21-month concept definition and preliminary design phase in support of Marshall Space Flight Center (MSFC) in Huntsville, Alabama. MSFC is responsible for managing Work Package 1 (WP-01) of the U.S.
Space Station. WP-01 is one of four Space Station work packages. It includes the
Habitation and Laboratory Modules, the Connecting Node Structure, the ECLSS and Internal Thermal Subsystems, and the Logistics Elements.
During the concept definition and preliminary design phase, numerous advanced technology
developments were completed. This paper reports the results of three of the more significant studies completed by Boeing.
Water reclamation is a critical operation for the station because of logistics weight
constraints and the criticality to crew satisfaction and safety. Water reclamation
techniques were developed using multifiltrat i on methods and reverse osmosis with both
longitudinal hollow fibers and spiral wound sheet structures. We have also conducted studies to characterize shower waste water preparatory to determining proper methods of water reclamation.
The pressurized modules are designed with micrometeorite/debris shields to reduce the
probability of penetration. Although there is a low probability of penetration, it is possible and we have tested methods of on-orbit repair using the Neutral Buoyancy Test Facility at MSFC.
The structural weight of the pressurized
modules is critical. A unique waffle grid structure was selected based on weight, stiffness and cost considerations. A full scale flight weight, flight quality prototype pressurized
module was fabricated in the MSFC Productivity Enhancement Facility using a computer controlled welding system.

Title: Space suit systems - technical and physiological constraints
Publication: IAC 1987 congress proceedings, 38th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  10–17 October 1987, Brighton, United Kingdom
Abstract:
This paper indicates the major issues pertinent to the design of a space suit system, and discusses the associated technical and physiological constraints. Prebreathing, required to prevent decompression sickness is strongly influenced by the change of nitrogen partial pressure and change of atmosphere composition, the astronaut experiences prior to EVA. Competing design drivers such as suit pressure and mobility as well as the critical design features of both the pressure garment and life support system are discussed. Safety aspects concerning human's hygiene and comfort are being indicated.
The close physiological relationship between diving and astronautics aids in the understanding of the physiological constraints of a space suit system. The transfer of techniques and knowledge between diving and space suit seems to promise fruitful results.
When the astronaut leaves the higher pressure of his spacecraft he has to undergo adequate decompression to prevent nitrogen bubble formation which may cause decompression sickness known as the "bends'. This condition requires hyperbaric treatment with pressure and oxygen. Based on the evaluationary process in EVA - with special emphasis on the pressure levels - the various concepts for accomplishing human adaptation are outlined and are available as guidelines for the design of a future space suit system.

Title: Space transportation architecture study overview
Publication: IAC 1987 congress proceedings, 38th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  10–17 October 1987, Brighton, United Kingdom
Abstract:
This paper covers the scope of the Space Transportation Architecture Study (STAS), summarizes the findings derived to date from this multi-task effort, and indicates its relationship to the recently initiated heavy-lift launch vehicle definition effort.
The study is being jointly funded and directed by the Department of Defense (DoD) and NASA. Purposes of the study are to identify attractive architectural and transportation system options, establish technology road maps and decision points for the implementation of the next generation of space transportation systems, and prepare conceptual design definitions, programmatic data, and technology plans for selected mid-to-late 1990s transportation systems. This STAS overview covers the mission model sets considered and the resulting preferred architecture options. Trends and findings to date are presented along with specific observations relative to requirements for future launch vehicles.

Title: Spacecraft technology trends: A view from the past
Publication: IAC 1987 congress proceedings, 38th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  10–17 October 1987, Brighton, United Kingdom
Abstract: Future spacecraft will be sent on missions to complete the exploration of the solar system, to return samples from celestial bodies, record the process of creation of stars, galaxies, and the universe itself, to provide a continuous record of Earth processes, and to maintain vital space communications. A key ingredient to pro- jecting the future is to comprehend the historic record and to understand the significance of trends. This paper focuses on spacecraft cost and life trends, as well as those of the major subsystems. Throughout the history of the "space age" there has been significant progress in the performance of spacecraft and their subsystems. However, variouâ* aspects of spacecraft performance lag behind what is technically feasible by a considerable margin. In addition, examination of the historical trend implies that future spacecraft will likely continue to be relatively unique in their design features. This is in contrast to the technically realizable future attributes such as large space platforms, modularity, system autonomy and on- orbit repair and servicing.

Title: A new approach of POGI phenomenon three-dimensional studies on the Ariane 4 launcher
Publication: IAC 1986 congress proceedings, 37th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  4–11 October 1986, Innsbruck, Austria
Abstract:
A pump-fed version of the current Orbit Maneuvering Subsystem (OMS) engine will increase engine performance and provide significant benefits for the NASA Space Transportation System (STS). These benefits include: (1) increased shuttle payload capability, (2) additional excess OMS propellant for scavenging and use in other systems, and (3) a high performance man-rated, storable engine for upper stage applications. A program has been initiated with the objectives to conduct the trade studies and design efforts necessary to define the preferred uprated OMS engine characteristics, and to fabricate and test critical components to demonstrate feasibility of the performance, life and operational goals.
Program scope consists of five (5) major tasks to be completed over a 19 month period. These tasks are summarized as follows: Task I - Engine definition study which includes engine/system integration, engine trade studies, turbopump configuration study and component arrangement,
Task II - Injector program consisting of Injector and cooled test combustion chamber design and fabrication, and injector testing and analysis, Task III - Turbopump program encompassing bearing and seal evaluation, turbopump assembly design fabrication and tests, Task IV - Thrust chamber program encompassing design, materials and manufacturing evaluation and Task V - a final engine system design update. Important to successful completion of this program are the trade studies performed during the engine system and major component design tasks. The Task I engine definition trade studies have been completed. Component designs are complete and the program is now in the early fabrication phase. Completion of this phase will lead to demonstration tests which will validate designs evolved from the trade studies.

Title: A proposed comet nucleus penetrator for the comet rendezvous asteroid flyby mission

Abstract:
