Title: Assessment of existing and future launch vehicle liquid engine development
Publication: IAC 1986 congress proceedings, 37th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  4–11 October 1986, Innsbruck, Austria
Abstract:
Recent expansion of spacecraft utilization for earth observation requires more economical spacecraft bus applicable to a wide variety of missions. In Japan, Engineering Test Satellite-Ill (ETS-III), 385kg three axis stabilized satellite carrying a vidicon camera, was launched successfully in 1982. Maritime Observation Satellite-1, which has the weight of 750kg and equipped with multispectrum electronic self-scanning radiometer (MESSR), visible and thermal infrared radiometer (VTIR), microwave scanning radiometer (MSR), etc., is now under development and will be launched in 1986 to make some experiments on sea surface observation. These satellites are relatively small comparing with future spacecraft and it was adequate to design as a uniquely-built spacecraft. However, as the spacecraft becomes larger, the conventional design approach of uniquely-built spacecraft has some disadvantage on integration, checkout and tests due to the complicated work of checking local parts, the capacity limitation of the test facilities, etc.
One of the practical solutions for these problems is a modular design.
Presently, we are in an advanced stage of spacecraft applications. Japanese Earth Resources Satellite-1 (ERS-1) is in the preliminary design phase and a next generation satellite for earth observation is now planned. We are required to develop the structures which have high performance for the installation of mission equipments and testability, in addition to the weight minimization efforts. Under these circumstances, to establish the basic technology for ERS-1 and future spacecraft, we developed a modular frame structure fabricated of CFRP and performed the structural tests such as modal survey, sinusoidal vibration and acoustic tests to verify the design. We adopted a new approach for the vibration test, i.e. module vibration tests, to deal successfully with the limitation of current shaker capacity. And we selected acoustic test to verify the high frequency design. The developed structure has high potential for future spacecraft due to easy handling and good testability. Based on our research and development results, we discuss the design, analyses, fabrication and tests of the modular frame structure in this paper.

Title: Challenges for space station logistics transportation
Publication: IAC 1986 congress proceedings, 37th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  4–11 October 1986, Innsbruck, Austria
Abstract:
The development of advanced aerospace vehicles has been typified by the use of high pressure propulsion systems. Earlier propulsion system technology typically operated at chamber pressures below 1000 psig (60.4 Kg/cm2) and gas generators/compressed gas systems below 3000 psig (211 Kg/cm2). Current systems like the Space Shuttle Main Engine (SSME) operate at chamber pressures of 3000 psig and gas generator/pump discharge systems up to 8000 psig (562 Kg/cm2). This trend towards higher pressure propulsion systems has resulted in higher operating efficiency, lighter engine weight per pound of thrust and a smaller physical envelope.
The higher engine pressures require careful design consideration and extensive testing including overstress-limits tests, to ensure meeting design goals. A primary requirement for high pressure systems is adequate sealing. Static seals must operate from -423°F to 4000°F (-253 to 2204°C) at pressures up to 8000 psig. Rotating seals must operate from -423°F to 2000 °F (-253 to 1093°C) at pressures up to 8000 psig. The design of seals to withstand these conditions throughout the entire engine mission life and environmental conditions propose a major challenge to designers.

Title: Continuous path control of space manipulators mounted on OMV
Publication: IAC 1986 congress proceedings, 37th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  4–11 October 1986, Innsbruck, Austria
Abstract: The authors previously proposed a new fabrication method of closeout for a regeneratively cooled thrust chamber, the CIP (Cold Isostatic Pressing) forming method, by which a low stiffness closeout is easily obtained. In this study, sintered aluminum alloy was chosen as a porous closeout material which had relatively a lower Young's modulus and a lighter weight. The forming conditions of the porous closeout and its elastic and plastic behaviors were investigated. Then the fatigue life of the high pressure chamber cooled by liquid hydrogen with the sintered aluminum alloy closeout was analyzed by means of non-linear FEM (Finite Element Method). The results showed that the optimum design condition for a long-life rocket thrust chamber could be achieved with a low-stiffness closeout consisting of a CIP formed aluminum alloy layer with a porosity of 17% and a TFE (polytetrafluoroethylene) insulation layer with a thickness of 20 mm. The chamber with this lowstiffness closeout had a prolonged fatigue life three times longer than that of a conventional chamber with an electroformed nickel closeout.

Title: NASA's robotic servicing role for space station
Publication: IAC 1986 congress proceedings, 37th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  4–11 October 1986, Innsbruck, Austria
Abstract:
The continuous trend to larger, heavier and retrievable spacecraft demands a new generation of stronger and stiffen masts in order to support large deployable structures. Such an Extendable and Retractable Mast was already built at DORNIER as a radio link mast for ground application (Fig. 1). By developing and refining that principle and adaption to the specific space requirements a design satisfying a wide range of requirements could be realized.
Two main space applications for an Extendable and Retractable Mast (ERM), the deployment of a Solar Array and positioning of an Unfurlable Antenna are presently proposed. Under ESA contract, Dornier System has elaborated an ERM design that establishes the basis for a mast family to cover a wide range of user demands (Fig. 2).

Title: Prospects for advanced rocket-powered launch vehicles
Publication: IAC 1986 congress proceedings, 37th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  4–11 October 1986, Innsbruck, Austria
Abstract:
Recent studies advent the use of solar thermal propulsion schemes as a way to provide a relatively high Isp and low thrust for application in orbital maneuvering situationsl1’2"3]. This would allow for greater capabilities in transferring satellites, large space structures and other payloads from Low earth orbit to a geosynchronous orbit. Because of the interest in the development of such a thruster, a heoretical model was determined to describe the energy transport throughout the solar collection chamber. The theory was developed as a steady-state one-dimensional heat transfer model with the interaction of conduction, convection and radiation modes of energy transport within the absorption chamber. The model was used to determine the thruster performance and efficiency.
The complex absorption chamber concept was determined by Shojil1! as an advanced thruster design for increased payload capabilities. The design of the solar concentrators, which supplies a fixed amount of solar energy to the absorption chamber, was considered to be a separate design problem and not considered in the analytical modeling. The heat transfer model was used to simulate the solar absorption chamber characteristics, which allowed for the various thruster geometries to be considered. The model assumed that all the solar flux received by the solar concentrator was uniformly distributed throughout the chamber. In the solar absorption design, a working fluid was introduced radially from the outer region of the chamber, heat was transferred from a simulated particle bed to the fluid by convection. Heat was also transferred throughout the chamber by conduction and radiation energy transport between the particle layers.

Title: Satellite navigation by stellar refraction (comparison of simulation results with first experiments and analysis of benefits for potential users)
Publication: IAC 1986 congress proceedings, 37th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  4–11 October 1986, Innsbruck, Austria
Abstract:
The purpose of this paper is to report technological developments for 2D-deployable, planar, tension-stabilized large membrane space structures, such as the solar cell array, the space radar, and the solar sail vessel. Since the concept of 2D-deployable array has been presented at 1980 IAF Congress, the studies on the 2D-deployable array systems and relating studies continue at ISAS. The major efforts of developments are focused on the design of blankets and the design of systems including the deployment mechanisms. The marked progress has been made in regard to the fabrication method of large blankets. It
provides the method that the blanket can be fabricated in a small facility, that the blanket is made in a folded state, and that the resulted package is a 2D-deployable structure. In order to promote the development of the 2D- array system, an experimental mission on board a space flyer unit is planned and the outline of the mission is described.

Title: The policy framework for space commercialization: Distinguishing rhetoric and reality
Publication: IAC 1986 congress proceedings, 37th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  4–11 October 1986, Innsbruck, Austria
Abstract:
The recently completed Space Station Human Productivity Study was an unprecedented analysis with the objective of establishing the integrated set of design and operational requirements that need to be met to maximize crew proficiency over their 90-day staytime on orbit. This study was conducted in response to NASA's key program objectives, "....to use man in a highly productive way....in a vigorous, creative, stimulating environment"....in order to be "customer friendly and dedicated to fulfilling customer needs...."
Traditional human factors and human engineering topics and important social and behavioral topics were included in the study. The study encompassed topics such as architecture, traffic patterns, decor, anthropometry, windows, stowage, internal environments, lighting, acoustics, safety, health maintenance, medical care, recreation, personal hygiene, food and water, housekeeping, waste management, restraints, mobility aides, communications, quality assurance, clothing, vibration, training, maintainability, tools, activity planning and scheduling, organization, autonomy, work stations, and data management.
These topical areas were analyzed to determine the requirements that could be justified based on historical evidence. Requirements that could not be justified were highlighted as issues. Over 200 of these issues were identified. Pians for resolving each of these issues were then prepared.
The results of the study included a requirements document and a set of management plans for resolving the issues.
KEY WORDS
Space Station Human Productivity Space Station Crew Interface Human Factors
Space Soeial/Behavioral Sciences Human Engineering

Title: A brief history of the first US JATO flight tests of August 1941
Publication: IAC 1985 congress proceedings, 36th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  7–12 October 1985, Stockholm, Sweden
Abstract:
This paper describes a simple antenna despun spacecraft with high efficiency GaAs solar cells for communications application. The spacecraft is planned for use of the coming generation of the Japanese domestic communications satellite (CS-3).
Most of recent communications satellites are of either 3-axis stabilized type with large solar wings or spin stabilized type with expandable solar cylinders. The size of solar arrays is important to satisfy the power requirement, which has been increasing as the increase of communications capacity per spacecraft.
The spacecraft described in this paper is designed by a different approach: i.e. to achieve high level of primary solar power by using high efficiency solar cells with limited area of solar arrays. The spacecraft has other design features also; i.e. the use of light weight CFRP main body structure and light weight electronics design including the use of MIC’s. The spacecraft is compatible with the Japanese H-I launch vehicle.
GaAs solar cells to be used for the spacecraft are expected to have an average efficiency of 17.5% at the beginning of life and 14.5% after 7 years in the geostationary orbit. The solar array consists of approximately 37,000 pieces of GaAs solar cells of 2 cm X 2 cm in size. The cells'are placed on light weight KFRP A1 honeycomb substrate panels by the shingle mount method. This provides an efficient use of the array area with respect to solar power generation. The output power available from the solar array is expected to be about 840 W at EOL equinox (7 years).
The main body (central cylinder) of the spacecraft consists of a single body CFRP cone fabricated by the filament winding method. The spacecraft has two equipment platforms supported by the cylinder, on one of which are held communication modules, and spacecraft bus electronics and the propulsion subsystem are placed on the other platform.
The spacecraft has a dry mass of approximately 470 kg, of which approximately 110 kg is allocated to communications transponders.
CS-3 is now in the design phase and expected to be launched in 1988.

Authors: ['Y. Ishizawa', 'T. Masuda', 'T. Shimamura', 'G. Shirako', 'T. Michida', 'T. Takai', 'T. Ono', 'K. Ichikawa']
Title: An outline of Marine observation satellite (MOS-1)
Publication: IAC 1985 congress proceedings, 36th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  7–12 October 1985, Stockholm, Sweden
Abstract:
National Space Development Agency of Japan (NASDA) initiated the development program of H-II Rocket, in 1985, which will play the role of Japan's main space launch vehicle in 1990's, with capability of placing a 2 ton satellite into geostationary earth orbit (GEO). After a couple of years trade-off studies, LOX/LH2 propulsion system with single Main Engine of staged combustion
cycle has been selected for the first stage of H-II Rocket, considering its high performance and
the accumulated experience in cryogenic propulsion system technology through development of the second stage of H-I Rocket, of which the first launch is planned in August, 1986. Preliminary design of the H-II Rocket first stage propulsion system is now being carried out according to the overall vehicle design policy;
" To realize low cost launching of satellites into GEO.
• To achieve high reliability with simple configuration.
• To minimize newly developed items.
In parallel with the preliminary design of the system, trial fabrication and tests of the main
components of Main Engine, named LE-7, and the vehicle propulsion system has begun. This paper
presents the basic plan of the overall propulsion system of the H-II rocket first stage. The detailed discussion of LE-7 engine will not be included.

Title: Anik and the space shuttle: A retrospective
Publication: IAC 1985 congress proceedings, 36th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  7–12 October 1985, Stockholm, Sweden
Abstract:
The review of the potential european missions trends through the next two decades shows an evolution of the relevant space segment towards heavier and larger spacecraft ; in particular, these missions could be accomodated on platforms having a long operational lifetime. Such missions would benefit from the in-orbit servicing on two levels :
- the mission itself, as the payload might be exchanged or resupplied with new samples or consumables,
- the platform design, which will be influenced by the in-orbit maintenance facilities.
Different scenarii are considered for the in-orbit servicing ; their applicability depends on the existing in-orbit infractructure and on the
mission type (orbital location of the spacecraft,...) ; most of them involve the Teleoperated Service Vehicle (TSV).
This vehicle has to perform four types of
missions : placement, retrieval and servicing of a spacecraft, logistic support to a space station ; to this aim, it has to fulfil two main functions : the orbital transfer and rendez-vous function is required by all its missions ; the servicing function is needed by some of these missions.
Therefore, it is constituted of two elements : a basic vehicle and a servicing kit which are
described in the paper. Three versions (space based, ground based, expendable) of this vehicle have been identified to support the different
servicing scenarii. A review of the servicing
operations and of the benefits of the utilization of the TSV is carried out.

Title: High-pressure propulsion advanced concepts for cooling
Publication: IAC 1985 congress proceedings, 36th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  7–12 October 1985, Stockholm, Sweden
Abstract: Two historic flights of the Manned Maneuvering Unit during early 1984 have clearly demonstrated man's ability to move freely and precisely in space unencumbered by tethers. The STS 41B mission in Feb. 1984 provided and allowed for the first time in space translations away from the shuttle of over 300 ft. Flown by Bruce McCandless and Bob Stewart, the two MMUs departed the shuttle payload bay and returned exactly as planned. Maneuverability of both flight units was reported by the pilots as excellent and as expected from their ground training. This paper describes the activities of Martin Marietta Aerospace Denver, Colorado under contract to the Johnson Space Center, NASA in the design, development, fabrication and test of the MMUs and presents comparisons of the design and operating-predictions with the orbital results of STS missions 41B and 41C. Almost without exception the on-orbit results were within the design predictions. Thermal stability of the MMUs and Flight Support Stations (FSS) were as predicted; the N2 propellant consumption rates on both flights (all four EVAs) was slightly higher than prediction; N2 recharge from the orbiter was demonstrated 3 times (50 lbs of recharge); control authority in the Payload Bay, during translations out to 300 ft. and the close proximity maneuvering during the docking attempts to Solar Maximum on 41C were reported as excellent and as trained. Engineering evaluations of the MMUs during both flights indicated a greater than anticipated sensitivity to center of gravity "offset" (axis cross coupling) which, once understood, cleared the "rumbling and rattling" comment by Bruce McCandless during the first MMU EVA. Prime, Backup and SAT STAB (Satellite Stabilization) modes all performed as predicted with a comment from Bruce that "we sure have a nice flying machine here". Maneuvering velocities during most phases of the four EVAs were less than predicted based on the aggressive flying by most of the crew during ground training in the simulator. Although the MMU was not able to hard dock with Solar Max on STS 41C (Figure 1) the data and experience gained on both STS flights clearly demonstrates MMU's ability to be employed in a vast series of tasks where untethered mobility is required. Bringing the MMU into the inventory of space tools opens a new chapter in man's evolving role on shuttle and space station. Utilization of the MMU will be limited only by the imagination of its users.

Title: NASA's pilot land data system development program
Publication: IAC 1985 congress proceedings, 36th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  7–12 October 1985, Stockholm, Sweden
Abstract: Space operation and space construction are the unique capability of the space station. These activities are featured by utilization of the vicinity space of space station. A result of preliminary study on the requirements of space construction and their interfaces with space operation indicated that the work of space construction include fabrication, assembly, test and operation. Choices of installation, commonality, dynamics of space station and interface with transportation have been considered as design factors of space construction facility. A configuration study has been made to see how the facility is related to the total space station system concerning these design factors. For future evolution, the space construction will be a central function of the space station and it should be so designed.

Title: Overview of Japanese technology development for space station
Publication: IAC 1985 congress proceedings, 36th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  7–12 October 1985, Stockholm, Sweden
Abstract:
The injector is a critical component in ali
liquid propellant rocket engines. It establishes
the combustion efficiency and many important
operating characteristics of the engine. Injector-
caused problems have resulted in expensive
delays and even mission failure on a number of
major vehicle programs.
The function of the injector is to atomize and
mix the propellants in a way that will result in
efficient, stable combustion in a small volume
while creating a benign combustion chamber wall
environment. Traditionally, injectors have been
designed to accomplish the atomization and mixing
by impinging streams or sheets of propellants on
one another. These streams or sheets are formed
by holes or slots in the injector face. Fabrication
considerations have generally placed a limit on
how small the injection orifices . can be. The
result has been that injectors often are a compromise
between the desire for a "fine" pattern for
combustion reasons and the dictates of fabricability.
A unique injector fabrication process called the
"platelet process" has been developed which
avoids the limitations on pattern fineness imposed
by conventional machining processes. Using
platelet technology, injectors have been fabricated
which contain thousands of closely spaced, individually
metered fuel and oxidizer orifices.
These orifices are typically an order of magnitude
smaller than those found on drilled injectors.
The platelet process also makes possible the
fabrication of an entirely new class of injector
elements which cannot be fabricated using conventional
fabrication technology. Typical of this
new class of elements are injector elements in
which the individual streams are self-atomizing or
in which the fuel and oxidizer are premixed at
the point of injection.
The micro-orifice injector provides a hign
degree of control over the combustion process.
It can be used to achieve nearly ideal combustion
efficiencies in very short lengths, while maintaining
good combustion chamber compatibility. The
control of the combustion process possible with
platelet injectors can also be used to optimize
injectors to meet special operating requirements.
Platelet injectors have been tested with all of
the common propellant combinations, including
O^/Hg, N^O^/MMH, and Og/RP-l. Operating
points have included both gas generator and main
chamber conditions to pressures in excess of
2,000 psia. Thrust levels have ranged from less
than 1 IbF to 40,000 IbF. Test results are presented
for several of the injectors. These results
illustrate the design flexibility and performance
capability of the platelet concept.

Title: Pulmonary function in microgravity: Spacelab 4 and beyond
Publication: IAC 1985 congress proceedings, 36th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  7–12 October 1985, Stockholm, Sweden
Abstract:
An advanced technology program to develop high pressure, storable propellant rocket engine components is being conducted in-house at the Air Force Rocket Propulsion Laboratory. The program (STAR Techt has consisted of three major tasks: Task I - Dual Thrust Injector, Task II - High Area Ratio Nozzles and Task III - Carbon-Carbon Chambers and Nozzles. Conceptual study and component design and analysis phases of all three Tasks were conducted. A decision was then made to proceed with fabrication of components to conduct experiments on high area ratio nozzles (400:1). The components are designed for N2O4/MMH propellants operating at 1,500 psia (l0.3MPa) and 3,750 lbs (I6,680N) thrust.
A description of the program is presented and discussed. For Task I, the topics are injector element concept selection for step (discrete, dual) thrust operation, injector design, combustion stability analysis, acoustic cavity design and cold flow facility to determine sprayfield characteristics for single element and full-scale injectors. The Task II discussion focuses on the parametric analyses which led to the selection of three 400:1 nozzle contours with which experiments will be conducted. A general description of the analytical methods used to characterize the fjowfields and performance loss mechanisms are presented. Heat transfer and design considerations for small, high pressure combustion chambers and large area ratio nozzles are also discussed. In Task III, the feasibility of using carbon-carbon material in thrust chambers and nozzles with N2O4/MMH propellants at high-pressure is being determined. The materials investigation, oxidation resistant coatings evaluation and initial designs are discussed.

Title: Reaching for the planet Mars: Humankind's evolving perspectives
Publication: IAC 1985 congress proceedings, 36th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  7–12 October 1985, Stockholm, Sweden
Abstract:
The recent more restrictive specifications issjj ed byvarious satellite communication organizations for the secondary lobes of earth station antennas has reproposed the problem of the architectural structure of the same. The question is whether, in order to meet such specifications, it will be or not necessary to substitute the well-tested axy symmetric Cassegrain antennas with offset type asymmetric ones. Undoubtedly the offset antennas in which the illuminated surface is free of block ing, have a secondary lobes envelope which is much lower than a Cassegrain. On the other hand, they rise some doubts on polarization purity and, above all, they are certainly bigger, heavier and more expensive than axy-symmetric antennas with equal gain.
The problem is particularly important for large diffusion small antennas which are supposed to be unexpensive as well, like the ones with D/3, ratio lower than 100.
The paper shows the results of a study on Cassegrain antennas from 2 to 6 m dish diameter, aimed to find the sensitivity of the off-axys radiation pattern with respect to some structural parameters like the quadrupode blocking, the primary spillover etc., in order to define some design tricks apt to extend as much as possible, the possible use of axy-symmetric antennas.
A simple criterion to design the subreflector supporting struts is proposed which substantially reduces the rise of the secondary lobes envelope.

Title: The EURECA design concept
Publication: IAC 1985 congress proceedings, 36th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  7–12 October 1985, Stockholm, Sweden
Abstract: This contribution makes use of some stellar astronomical results based on the galactic distribution of open clusters of different ages and on C. C. Lin's gravitational density wave theory of the large scale galactic spiral structure. Relying upon the cluster distribution it is possible to determine the pijoh angle (i) and angular velocity ( Cl ) of the spiral pattern. It turns out that the orBit of the Sun is close to the so called co-rotation circle. Consequently, if we assume that our case is about average and accept the idea that the longevity of a civilization might be limited with high probability by catastrophic events threatening during the crossing of the arms, the intelligent life is presumably concentrated on a belt in the Galaxy which is a narrow annulus including the co-rotation circle and the galactic orbit of our Sun. It is possible to select loci of coevality in the belt which localize the zones where societies at least as old as ours are primarily expected.

Authors: ['S. Kitazume', 'R. Ohrui', 'H. Honda', 'T. Kimura', 'T. Koike', 'Y. Morishita']
Title: The eclipse simulation tests of 12GHz 200 W TWTA for broadcasting satellites
Publication: IAC 1985 congress proceedings, 36th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  7–12 October 1985, Stockholm, Sweden
Abstract: The environmental effects on a proposed large flexible space structure, namely, the Hoop/Column antenna system are studied. Mathematical models for the disturbances resulting from the interaction of solar radiation pressure with the vibrating and at so thermally deformed antenna structure are developed, Expressions for the stabilizing gravity-gradient torques are also obtained. The uncontrolled transient response of the antenna system shows that the structure would tumble in orbit due to the expected disturbances. Linear quadratic regulator techniques are used to develop control laws for the actuators which could provide both shape and orientation control. The controlled response of the system is simulated for various initial conditions. The steady state RMS pointing accuracy and the antenna surface accuracy are met in all the cases considered here. In order to reduce the control effort required to maintain the shape and orientation, the thermal deformations will have to be minimized. In the preliminary design of the system, materials should be considered which have a higher thermal conductivity and a lower coefficient of linear expansion, within cost constraints.

Title: The scientific payload of the HIPPARCOS astrometry satellite
Publication: IAC 1985 congress proceedings, 36th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  7–12 October 1985, Stockholm, Sweden
Abstract:
This paper presents the development work carried out by Aerospatiale on the structure of the direct TV satellites TV-SAT and TDFl.The structure is divided in three main modules (communication module, service module and propulsion module) and a satellite adapter equipped with separation nuts.
The development includes design and analysis, fabrication and tests (static loading tests of the structure and functional tests on separation nuts.
Whenever it is possible, GFRP is used to get a structure as light as possible.

Title: Towards establishing a multi-planet species
Publication: IAC 1985 congress proceedings, 36th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  7–12 October 1985, Stockholm, Sweden
Abstract: The near future will witness the construction and deployment of large space structures intended to serve as advanced research laboratories, production facilities for high quality materials, communication systems, or the like. The German Aerospace Research Establishment (DFVLR) contributes to this trend by performing design preparations for typical components of space structures. Emphasis is placed on the characterization of fiber- reinforced materials under space conditions, the development of computer programs for optimal design and analysis practices, and the construction of space-type frameworks for test and validation purposes.

Title: An antenna despun spacecraft with GaAs solar cells for communications application
Publication: IAC 1984 congress proceedings, 35th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  8–13 October 1984, Lausanne, Switzerland
Abstract:
This paper describes a simple antenna despun
spacecraft with high efficiency GaAs solar cells for
communications application. The spacecraft is
planned for use of the coming generation of the
Japanese domestic communications satellite (CS-3).
Most of recent communications satellites are of
either 3-axis stabilized type with large solar wings
or spin stabilized type with expandable solar
cylinders. The size of solar arrays is important to
satisfy the power requirement, which has been
increasing as the increase of communications capacity
per spacecraft.
The spacecraft described in this paper is
designed by a different approach: i.e. to achieve high
level of primary solar power by using high efficiency
solar cells with limited area of solar arrays. The
spacecraft has other design features also; i.e. the
use of light weight CFRP main body structure and
light weight electronics design including the use
of MIC’s. The spacecraft is compatible with the
Japanese H-I launch vehicle.
GaAs solar cells to be used for the spacecraft
are expected to have an average efficiency of 17.5%
at the beginning of life and 14.5% after 7 years in
the geostationary orbit. The solar array consists
of approximately 37,000 pieces of GaAs solar cells
of 2 cm X 2 cm in size. The cells'are placed on
light weight KFRP A1 honeycomb substrate panels by
the shingle mount method. This provides an efficient
use of the array area with respect to solar
power generation. The output power available from
the solar array is expected to be about 840 W at EOL
equinox (7 years).
The main body (central cylinder) of the spacecraft
consists of a single body CFRP cone fabricated
by the filament winding method. The spacecraft has
two equipment platforms supported by the cylinder,
on one of which are held communication modules, and
spacecraft bus electronics and the propulsion subsystem
are placed on the other platform.
The spacecraft has a dry mass of approximately
470 kg, of which approximately 110 kg is allocated to
communications transponders.
CS-3 is now in the design phase and expected to
be launched in 1988.

Title: Simple method for precise geometric coof digila ilage
Publication: IAC 1984 congress proceedings, 35th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  8–13 October 1984, Lausanne, Switzerland
Abstract:
On 4 April, 1983 the second Inertial Upper Stage (IUS) flight vehicle was carried into low Earth orbit by the Space Shuttle Orbiter (STS-6). The first stage solid rocket motor (SRM-1) successfully completed its portion of the mission to transfer the IUS vehicle second stage and the Tracking and Data Relay Satellite (TDRS) payload to geosynchronous transfer orbit. However during the second stage (SRM-2) bum, an uncommanded change in thrust vector occurred. The IUS lost its control stability after providing 96% of the total transfer energy required to place TDRS-A in its desired geosynchronous orbit. The resultant tumble of the IUS and TDRS placed the combined payload into an elliptical orbit which was 245 miles lower at apogee and 8650 miles lower at perigee than the required 22,236-mile circular orbit. Special uplink commands by Boeing and Government personnel separated the TDRS from the IUS and permitted the team of NASA, Spacecom and TRW to stabilize and raise the spacecraft to its operational geosynchronous orbit on June 28, 1983 through a series of TDRS reaction control thruster firings.
The flight anomaly initiated an extensive investigation to establish the cause and corrective action. This paper addresses all of the anomalies which occurred during the IUS flight on STS-6. Included are discussions of 1) the review of flight data, 2) the evaluation of the possible causes, and 3) the results of supporting analytical and component test efforts, 4) the resulting enhanced design, processing and test requirements and 5) the test program which was established to verify the design enhancements and establish the confidence needed to proceed with future flights.
The results to date show that 1) the causes have been established, 2) the analysis models verified, 3) all corrective actions complete, 4) new flight hardware fabricated and 5) final confidence testing is nearing completion. The IDS is ready to resume its role as a key element of the Space Transportation System.
