Title: The challenge of advanced space transportation and propulsion systems
Publication: IAC 1984 congress proceedings, 35th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  8–13 October 1984, Lausanne, Switzerland
Abstract:
The past years have seen a major expansion in the use of space vehicles and satellites for many new roles. If past trends are an indication of the future, the coming decades will see an even greater expansion in space transportation, space transfer systems and their usage for space missions. This expansion wi 11 provide the benefits of space utilization to an ever increasing spectrum of the world's population. This growth will be faci 1 itated by both near- term design refinement and more technologically advanced means to reduce space transportation costs.
For the space vehicle and propulsion designer there are many challenges associated with such growth. The challenges are to develop advanced vehicle and propulsion system designs that provide higher performance, greater reliability and safety, lower weight, and for reusable applications, increased life and reduced servicing. The challenge is also to define and develop systems that can be developed, produced and operated efficiently, and at low cost. In addition, their is a challenge in developing the technology for new designs and concepts at acceptable costs and within prescribed schedules.

Title: A spacecraft design for shuttle
Publication: IAC 1983 congress proceedings, 34th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  10–15 October 1983, Budapest, Hungary
Abstract:
The Earth Radiation Budget Satellite (ERBS) is an application research satellite that will study the components and dynamics of the Earth's radiation budget on a long-term, large-spatial scale. Data thus collected will form the basis for extensive climatology models designed to predict longterm climate and weather trends.
ERBS is the first spacecraft designed uniquely for use on the Space Transportation System (STS).
It consists of three major parts; the base module, the keel module and the instruments. The base module and the instruments. The base module spans the orbiter bay (15 feet) and mounts directly to the orbiter sills by trunnions. The keel module attaches to the bottom of the shuttle bay. The instrument module supports two of the three instrument experiment packages.
Data collected by the scientific instruments and generated by the operational subsystems are processed by the command and data handling subsystem for real-time transmission or storage into tape recorders. The communications subsystem receives and transmitts to the TDRSS using an electronically switched spherical array antenna.
Two solar array panels generate electrical power. A charge control of 2-50 AH nickel-cadmium batteries is done using a series regulator that works the solar array at its maximum power point until the batteries are fully charged. An undervoltage/over current switch automatically disconnects the nonessential bus should the primary bus drop below commanded levels or bus current exceeds commanded levels.
The Orbiter's remote manipulator system (RMS) deploys the spacecraft into a 300 km circular orbit. Several hours later the spacecraft's orbit adjust propulsion system (OARS) is used to raise the orbital altitude to 600 km.
The momentum biased attitude control subsystem (ADCS) maintains the spacecraft in the normal, nadir pointing mode or executes special pointing mode reorientation maneuvers.

Title: Overview of space station operations
Publication: IAC 1983 congress proceedings, 34th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  10–15 October 1983, Budapest, Hungary
Abstract:
Based on studies currently underway in Europe and the United States, the operational requirements for a multipurpose manned space station to be launched by about 1990 are discussed. A circular orbit inclined 28.5° to the equator and with a nominal altitute of 450Km is indicated for the initial station. Crew exchange and logistic resupply every 90 to 120 days would be required with an initial crew complement of 6-8 and growing later to 20-24 people.
In its mature configuration, the station, in addition to supporting diverse experiment operations, would provide a capability for satellite service and repair, upper stage basing and servicing, payload-upper stage mating, checkout and launch, structural fabrication and/or assembly and operation of tethered satellites.
For purposes of this overview, the authors have assumed that an international cooperatively developed manned space station will be flying in the 1990's, that it will be launched and supported logistically by the space shuttle and that it will be configured to be capable of growth to accommodate projected mission needs to the turn of the century and beyond. Such a development would be a logical follow-®n to Spacelab and Skylab and would phase well;with full maturity of the Shuttle Spacelab system.
In preparing this paper, the authors have had the benefit of information developed during studies by American and European space station government contractor teams, as well as the benefit of personal experience in the Gemini, Apollo, Skylab, Spacelab, Shuttle and Tracking and Data Relay Satellite programs. Much of the information presented has been synthesized from the current space station studies.
These studies, generally, have compiled the best current information available on potential space station needs over the next 20 years and then translated these needs into the characteristics that a space station would require to meet these needs—not in terms of architecture, but in terms of operating environment and capabilities. These studies, which are continuing, will next address architecture and system design in preparation for system development starting within the next 2 or 3 years.

Title: Transmitting antenna for direct broadcasting satellites with radio frequency beam fine pointing capability
Publication: IAC 1983 congress proceedings, 34th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  10–15 October 1983, Budapest, Hungary
Abstract: The design objectives and electrical performance data of a circularly polarized offset reflector antenna for the illumination of the FRG are presented. The requirements are based on the WARC regulations settled for direct broadcasting satellites. The antenna consists of an offset paraboloid reflector with an elliptical corrugated feedhorn with RF-sensor. Measured radiation pattern, gain figures and RF-sensor performance data are presented. Pattern degradation caused by reflector tilting for beam fine pointing and thermal deformations are considered.

Title: Injector design efficiency increases
Publication: IAC 1982 congress proceedings, 33rd  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  27 September–2 October 1982, Paris, France
Abstract:
The injector designer is constantly faced with the requirement to approach the absolute minimum of propellant distribution distortion. It is known and accepted that both performance and cooling problems are minimized as "perfect" propellant distribution and manifolding are approached.
This paper describes how a very low-cost effort yielded a major increase in Isp and a major decrease in cooling requirements by utilization of the Aerojet platelet design, not only in the injector orifice section, but in the fabrication of the entire injector manifolding scheme.
The effort exceeded the targeted increase in performance and, in this particular application, suggested the possibility of operation without use of a regeneratively cooled combustion chamber due to the near-perfect formation and control of the combustion-side boundary layer.
These results, combined with accurate reproducibility, provide potential for reliability and performance in many applications.

Title: MESA - A new approach to low cost scientific spacecraft
Publication: IAC 1982 congress proceedings, 33rd  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  27 September–2 October 1982, Paris, France
Abstract: Boeing Aerospace Company has developed a low cost spacecraft called the Modular Experimental platform for Science and Applications (MESA). The initial Boeing MESA design is incorporated in the Swedish Viking spacecraft which will be launched in a stacked configuration with the French SPOT spacecraft on the Ariane launch vehicle in 1984. This paper considers international market requirements for scientific spacecraft covering traditional needs as well as those likely to develop from recent technological trends. Satellite system cost drivers are examined and methods of providing cost effective missions are treated. The Viking configuration of the MESA satellite platform is described, including its ability to accommodate alternative payloads, subsystems, and mission design requirements. The MESA concept is described. This concept allows the economical placement and maintenance in orbit of a variety of payloads using relatively low cost, reliable, flight proven, off the shelf hardware in a share the ride launch. Modular kit design is used to promote low cost mission flexibility. The MESA concept is shown to encourage early tailoring of mission design and platform requirements so as to achieve a cost effective mission.

Title: Recent progress in composite materials application for space system
Publication: IAC 1982 congress proceedings, 33rd  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  27 September–2 October 1982, Paris, France
Abstract:
The economic aspects of rocket launchings, in particular the expected masses of satellites to be put into orbit in the future, necessitate considerable increases in the payload capacity of the launcher rockets at present in use. Alongside modifications to the engines or the development of complete upper stages for rocket through the use of efficient fibre-reinforced plastics (FCM) can load to a considerable increase in the payload.
The influence of a rocket's structural mass on the attainable payload in transfer orbit is shown from performance calculations for the European launcher rockets ARIANE 1, 3 and 4. Rocket structures which could advantageously be replaced by structures of FCM are presented and first estimates of the mass of composite material structures are given.
An intermediate stage structure from the second stage of ARIANE 1 is presented as an applied draft example of an FCM structure. The strength layout and the precision-winding production process are introduced and compared to the conventional metal construction. The structural concept presented is based on a shell of sandwich construction, which consists of two skins with interposed stringers or annular ribs. This concept is flexible and makes it possible to adapt the structural design to local problems of force induction or cut-outs.
Tension/compression struts made from CFRP were also developed and qualified for aviation and aerospace applications. For load transmission between CFRP tube and aluminium fitting a positive connection for both tension and compression is used. CFRP- struts save about 50 Î of conventional fabricated aluminium struts.

Title: SETI-games and the book of earth. How signals can transmit the most useful information
Publication: IAC 1982 congress proceedings, 33rd  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  27 September–2 October 1982, Paris, France
Abstract:
The goal of SETI~France is to establish a strategy for communicating with extraterrestrial intelligences. Games designed to simulate the search for signals have proved* such a search to be very difficult. Attempts to communicate an understandable message have proven just as 'difficult.
A "communication SETI-game" performed on March 12 1982 was indeed negative in that neither group, using flashlights and their own code, was able to be understood by its "rival". Group A tried to represent through coded pulses the numberhp and a model of the solar system? group B did not understand any of the information.
Group B then broadcast a symbolisa,tion of the water molecule and its important cycle through the atmosphere and back into the oceans. Group A, in turn, understood nothing. The fact that it believed B's message had to do with the solar system points out how biased a receiving party is in expecting a message to deal with whatever it, itself, would send.
A reflexion on the nature of information leads us to the conclusion that information is relative. A common frame of reference must exist between correspondents before information can be conveyed. More common the frame that is shared, the greater the information.
For this reason we must expect that communication with a civilization most similar to our own will yield the richest type of information? The existence of such similar worlds is expected from the banality of the biochemical constituent atoms in terrestrial forms of life. Differences in the final products might be large but the frame of reference, necessary for the transfer of information, is expected to be shared between the Earth and many other intelligent worlds.
A communication link would then be expected, if civilization lifetimes are sufficiently large. The fact that we have discovered no strong hertzien signal in the Galaxy to be credited to another intelligence raises the question of a civilisation's evolution and the possibility that technical expansion of the terrestrial type is not a current and a lasting evolutionary pattern in the Galaxy.
Our reflexions on cosmic messages led us to design a Book of the Earth, to be published this fall, consisting of a collection of photographies depicting our planetary frame, the life and intelligence it harbored, addressed to ourselves and to the cosmos.
The pool of photographies was assembled by means of the Kodak 1982 contest, open to amateurs and to photo clubs. Kodak helped structure a selection process to boil down the 50t000 entries to a couple hundred images for the Book. Our jury included specialists and dignitaries from most fields represented in the Book? they led the selection process and provided pictures where themes had been insufficiently covered by the contest participants.
Messages from both international dignitaries and from french teenagers complete the Book of the Earth.

Title: Use of a geosynchronous satellite within the SARSAT/COSPAS system
Publication: IAC 1982 congress proceedings, 33rd  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  27 September–2 October 1982, Paris, France
Abstract:
The SARSAT/COSPAS program will provide the maritime and aeronautical communities with a mean to detect and locate distresses 24 hours per day, on the earth surface, using low cost radio beacons transmitting at 406 MHz.
The present design of the system relies on the use of near polar low orbiting satellites. To meet IMCO desire of immediate alerting the adjunction of a geosynchronous space segment to the present SARSAT/COSPAS system is examined.
After a brief summary of the characteristics of the SARSAT/COSPAS system, the link between a 406 MHz beacon and a geosynchronous satellite is analysed. The link budget, the capacity and the principles of the ground processing are outlined. Real life experimentations using environmental data collection systems are enviewed.

Title: An overview of United States manned space flight from Mercury to the shuttle
Publication: IAC 1981 congress proceedings, 32nd  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  6–12 September 1981, Italy, Rome, Italy, Italy
Abstract:
This paper is an overview of the U.S. manned-space-flight programs beginning with Project Mercury and continuing to the present status of the Space Shuttle Program. The nature of previous programs is discussed as to design and mission philosophy, characteristics of the launch vehicle and spacecraft, mode of operation, significant flight results, and the manner in which the experience from one program affected the nature of the next. Interesting physical and performance comparisons of spacecraft, launch vehicles, and ground-support systems are discussed.
The Space Shuttle is shown to clearly represent a major departure from the trend established in previous programs. Some of the major consequences of this difference will be revealed in a discussion of the design features of the Shuttle as well as the more significant new advancements in technology that were required during the development program. Finally, some interesting aspects of the first orbital flight are discussed.

Title: Development of an animal holding facility for space shuttle studies
Publication: IAC 1981 congress proceedings, 32nd  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  6–12 September 1981, Italy, Rome, Italy, Italy
Abstract:
In this paper is described the development status and design details of NASA's Research Animal Holding Facility (RAHF), currently being fabricated at Lockheed Missiles and Space Company (LMSC) for its first flight on the Spacelab-3 mission on the Space Shuttle in IQS1!. The RAHF is being developed as part of NASA's Life Sciences Flight Experiments Program (LSFEP), the primary objective of which is the flight of Spacelab missions dedicated to the Life Sciences. Dedicated Life Sciences Spacelab missions will provide the opportunity for scientists and astronauts to conduct Life Sciences research and development in the unique environment of near-Earth orbit space. Research carried out on animals in the Spacelab will complement parallel human studies of acute physiological responses associated with space flight. This spaceflight laboratory environment will also afford the opportunity to study basic phenomena associated with gravitational biology in zero gravity. These and other studies support NASA's long-term objective of making the space environment more readily available to mankind.
To support the objectives of NASA's Life Sciences Flight Experiments Program requires functioning laboratory animal housing facilities approximating those in ground-based laboratories. The RAHF supports these objectives by providing life-support and housing for the experimental animals required in Spacelab to support various Life Sciences investigations.
The adequacy of facilities to maintain and house small experimental animals is critical to successfully attaining experiment goals. To assist the Principial Investigators to these ends and provide mission flexibility during subsequent flights, NASA has developed a modular RAHF system. In addition to providing general housing for various animal species, the RAHF is designed to minimize disturbance of the specimens caused by vehicle and mission operations. The RAHF system provides life-sustaining capabilities, such as food, water, and waste removal as well as environmental control. Modularity of construction to accommodate a variety of small animals and associated instrumentation insures RAHF's continued use as the sophistication of experiments increases on subsequent missions.
The RAHF system will accommodate either twenty-four 500-g rats or Ik1! mice, or a mixed number of rats and mice. An alternative design accommodates four unrestrained or restrained squirrel monkeys. The RAHF system may be housed in either a single or double Spacelab rack. Because Spacelab is launched vertically, the cages are installed on their sides to provide proper orientation for operation of the waste management system in the prelaunch one-gravity environment.
Lockheed Missiles and Space Company developed the RAHF system design and is building and assembling the first flight systems that, together with NASA-designed and built rodent cages, will be flight-tested on the Spacelab-3 mission. The Spacelab-3 mission will serve as a pathfinder for subsequent Spacelab missions dedicated to Life Sciences by allowing careful evaluation and testing of critical RAHF systems housed with animals in a spaceflight environment. This flight test will also provide the opportunity to acquire baseline spaceflight data from animals unburdened with extensive instrumentation and to evaluate animal restraint and data-collection systems required for more ambitious experiments. Spacelab-3 will also allow investigators selected for later flight missions opportunities to participate in developing recommendations and plans for the utilization of the flight animals. Rats, mice, and squirrel monkeys will be flown in two RAHFs dedicated to rodents and primates, respectively.
Currently, the first flight RAHFs will be delivered to Ames Research Center in early 1982. After delivery, the RAHFs and their associated support instrumentation systems will be assembled into the final Spacelab-3 payload configuration and subjected to various tests. These activities will be performed by the Management and Technical Services Company (MATSCO), a subsidiary of General Electric Space Division, under the direction of the Life Sciences Flight Experiments Project Office at Ames.

Title: Intelsat system summary and initial launch operations
Publication: IAC 1981 congress proceedings, 32nd  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  6–12 September 1981, Italy, Rome, Italy, Italy
Abstract:
This paper describes the technical and operational aspects of the first 2, in a series of 12, INTELSAT V satellites built by Ford Aerospace & Communications Corporation (FACC) for the International Telecommunications Satellite Organization (INTELSAT). The successful launch of the FM-2 and FM-1 satellites took place on 6 December 1980 and 23 May 1981, respectively. Following nominal transfer orbit operations, the satellites were placed into geosynchronous orbit by successfully firing solid apogee kick motors. After oné drift orbit, the satellites were maneuvered and reconfigured for synchronous orbit operation. Transition to the three-axis-stabilized mode was successfully executed as planned. Following solar array and antenna deployments, a series of detailed functional tests were performed to validate the state of health and performance characteristics of the satellites. All redundant spacecraft hardware, mechanisms, and critical operational modes were verified to be working properly and all test results agreed quite well with prelaunch factory tests. These tests confirmed there had been no infant mortality during the launch and orbit injection process of either satellite. Communications tests validated that the critical payload elements (antennas, feeds, and transponders) had experienced no adverse effects by launch.
This paper will review the INTELSAT V satellite design, launch preparations, subsequent flight operations, and results of on-orbit testing. The paper will review the operational plans to transition from the INTELSAT IV-A to the INTELSAT V series and the trend in international communications satellites.

Title: Liquid bipropellant engines for large telecommunications satellites
Publication: IAC 1981 congress proceedings, 32nd  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  6–12 September 1981, Italy, Rome, Italy, Italy
Abstract:
As telecommunications satellites become larger and longer-lived as a result of the launch capability provided by Titan 34D, Space Shuttle and Ariane, integrated liquid bipropellant propulsion systems will replace solid propellant motor/liquid monopropellant thruster propulsion systems for apogee and on-orbit maneuvers. On going programs, e.g., INSAT and L-SAT, are representative of this trend.
The Aerojet Liquid Rocket Company has two liquid bipropellant engines (NTO/MMH) for use on large telecommunications satellites, i.e., AJ10-181, 22 N Thrust Reaction Control Thruster and AJ10-210, 445 N Thrust Liquid Apogee Engine.
Extensive hot-fire and other testing has been accomplished with these engines over a period of several years.
Such issues as engine design, delivered performance (steady state and pulse), and durability and life are discussed. A design, including envelope, is presented for each engine.

Title: The European large telecommunications satellite programme: Demonstration mission and future perspectives
Publication: IAC 1981 congress proceedings, 32nd  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  6–12 September 1981, Italy, Rome, Italy, Italy
Abstract:
The European Space Agency Large Telecommunications Satellite (L-SAT) programme has been conceived against a background of a predicted rapid growth in satellite communications and a trend towards larger and more powerful satellite designs.
The programme objectives are the development of a multipurpose platform matched to a range of future mission needs, the development of a multi-element advanced communications payload, and the launch of a single flight model carrying this payload to support a range of communications missions. This paper outlines the main features of the satellite design and then goes in more detail into the payloads and their foreseen utilisation for tests, demonstrations and preoperational systems.

Title: Development of electron bombardment mercury ion engine
Publication: IAC 1980 congress proceedings, 31st  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  22–28 September 1980, Tokyo, Japan
Abstract:
Ion propulsion offers a significant weight-saving payoff when used for north- south stationkeeping on satellites in geosynchronous orbit or orbital rising of heavy structures from parking orbit to geosynchronous orbit. There have been electron bombardment ion engine flight tests in U.S.A. and some flight tests demonstrated the ability to operate in space with no difference from ground tests.
In Japan, National Aerospace Lab.oratry (NAL) has developed the same type of electron bombardment engines from 1965. Succeeding to the studying results (Nakamura, 1978; Azuma, 1978) Mitsubishi Electric Corporation (MELCO) has been developing the 5 cm electron bombardment mercury ion engine (IEE) for Engineering Test Satellite IOE (ETS-IU) to be launched by National Space Development Agency (NASDA) in the summer of 1982. The development of IEE has been carried on from 1975 as follows:
1975-1976 preliminary design, ... ‘ " ~
1977- 1978 basic design,.
1978- 1979 detail design with fabrication and development- tests of engineering
models (EM),
1980 fabrication and qualification tests of prototype models (PM).
Qualification tests of PM finished in July 1980, and design verification of IEE was accomplished. At present flight models (FM) have been fablicated. FM will be delivered in December 1980 after the performance verified by acceptance tests.

Title: Ignition system for oxygen/hydrogen auxiliary propulsion systems
Publication: IAC 1980 congress proceedings, 31st  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  22–28 September 1980, Tokyo, Japan
Abstract:
When the oxygen/hydrogen bipropellant combination was selected for use in the Space Shuttle Main Engine, it became apparent that many advantages may result if the Auxiliary Propulsion System Engines were to use the same propellants. A new ignition system, possessing a dramatically new level of reliability, durability and response, is required because the oxygen/hydrogen combination is not hypergolic and the projected missions will require a very large number of fast-response engine statts.
The objective of this program was to obtain basic data for spark torch ignition methods at operating conditions typical of a Space Shuttle Orbiter Auxiliary Propulsion System. The research included ignition analysis and igniter design, fabrication, and hot-fire test.
Extensive testing of spark torch igniters was performed (chamber pressure, 206.8 N/cm2, 300 psia, nominal) in the Igniter-Only and Igniter-Complete Thruster (thrust, 6672 N, 1500 IbF, nominal) operational modes. Reliable, repeatable ignitions were obtained with spark energies of 1 to 10 millijoules. Hot-fire test results showed there is no effect of back pressure (1.013 x 10^ to 1.333 x lO-^ N/m^, 7.60 x 10^ to 1 x 10“4 mm Hg) or low temperature (02, 170°K, 306°R; H2, 107°K, 193°R) on the response of the igniter or the ignition delay of the thruster over the ranges tested. Igniter durability and pulse capability were demonstrated with 150 sec of continuous operation and 1000 consecutive pulses, respectively. Durability was further demonstrated with a series of 2500 Igniter-Complete Thruster ignitions at nominal chamber pressure. No limiting variables were encountered. The hot-fire test results showed the spark torch igniter is capable of meeting fully the typical Space Shuttle Orbiter Auxiliary Propulsion System mission requirements.

Title: K band tracking system for the domestic satellite communication system
Publication: IAC 1980 congress proceedings, 31st  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  22–28 September 1980, Tokyo, Japan
Abstract: This paper is concerned with system design and operational results of a tracking system for an earth station antenna operating in the 20 and 30 GHz bands. The antenna is either an 11.5 m diameter axisymmetrical Cassegrain antenna or an equivalent offset Cassegrain antenna. Monopulse tracking technique using higher- order waveguide modes is utilized. An investigation was conducted to clarify the rainfall effect and the effect of oscillator phase noise on the tracking receiver. The result is that the tracking system can be operated normally even when rain attenuation reaches 20 dB. Experiments were performed using the Medium Capacity Communications Satellite for experimental purpose (CS). No cross coupling was seen in the pull-in patterns. Sufficiently good results were obtained in tracking accuracy; less than 0.005° (peak value) under normal conditions, and less than 0.01° under an average wind velocity of more than 20 m/s.

Title: LEASAT
Publication: IAC 1980 congress proceedings, 31st  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  22–28 September 1980, Tokyo, Japan
Abstract:
The United States Navy, as executive agent for the Department of Defense, announced in October 1978 the award of the LEASAT contract to Hughes Communications Services, Incorporated (HCSI), a wholly owned subsidiary of Hughes Aircraft Company. The LEASAT system will provide worldwide communications satellite services to land mobile, airborne, shipborne and fixed earth stations of the U.S. Navy, Marine Corps, Army, and Air Force. »
Hughes' Space and Communications Group is to design, develop, fabricate, integrate, and test five satellites, one operational control center, four satellite control stations, and two movable ground stations. HCSI is to arrange for the launch services of the Space Shuttle from the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA), perform the satellite launch control and mission operations, and deliver communications services for 5 years to the other Department of Defense users. The ownership and operation of the satellite and associated satellite con- - trol earth stations are retained by HCSI. f '
, f
This paper describes the system design, the satellite design (including its unique:.; use of the Space Shuttle launch vehicle), and the operational ground segment-bf the system.

Title: Material and structural approaches for large space structures
Publication: IAC 1980 congress proceedings, 31st  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  22–28 September 1980, Tokyo, Japan
Abstract:
The development of large space structures projected to occur by the year 2000 will require significant technology developments to achieve structures that are thermally stable and possess long life in the space environment. Structural systems used for precision reflectors and antennas will require materials and structural elements that minimize distortion caused by temperature variations encountered during orbital flight. Methods of reducing structural temperature variations combined with material formulations which minimize structural distortions caused by temperature changes are, therefore, of primary concern in developing future structural and material systems for large space structures.
Long life in the space environment is also an area requiring development as is evaluation of methods to protect materials from degradation resulting from the space environment, e.g., ultraviolet exposure. This paper, utilizing results from a NASA Johnson Space Center contract, discusses: low distortion, earth- prefabricated materials that are suitable for orbital construction of large space structures; the design and on-orbit fabrication, using these materials, of lightweight, stiff structural elements called geodetic beams; and structural tests of segments of these beams.

Title: Structural and thermal design of a CFRP antenna for communication satellite
Publication: IAC 1980 congress proceedings, 31st  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  22–28 September 1980, Tokyo, Japan
Abstract:
A shaped beam hom-refleeter antenna suitable for Japanese domestic satellite communication system has been designed» In structural design, CFRP (Carbon Fiber Reinforced Plastic) is adopted for its high specific strength/elasticity and low thermal expansion coefficient. Structural analysis based on Finite Element Method (FEM) is used extensively, mainly to decide the detailed structure which satisfies the rigidity requirement. In thermal design, the coating pattern suitable for this antenna is selected from the thermal calculation result based on nodal method.
The antenna is evaluated by a series of environmenta1 tests, including vibration and thermal vacuum tests, tô establish the satellite antenna design.

Title: Advancement in chemical rocket technology
Publication: IAC 1979 congress proceedings, 30th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  17–22 September 1979, Munich, Germany
Abstract:
It is important for an economical single-stage-to-orbit (SSTÛ) vehicle design to be a merger of the appropriate structure and propulsion system technology. The largest portion of the cost savings can be obtained by simplicity of operation of the (SSTO), and this depends heavily on the propulsion system design and integration with the vehicle. This marriage not only involves the selection of the propulsion cycle and its operational mode (that is, tripropel 1 ant parallel burn or series burn), but the tailoring of the nozzle(s) to meet the mission and system packaging requirements. This paper examines some of the unique nozzle concepts that have recently emerged to obtain the best performance from the integrated propulsion vehicle system.
Propulsion systems and nozzles discussed in the paper include: (1) dual fuel engine for series burn SSTO, (2) dual expander engine for parallel and series burn SSTO, (3) dual throat engine for parallel burn and (4) scarfed bell/plug cluster nozzl e.

Title: Annual survey of spaceflights safety systems: 9th supplement: Survey period July 1978 - June 1979
Publication: IAC 1979 congress proceedings, 30th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  17–22 September 1979, Munich, Germany
Abstract:
Total manned spaceflight safety encompasses not only the safety of crewmembers and supporting ground-based personnel, but also the space vehicles, payloads, support equipment and the general public and property within the flight envelopes. Extensive safety programs, equipment and training are required to effect overall safety for manned spaceflight programs. NASA and ESA are nearing completion of two major space- flight systems, the Space Shuttle and Spacelab, initiating the beginning of an extensive range of future space undertakings with unlimited possibilities. Safety requirements and provisions to satisfy the requirements are continually evolving as a mandatory part of every space program. This survey identifies and documents salient safety studies, analyses, systems, and developments aimed toward providing spaceflight safety for the Shuttle era and beyond.
The first Space Shuttle Orbiter will have completed the orbital flight test phase and will be in routine earth^to-orbit service for over -a year before an on-orbit rescue capability becomes available. Extravehicular systems available for enhancing crew and vehicle safety during this period are discussed and several major hazards affecting Shuttle systems and equipment identified. Soviet spacesuit design and parachute systems for crew recovery are reported, and European Spacelab materials and atmospheric contamination measurement activities are presented. Water immersion testing, spacecraft lighting and color, and manned remote work station studies as related to safety for future long-duration spaceflights and large space construction are discussed. The survey concludes with brief comments concerning safety in space colonies and bases of the 21st century.

Title: Economics of satellite communications systems
Publication: IAC 1979 congress proceedings, 30th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  17–22 September 1979, Munich, Germany
Abstract:
This paper is partly a tutorial, telling systematically how one goes about calculating the total annual costs of a satellite communications system, and partly the expression of some original ideas on the choice of parameters so as to minimize these costs.
The calculation of costs can be divided into two broad categories. The first is technical and is concerned with estimating what particular equipment will cost and what will be the annual expense to maintain and operate it. One starts in the estimation of any new system by listing the principal items of equipment, such as satellites, earth stations of various sizes and functions, telemetry and tracking equipment and terrestrial interfaces, and then estimating how much each item will cost. Methods are presented for generating such estimates, based on a knowledge of the gross parameters, such as antenna size, coverage area, transmitter power and information rate. These parameters determine the system performance and it is usually possible, knowing them, to estimate the costs of the equipment rather well. Some formulae based on regression analyses are presented. Methods are then given for estimating closely related expenses, such as maintenance and operation, and then an approximate method is developed for estimating terrestrial interconnection costs.
It is pointed out that in specific cases when tariff and geographical information are available, it is usually better to work with specific data, but nonetheless it is often desirable, especially in global system estimating, to approximate these interconnect costs without recourse to individual tariffs. The procedure results in a set of costs for the purchase of equipment and its maintenance, and a schedule of payments. Some payments will be incurred during the manufacture of the satellite and before any systems operation, but many will not be incurred until the system is no longer in use, e.g. incentives. In any case, with the methods presented in the first section, one arrives at a schedule of costs and payments for all the items and the years in which they will be incurred. The - second category of costing problems is one of financing or engineering economics. All the costs are first "present valued" to some reference period using fates of return appropriate to the particular situation.
One finally arrives at sets of annual costs which can be used as the basis for setting lease costs or revenue requirements and tariffs. The correspondence between methods using discounted rates of return and capital recovery formulas on one hand and those using various depreciation schedules, such as is typical of regulated industries on the other hand, is discussed.
The remainder of the paper is devoted to discussing the relationship between critical parameters, such as replacement schedules, design lifetime, satellite power and earth statioh antenna size, and the overall costs.
It is shown that optima for these parameters may exist and can be calculated. In particular, the optimization of satellite replacement schedules to minimize the present value of total investment over a very long period is presented, along with simplified versions of the theory suitable for system planning.
The choice of EIRP is also discussed and a procedure for choosing the value that minimizes the costs is shown.

Title: Orbital transfer vehicle propulsion concepts and technology
Publication: IAC 1979 congress proceedings, 30th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  17–22 September 1979, Munich, Germany
Abstract:
The Orbital Transfer Vehicle (OTV), part of the planned U.S. Space Transportation System (STS), will be carried into low earth orbit by the Space Shuttle Orbiter where it will extend the operating regime of the STS to higher altitude orbits, geosynchronus orbits and other space missions.
Based on studies completed by NASA, high performance requirements of a reusable orbital transfer vehicle necessitate the use of oxygen/hydrogen propellants and an advanced,' high-performance, pump-fed main propulsion system in the thrust range of 10,000 to 20,000 pounds.
OTV Engine Phase A studies are in progress under sponsorship of the NASA Marshall Space Flight Center in which candidate main engine concepts are being assessed and comparisons made of performance capability, system complexity, and state of technology readiness. The concepts include the staged- combustion, expander and gas generator engine cycles. Trends in chamber pressure, engine envelope, and weight as a function of thrust level are discussed for each engine cycle.
Major engine components and subsystems for this type propulsion system
have been undergoing technology development and demonstration under NASA Lewis Research Center sponsorship at a thrust of 20,000 pounds and chamber pressure of 2000 psia. The staged-combustion cycle concept was selected for carrying out this technology development since this cycle offers the greatest performance potential as well as the greatest required technology advancements. The technology developed is, however, generally applicable to the other engine cycle concepts as well and the continuing effort is discussed.
Technology development and demonstration have also been in progress on components for an O2/H2 integrated altitude control system applicable to OTV.
The design, fabrication, and demonstration test of a 25-pound thruster, with unique spark torch ignition, is discussed and performance and operating characteristics are presented.

Title: Trends in the design of future communications satellite systems
Publication: IAC 1979 congress proceedings, 30th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  17–22 September 1979, Munich, Germany
Abstract: This paper presents a review of the trends in communication satellite technology. In the near term the development of moderate size, dedicated satellites is to be expected. In the long term international coordination of orbit and spectrum allocations, introduction of higher-frequency bands, spectrum conserving techniques and the concept of large communication platforms deserve particular attention. Means to improve the cost effectiveness of satellite communications system and technology aspects are considered. Finally some German contributions to these developments are presented, mainly concerning high-power TWT's in the 12 GHz and 20 GHz range.

Title: Biological specimen holding facilities for Spacelab experiments
Publication: IAC 1978 congress proceedings, 29th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  1–8 October 1978, Dubrovnik, Yugoslavia
Abstract: This paper describes the use of biological specimen holding facilities in life- science experiments that will be flown on the Spacelab in the 1980s. Design, development, integration, and testing of two prototype holding facilities are discussed. One of these units housed 36 laboratory rats in individual cages; supplied conditioned air, food, and water; provided for waste management; and included instrumentation to measure environmental parameters and animal activity. The other unit housed one unrestrained 14-kilogram rhesus monkey in an environmentally controlled enclosure complete with food, water, and waste-collection equipment. Timer- controlled fluorescent lights in both units permitted automatic day-night cycling. Both units were designed to satisfy animal metabolic, volumetric, and atmospheric requirements; to be compatible with Spacelab interfaces; and to be operated by NASA payload specialists. After use for crew training at Ames Research Center, the units were integrated with 25 other experiments into the Spacelab Simulator at Johnson Space Center, where a three-man crew successfully performed a 7-day mission.

Title: Design of an experimental data collection system using a commercial communication satellite
Publication: IAC 1978 congress proceedings, 29th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  1–8 October 1978, Dubrovnik, Yugoslavia
Abstract: This paper describes the system design procedure followed for defining the configuration of an experimental satellite data collection system using a commercial communication satellite. The institutional framework in which the experiment took place is first introduced and the system design constraints derived from the agreements stipulated between the participating organizations are discussed. The basic steps followed in the system design procedure are then illustrated for the three major system components, namely, the satellite link, the ground transmit terminals and the central receive station. Finally, the conclusion reached after monitoring the performance of the system for a period of about eight months are presented.

Title: Development logic and performances of the Ariane launch vehicle structures
Publication: IAC 1978 congress proceedings, 29th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  1–8 October 1978, Dubrovnik, Yugoslavia
Abstract:
In the year 1973 Europe decided to undertake the development of the ARIANE Launch Vehicle to be made operational in 1980. In order to ensure the success of the ARIANE operation, a rapid development and a competitive price had to be foreseen which led to the use of proved technologies. Thus, the classical metals, the conventional fabrication techniques in the aeronautics industry with standardised dimensions have been employed for the structural components of the Launch Vehicle} only the cryogenic third stage used the already more advanced technologies.
However, the objectives of the Launch Vehicle performances required a reduction, to the maximum extent, of the structural mass. Besides, being an European programme, the structures have been developed all over Europe. Also, to respect these performance objectives and to ensure a homogeneous development the CENTRE NATIONAL D'ETUDES SPATIALES (Overall manager of the Programme) with the help of the AEROSPATIALE has elaborated the management specifications and the general specifications for design and testing (static, dynamic as well as thermal) of structures.
After a brief description of the primary structures of the launch vehicle, the development logic of these structures will be dealt with while emphasizing on the overall system imputs used, their verification and the design and testing phase of these structures. Thus the static and thermal loads acting on the launch vehicle have been calculated right at the beginning of the Program- me and their verification at a later date has not implicated these initially computed values.
The various structural components have ‘been, to the best extent, designed employing the modern analysis methods (Finite Elements) and particular attention has been paid to resolve the interface problems that cropped up among these structures.
Today the ensemble of the ARIANE Launch Vehicle structures has withstood, with success, the qualification tests (Static as well as dynamic and thermal) and in course of this presentation, the tests conducted on the most complex structural components will be detailed.

Title: Shuttle demonstration of large space structure fabrication and assembly
Publication: IAC 1978 congress proceedings, 29th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  1–8 October 1978, Dubrovnik, Yugoslavia
Abstract: The purpose of this paper is to describe a program aimed at the early on orbit demonstration of a large space structure fabrication and assembly capability. Requirements for the demonstration concept have been formulated. The concept that has been selected to meet these requirements is a Large Space Structure Platform consisting of a triangular prism of 31.5 m length. Sensors can be mounted on this platform to perform earth observation measurements from space. Structural elements of the platform are fabricated using an automated beam builder in the Shuttle Orbiter payload bay. Special fixtures are designed to assemble the structure with the aid of the Remote Manipulator System and two astroworkers in an EVA mode. Results are shown of the platform preliminary design in terms of a design layout with related structural, thermal, mass properties and control dynamics data. The assembly scenario is described. Estimates of the total construction time and Orbiter support requirements are also presented.

Title: The INTELSAT system and its future challengers
Publication: IAC 1978 congress proceedings, 29th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  1–8 October 1978, Dubrovnik, Yugoslavia
Abstract:
The successful implementation and growth of the INTELSAT system over the last lU years has in large measure been the result of close and continuing cooperation between the. organization and its users. INTELSAT has changed in many ways - from a small organization with limited membership to a global organization with over 100 members ; from limited operation in the North Atlantic Region to a global system providing 60 percent of the world's overseas international traffic; from fixed point-to-point public international telecommunications traffic to a wide range of mobile and fixed international and domestic telecommunication services. By year- end 1978, it is anticipated that INTELSAT will be providing in addition to its primary expanding international fixed service, domestic telecommunications services to ih countries and currently, many additional services, such as television distribution and global maritime telecommunications, are under active study.
Planning for the provision of the necessary space segment resources and implementation, maintenance and operation of the global system has been no simple task. It involves all of the organs of INTELSAT, more particularly the Board of Governors, its advisory committee, and the Executive Organ. Institutional arrangements had to be developed that permitted satisfaction of user requirements in the system through effective integration of planning for operation of the space and earth segments.
INTELSAT, as can be seen from its brief history, must face tomorrow with a versatile and flexible outlook. If our organization is to continue to be successful, it must continue to be sensitive to new and different needs of our Signatories and users as well as to new opportunities to increase the reliability, the effectiveness and the cost efficiency of INTELSAT service. Equally important, INTELSAT must, along with others, seek solutions to the problems posed by increasing demand upon the geo-synchronous orbital arc; utilizable radio frequency spectrum, proliferating satellite systems ; and related issues.
The paper focuses attention on the fact that INTELSAT will bring in operation the INTELSAT V spacecraft in 1980 which is presently under procurement. Along the coming of the new satellite - a new type of earth terminal, at ll/lU GHz, will be incorporated into the system and introduction of advance communication techniques would allow a more efficient use of the committed INTELSAT resources.
In the second half of the 80's the increasing demand on traffic would require larger capacity satellites and the planning for the INTELSAT V Follow-on Program has been underway for some time. The paper summarizes the present status of the definition of the follow-on systems and will include descriptions of spacecraft concepts and of system configurations.
The paper addresses future directions in INTELSAT research and development.
It emphasizes the technologies needed for INTELSAT to provide its regular international services, as well as new services under study. These technologies include: multibeam and shaped beam antennas; intersatellite communicatiors links ; advanced propulsion, stabilization and orientation techniques, including ion engines; onboard satellite switching and signal regeneration; new spectrum/orbit-efficient communication schemes; advanced battery and solar cell array development; fabrication techniques for large structures in space, modularization techniques and lightweight structural design.
In the 1990's, large-scale space stations equipped with complex orbital antenna farms and multiple communications packages for a variety of uses would be technically feasible. Such space stations, implemented under the INTELSAT framework, would appear to provide many technical and operational advantages, as well as potential for substantial cost savings to consumers for future years.

Title: The collection of lunar mass driver payloads in earth-moon space
Publication: IAC 1978 congress proceedings, 29th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  1–8 October 1978, Dubrovnik, Yugoslavia
Abstract:
The mass driver is conceptually a special type of linear synchronous motor, envisioned for use in future space operations. The idea of a lunar mass driver is one in which small passive carrier vehicles (buckets), guided by dynamic magnetic constraint forces, are accelerated along a linear guideway by pulsed magnetic fields.
At peak velocity, each bucket releases a payload of lunar soil on a free-flight trajectory to a nearby point in free space. The buckets then decelerate and return for another launch cycle. Some of the problems associated with the collection of the incoming lunar mass driver payloads at the point in Earth-Moon space are revealed and treated. A summary of the development of this collection concept, or "mass catcher" concept, is presented. Relevant subject areas include the future material needs in space, sources of the material, and use of the mass driver to acquire this material for use in space operations. Following a brief survey of the various design options for the mass catcher, a broad development of the catcher dynamics is presented, including discussion of the orbital conditions and of the various perturbing effects which exist at the catcher site. The basic requirements and design constraints for several mass catcher subsystems are summarized, and pertinent recommendations for further research in the catcher design problem are offered.

Title: A prototype carbon dioxide and humidity control system for shuttle mission extension capability
Publication: IAC 1976 congress proceedings, 27th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  10–16 October 1976, Anaheim, United States
Abstract: The primary objective of this paper is to describe an advanced regenerable carbon dioxide (CO^) and humidity control system being developed for the NASA JSC. The system offers substantial weight advantages compared to the baseline Shuttle Orbiter expendable, lithium hydroxide (LiOH) CC^ removal system for extended missions beyond the nominal design of 4 men for 7 days. The regenerable HS-C system offers a potential weight savings of 431 kg for a 7 man, 30 day mission. A regenerable sorbent material designated as HS-C coadsorbs C0„ and water (H2O) vapor from the cabin atmosphere and desorbs the CO2 and H2O vapor overboard when exposed to space vacuum. In addition to comparison of the regenerable system with the baseline Shuttle expendable system, HS-C mission simulation test results and the flight prototype regenerable system, currentl> being fabricated, are presented. The paper shows the integration of the system into the Shuttle Orbiter vehicle; exclusive of cryogenic fuel cell power expendables, the available packaging envelope is sufficient to stow all expendables necessary for HS-C operation on 30 day extended missions.

Title: Future low-cost space transportation system analysis Part II: Preliminary concept evaluation
Publication: IAC 1976 congress proceedings, 27th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  10–16 October 1976, Anaheim, United States
Abstract:
This is the second part of a comprehensive analysis of the most economic technical solution for low-cost transportation of large quantities of cargo into space. The first part („me- thodical Approach") was presented at the 1975 IAF Congress and published in „Raum- fahrtforschung. No. 2/76".
The Space Shuttle with 30 Mg LEO (Low Earth Orbit) payload capability will become operational in the early 80ies. By 1985 it will increase the transportation capacity into LEO with 60 launches p.a. to a new level of 1200 Mg (FIG. 1). The transportation cost will be reduced to half of the present level with expendable launch vehicles or some 700 $/kg payload mass (1976) based on recurring cost only. The specific cost for GEO (Geosynchronous Earth Orbit) transportation will be about 20 000 f/kg (1976) by using an additional solid motor assembly for transfer and injection. By using a Space Tug these costs could come down to about 7 000 $/kg.
The Space Shuttle (+ Tug) may satisfy the requirements for the eighties, but probably not for the following decades. It is still too expensive and too limited in payload capacity (massand volume), if we consider larger space stations and space power systems in geosynchronous orbit. We can expect a decision on a next generation "Low-Cost Cargo Carrier Vehicle (LCCV)" by the mideighties and it is not too early now, to start the systems analysis ofthat new transportation system to come.
FIG. 2 indicates the trend and requirements for the reduction of transportation cost to geosynchronous orbit in terms of MY/Mg (man-years per megagram or 103 kg). This term is being used to eliminate the cost increases/inflation and exchange rate influences. (It does not, however, take into consideration of the general gains in productivity). A conversion factor for MY to US-Dollars is indicated in FIG. 2.
The design goal is to conceive a transportation system which is capable by the year 2000 to come down by two orders of magnitude in specific cost compared to the present situation. Only this order of magnitude in cost reduction would allow to increase the total transportation volume to the level required for larger power stations in space without excessive and unrealistic expenditures for space transportation.

Title: The space shuttle - Key considerations
Publication: IAC 1974 congress proceedings, 25th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  30 September–5 October 1974, Amsterdam, Netherlands
Abstract:
Although the United States achieved leadership in manned space exploration as a result of the successful Apollo and Skylab programs, the high cost of space operations, coupled with a change in national priorities, made it necessary to find a method for substantially reducing the cost of space operations. As a result the United States decided, in 1972 to proceed with an entirely new type of space transportation system, designed to help transform the space frontier of the 1970s into familiar territory, routinely accessible, at low cost, in the 1980s and 1990s.
The paper first reviews the current program status of the reusable Space Shuttle and describes the hardware being developed. A typical mission is then described in some detail which includes the parameters associated with the significant flight operations. This description flows through all operational modes from lift-off, staging events, orbital maneuvers, reentry, landing and refurbishment for the next flight.
The principle part of the paper contains information about the many accommodations aboard the Shuttle to support the user payloads. Factors described include crew provisions, payload specialist functions, pointing and position stability, on-orbit thermal constraints, electrical power, data communications, structural attachments and space manipulator, kits required for extended missions, and other payload provisions. The Spacelab and Space Tug are mentioned briefly, however, payload accommodations are the chief concern of the Shuttle element of the Space Transportation System.
While the Shuttle represents a second generation system with much of the technology based on previous space programs, there are two areas where technology transition into development hardware is critical to successful development of the Space Shuttle system. These areas are the Orbiter thermal protection system and the Space Shuttle main engines.
All major contractors and subcontractors are on board. Detail design and hardware fabrication are underway and component testing has been initiated. The program is on schedule and within our cost targets. In conclusion, the paper summarizes the present status of the Shuttle development by reviewing the program schedule, hardware in development and payload accommodations the Shuttle provides to the user.

Title: United States manned spacecraft reliability experience
Publication: IAC 1974 congress proceedings, 25th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  30 September–5 October 1974, Amsterdam, Netherlands
Abstract:
Completion of the Skylab Program on February 8, 1974, signaled the end of the fourth major U.S. manned spacecraft program and the thirtieth manned spacecraft flight. More than 7000 hr of manned flight commencing with Project Mercury and extending through the Apollo Program were accumulated. The experience gained from the four major space programs in little more than 15 years provided the impetus for formulating the reliability approaches being used in the present Space Shuttle Program.
Two key spacecraft design guidelines were used to the degree practicable in Project Mercury, which was the first manned space-flight project. They were: (1) no single failure shall cause an aborted mission, and (2) no single failure during an aborted mission shall result in loss of life to crew members. Use of proven components was emphasized in Project Mercury spacecraft design. A requirement existed that all failures and anomalies would be resolved before space flight.
Approaches similar to the project Mercury reliability controls were used in the Gemini Program spacecraft, which were two-man spacecraft used to conduct research in rendezvous techniques. Basic design changes that enhanced reliability based on Project Mercury experience were made in the Gemini Program.
The Apollo Program (U.S. manned lunar landing missions) was designed using a number of key design and assurance principles derived from previous manned spacecraft program experience. Because the command module spacecraft hardware was essentially the same for the Skylab Program (with some modifications), the design and assurance principles were complied with fully for the Skylab Program. Additional testing was necessary to ensure confidence in the longer-duration Skylab missions. Reliability practices for experiments required some revisions or tailoring because the loss of a single experiment did not mean the loss of a major mission objective.
Specific reliability disciplines have evolved from previous spacecraft programs, and these disciplines currently are being applied to the latest U.S. manned space-flight program, the Space Shuttle Program, which involves a reusable orbiter vehicle. A summary of the major reliability tasks and innovations being used on the Space Shuttle Program is presented.

Title: Progess in the development of the reverse osmosis process for spacecraft wash water recovery
Publication: IAC 1972 congress proceedings, 23rd  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  8–15 October 1972, Vienna, Austria
Abstract:
The major expendable required by manned space missions is water. Drinking water requirements increase proportionately with mission duration; however, the requirements become even more important as missions become longer. The present Skylab water system requires over 4540 kg of stored water and tankage for supplying potable water, with minimal water for personal hygiene.
Wash water consists principally of the water and soap used for personal hygiene, including showering, as well as detergent and residue from washing clothes. In addition to the soap (which may contain a mild antiseptic) and detergent (which is a major component), the wash water contains various microorganisms and particulate matter. Dissolved solutes, in addition to those from the soap and detergent, include sodium and potassium chloride, ammonia, urea, lactic acid, etc. Upon recovery and reuse of water, the latter components may build up to appreciable concentrations unless they are actually removed in solid form, such as, for example, by absorption or ion exchange demineralization. In the latter case, the weights of expendables would be further increased.
In considering various processes for recovery and reuse of wash water, the reverse osmosis (RO) process was considered as a means for water recovery and concentration of the dissolved solids. Reverse osmosis is an extremely attractive process for recycling large volumes of wash water onboard manned spacecraft because its specific energy and volume requirements are substantially less than for other processes.
This paper reviews some of the work being done to develop RO membranes for wash water recovery, compatible cleansing agents, tentative wash water standards by the National Academy of Sciences and trade-off analyses for system design and optimization.

Title: Algorithm for roving vehicle motion control
Publication: IAC 1970 congress proceedings, 21st  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  4–9 October 1970, Constance, Germany
Abstract:
A significant advance in the design of completely automatic roving vehicles requires the development of a large number of devices, starting with the control system. Here the problems of choice of strategy and tactics of vehicle behaviour are of great importance. An approach to the solution of these problems depends on numerous external factors and, primarily, on the specific conditions of the vehicle motion.
At the present time the general problem of control algorithm theory is not yet completely solved, and different trends exist in the approach to its development.
One possible version of motion control algorithm for roving vehicles intended for self-dependent motion in a given direction (or to the given point) is presented in the report. A form of one or another version of the control algorithm is basically determined by the information which is used for the control program synthesis.One of the versions considered is based on the assumption that local surface relief data is obtained with the aid of a stereoscopic TV system. The object of the algorithm is the determination of forbidden zones, search for an optimum route within the survey zone, and synthesis of an appropriate programme of roving vehicle motion control.

Abstract: The calculation of the three-dimensional flow field about hypersonic lifting bodies is very difficult because of the complex equations governing the flow at hypersonic speeds. A way to avoid these difficulties is the application of the wave- rider concept which makes use of simple and fundamentally known flow fields by replacing stream surfaces with solid surfaces. Title: Thermal protection systems for the space shuttle
Publication: IAC 1970 congress proceedings, 21st  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  4–9 October 1970, Constance, Germany
Abstract:
During the past decade, there has been considerable research and development relating to the aerodynamics, design, fabrication and test of prototype lifting re-entry vehicles. A few of these vehicles have been flight-tested and there has been a continuing search to determine where this technology can be applied to make major advances in the overall aerospace activities of the United States. In the aggregate, the United States has spent about $600 to $700 million during the 1960’s on lifting re-entry vehicle technology. The space shuttle program provides an application that will fully utilize the technology from this past decade of progress and will challenge our ingenuity during this next decade. The reusability of boosters and spacecraft will permit a quantum jump in the reduction of space launch and recovery costs.
To be successful as an efficient transportation system, the space shuttle must have an acceptable payload weight fraction. Current studies indicate that the payload weight fraction is not only extremely small, but also difficult to establish because of the major uncertainty in inert weight for the vehicle structures and thermal protection systems (TPS). The structural components and TPS together constitute about 50—60% of the orbiter or booster inert weight; the thermal protection system here being defined as the heat shield, insulation, and attachments necessary to protect the primary structure of the space shuttle.

Title: Zero-gravity testing of a waste management system
Publication: IAC 1969 congress proceedings, 20th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  5–10 October 1969, Mar del Plata, Argentina
Abstract:
The zero-gravity flight test program was conducted to evaluate the design concept of accomplishing waste collection by an airflow technique in a zero-gravity environment. The waste management system to be evaluated was required to collect, inactivate by a vacuum drying process, and store the urine, feces, emergency diarrheal disorders, vomitus and debris generated throughout the mission of the space vehicle. The system also incorporates provisions for volumetric determination of each micturition of each crew member as well as a crewman personal hygiene cleaner.
The flight test program in a KC-135 aircraft verified the most critical parameters of waste collection, liquid/gas separation and volume determination. By varying the airflows for collection, and through use of a specially designed waste dispenser, test data were accumulated during the 20-30 sec of zero-gravity achieved in each parabolic trajectory. These data permitted evaluation of the test configurations so that comparative conclusions could be obtained in arriving at a final design for the actual space vehicle.

Title: A systematic method of thermal design of spacecraft
Publication: IAC 1968 congress proceedings, 19th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  13–18 October 1968, New York, United States
Abstract: The spacecrafts considered here are divided into the hull and the inner canister systems, and the thermal characters of the simplified configurations of these systems are analysed based on the linearized nodal analysis. The result gives the analytical expressions of the temperature variation during the orbital motion and the temperature distribution over the spacecraft surface as the function of the heat transfer rate and the heat capacity of the each node of the spacecraft. This relations are confirmed by the simplified model tests in the space simulators. Following this analysis, the thermal model of the spacecraft is constructed and tested. The thermal behavier of the real spacecraft is reduced from this data systematically with considerable savings of the simulator time as well as the computer time. I.

Title: Advanced two-gas sensor technology research
Publication: IAC 1968 congress proceedings, 19th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  13–18 October 1968, New York, United States
Abstract:
Manned spacecraft now use a single-gas atmosphere system that operates on oxygen. For U. S. manned missions of 45 days or more, a two gas system is planned. This gaseous atmosphere will be composed of oxygen and either nitrogen or helium or some other inert gas. A sizable effort begun in 1965 has resulted in the design and fabrication of a reliable mass spectrometer system for sensing and controlling a two-gas atmosphere.
The unit is lightweight (6-1/2 lb), has output voltages compatible with existing telemetry and control devices, and is remarkably reliable. It's reliability was tested and proven in a 60-day, four-man simulated run in which an oxygen-nitrogen atmosphere was used, with the following results:
1. The system continuously monitored the partial pressures of water vapor, nitrogen, oxygen, and carbon dioxide, and controlled the oxygen and nitrogen concentrations with desired accuracy.
2. The response rate was fast enough to keep the FO2 within the range of 150-160 mm Hg.
3. There was no performance degradation over the test period.

Title: Axisymmetric viscous interaction with small velocity slip and transverse curvature-effect of Prandtl number and ratio of specific heats
Publication: IAC 1968 congress proceedings, 19th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  13–18 October 1968, New York, United States
Abstract:
During the past three years, new feats of space exploration have added to our knowledge of the planets. Probes have circumnavigated Mars, Venus and the Moon and landed on the last two. Meanwhile, much advance planning has been done on future missions. Among numerous other problems, the question of probe survival during their penetration in the atmosphere of planets has received close attention.
This paper is a review of the progress made in the understanding of the radiation processes which take place around probes during planetary entry. Currently three kinds of atmospheres seem to be of interest: air (Earth), nitrogen-carbon dioxide mixtures (Venus and Mars) and hydrogen- helium mixtures (Jupiter). The design of systems that make the best use' of available technology -L_;5 involves a wide choice of trajectories, with varying atmospheric entry patterns. Velocities up to 55,000 fps (l6 Km/sec) have been studied for earth re-entry and up to 190,000 fps (60 Rm/sec) for Jupiter entry. The density ranges relevant to radiation exchanges are pretty much the same for all atmospheres.
It is convenient to group the recent advances in this domain into three parts: emissive properties, shock layer techniques and non equilibrium phenomena.

Title: Same title as paper # 1968-P94
Publication: IAC 1968 congress proceedings, 19th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  13–18 October 1968, New York, United States
Abstract: Grain configurations for solid propellant rockets are classified by relative web thickness and mean vector direction of burning surface into a topological continuum. This ranges from the thin web dendrite (web equal to 1/6 of charge radius and entirely in the cross- section plane) thru the wagonwheel- and star-perforated grains Q to J web range and partial use of end effects in burning surface area control) to the slotted, conocyl, and finocyl grains (web 0.6-0.8 of radius and burning front partially in the axial direction). These geometrical principles relate to the mission by the ratio of thrust-to-duration squared (F/t1) which requires a dendrite grain for F/t2 X 3000 Ibf/sec2 and a slot or finocyl for F/t2 x 30 Ibf/sec2. This effect is counterbalanced by the range of burning rates available. Burning rate, relative web thickness, chamber pressure, length-to-diameter ratio, and volumetric loading affect Fjt2 attainable in a descending significance. The prevailing style of grain design in any era, although optimized mathematically within itself, depends more on technological breakthroughs in materials and propellant properties, than on factors of ballistic performance Grain, design is primarily a graphic subject. There are two aspects : performance attributes and description of the grain configuration.

Publication: IAC 1968 congress proceedings, 19th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  13–18 October 1968, New York, United States
Abstract: Research and Advanced Development has classically been conducted at the subsystem level. This paper describes a new system level Advanced Development (AD) concept and presents a task which used the knowledge derived fiom such an AD program : a Mars entry and landing mission. A system design was developed and most of the essential elements were designed, developed and fabricated. The assembled system was then functionally and environmentally tested: heat-sterilized and impact-tested. The resulting benefits are: the reduction of the flight project cost and schedule; development of subsystems which are oriented toward future missions and systems; exposure and solution of system problems which would not become apparent in subsystem AD; and identification and maturing of engineering technologies inherent in all system effort.
