Title: The morphological continuum in solid propellant grain design
Publication: IAC 1968 congress proceedings, 19th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  13–18 October 1968, New York, United States
Abstract: Grain configurations for solid propellant rockets are classified by relative web thickness and mean vector direction of burning surface into a topological continuum. This ranges from the thin web dendrite (web equal to l/6 of charge radius and entirely in the cross-section plane) thru the wagonwheel- and star-perforated grains (£ to ■§■ web range and partial use of end effects in burning surface area control) to the slotted, conocyl, and finocyl grains (web 0.6 - 0.8 of radius and burning front partially in the axial direction). These geometrical principles relate to the mission by the ratio of thrust-to-durâtion squared (F/t^) which requires a dendrite grain for F/t^ ; 3000 Ibf/sec^ and a slot or finocyl for F/t^ ; 30 Ibf/sec^. This effect is counterbalanced by the range of burning rates available. Burning rate, relative web thickness, chamber pressure, length-to-diameter ratio, and volumetric loading affect F/t^ attainable in a descending significance. The prevailing style of grain design in any era, although optimized mathematically within itself, depends more on technological breakthroughs in materials and propellant properties, than on factors of ballistic performance Grain design is primarily a graphic subject. -There are two aspects: performance attributes and description of the grain configuration.

Title: Assessment of the attitude perturbations of a spinning satellite on an orbit of large eccentricity
Publication: IAC 1967 congress proceedings, 18th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  24–30 September 1967, Belgrade, Yugoslavia
Abstract: A method is presented for assessing the attitude perturbations of a spin-stabilized satellite describing a highly eccentric orbit (e > 0.9). In contrast with worst case estimates or with a detailed computer study of a particular attitude history, the approach is analytical in nature and is aimed at putting the strictly necessary constraints on the satellite designers. It combines integration along the orbit with considerations on the dependence of the disturbing torque impulse on what occurs at perigee, account being taken of the orbital history. Meaningful expressions may then be obtained for the average torques due to: the interaction of the satellite residual magnetic moment with the magnetic field in various regions of space; the gravity gradient; the eddy-currents (despin and precession) ; the aerodynamic drag and the solar radiation pressure. The study is illustrated by an example in which the above approach is used to critically assess various design parameters for an actual satellite.

Title: Integrated design of composite materials
Publication: IAC 1966 congress proceedings, 17th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  9–15 October 1966, Madrid, Spain
Abstract:
Three years ago at the XIVth Congress, we presented our first attempt to describe the behavior of composite materials on a rational basis.1 Since then, composite materials have been under intensive research and development as a result of advances in the fabrication of boron and other high- performance filaments and whiskers. The purpose of this talk is to present the state of the art of composite materials as of 1966. Emphasis is placed on the micro and macromechanics analysis from which design methodology of composite materials can be derived.
A very popular application of composite materials is in the form of plates and shells consisting of layers of unidirectional composites. It is a commonly accepted assumption that each constituent layer is quasi-homo- geneous. This assumption leads to the use of the theory of laminated anisotropic plates and shells which has been treated by many authors.2-5 The buckling problem of anisotropic laminated shells have been solved by CHENG and HO,6 and TASI.7 Composite materials offers an opportunity to perform integrated design which combines the traditional structures design with materials design. In addition to the structural analysis of anisotropic laminated plates and shells, micromechanical relations, which links the composite moduli with the properties of the constituent materials, must be known to effect a complete systems integration.

Authors: ['M. J. Vaccaro', 'H. Y. Grubbs', 'S. Deutsch', 'J. E. Haaland', 'N. M. Burns']
Title: Lunex II: a study on manned lunar exploration
Publication: IAC 1966 congress proceedings, 17th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  9–15 October 1966, Madrid, Spain
Abstract:
In earlier studies,1 a series of simulations were conducted using a variable- volume simulator to establish cabin free-volume design criteria for lunar surface vehicles. Using performance and physiological measures1,2,3,4 in evaluating vehicle interior volumes during a series of 3-hr, 10-hr and 72-hr simulations, a minimum free volume was determined which did not seriously compromise either the subjects’ performance of simulated mission tasks or their physical well being. Data, obtained on two-man crews performing representative lunar mission segments, provided critical design data for over-all size, weight and trans-lunar stowage space required for a lunar surface vehicle. These parameters in turn affect the amount of space available on such a vehicle for scientific equipment and lunar surface sample collection.
The LUNEX II was designed to simulate a lunar mobile laboratory, one of several concepts NASA is evaluating for manned lunar exploration. This lunar vehicle is intended to house a two-man crew in a shirt-sleeve environment for a nominal 14-day lunar mission with a maximum stay-time of 21 days. During this mission the crew would conduct a scientific lunar exploration requiring extra-vehicular excursions in pressurized suits on the lunar surface. Crew members would also perform on-board scientific
system monitoring and preliminary analyses of lunar surface samples. In addition, vehicle driving, navigation, system monitoring and routine housekeeping tasks would need to be performed. The stationary LUNEX II simulator housed two test subjects for a full-term 14- to 21-day lunar surface mission requiring the performance of tasks related to the lunar mobile laboratory concept. No attempt was made to provide a completely closed ecological system or to simulate unusual environmental conditions.

Title: Mechanical design evolution of the Mariner spacecraft
Publication: IAC 1966 congress proceedings, 17th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  9–15 October 1966, Madrid, Spain
Abstract:
The Mariner II (Venus 1962) and Mariner IV (Mars 1964-5) spacecrafts represent successfully executed designs for grossly similar missions completed a few years apart. The Mariner II design was constrained by available time to be a minor modification of the existing Ranger spacecraft. To meet increased mission requirements, the Mariner IV was of necessity a new design. It reflected the experience gained from Ranger and Mariner II and also the fresh ideas which emerged from advanced project studies. Thus, it was a true second generation spacecraft design. Some evolutionary trends can be observed in the Mariner spacecraft which indicate increased understanding and education and illustrate the increased efficiency and reliability attained. Discussion of these trends in this paper will be limited to the areas of configuration, structural design, temperature control, mechanical devices, and mechanical system operations. These areas interact significantly such that any one discussion will consider overlapping effects of the others. Since the two designs to be discussed were created primarily by the same people, the trends observed may not be general. However, they are at least indicative of what the experienced engineers would do when given a fresh start without the undue restriction of having to utilize a previous design. The trends noted are of course most valid for attitude stabilized interplanetary spacecraft in the same general weight classification as the Mariners. However, some of them are also applicable to other spacecraft designs.

Title: Design and performance of the ranger block III unmanned lunar spacecraft television system
Publication: IAC 1965 congress proceedings, 16th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  13–18 October 1965, Athens, Greece
Abstract:
The Ranger television system, designed and fabricated by the Astro-Electronics Division of the Radio Corporation of America for the Jet Propulsion Laboratory, was the payload for the Ranger Block III unmanned lunar spacecraft missions and obtained the first high-resolution photo graphs of the lunar surface. The Ranger Block III program consisted of four lunar probes, Rangers VI-IX, launched between January 1964 and March 1965, and programmed to photograph and impact on selected lunar locations near or in terrain nearly identical with that of intended manned landings. The Ranger TV system, which obtained over 17,000 high-resolution photographs in Rangers VII, VIII, and IX, successfully demonstrated an electronic system capable of deep-space operation with exceptionally high-quality cameras and a high-powered communications system. The mission objective was to obtain the lunar photographs to aid in the design of manned landing vehicles and to provide information of interest to the world scientific community.
The TV system is discussed in detail; its development is traced from the original design criteria, constraints, and trade-offs, through the complete evolution of a flight-ready system. The flight sequence, trajectory requirements, and effects imposed on the equipment operation are evaluated.
The TV System consists of two separate chains of equipment designed to provide the greatest probability of receivin g video pictures to meet the mission objective. Each chain contains slow-scan video cameras, camera electronics, sequencing circuits, transmitters and power amplifiers, power su pplies, and associated control circuitry.

Title: Spacecraft temperature-control coatings : selection, utilization and problems related to the space environment
Publication: IAC 1965 congress proceedings, 16th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  13–18 October 1965, Athens, Greece
Abstract:
The thermal design, fabrication, launch, and operation of a spacecraft is a complex balancing of various factors, each of which must be weighed in the light of overall mission requirements, performance, and reliability.
The selection and the use of thermal-control surfaces are discussed. Included are historical background, radiometric and physical requirements, range of surface properties available to the designer, criteria for selection, space environmental effects on radiative properties, and a prognosis of future technology.
The requirements for and constraints on spacecraft thermal design as related to selection of surfaces are described, and specific examples are given. The fundamental properties that establish the radiative characteristics of surfaces and the methods of measurement are described.
The range of theoretical coatings available is discussed in term of practical engineering limits such as applicability, mission requirements, prelaimch and launch environments, and reliability and stability to the space environment. The effects of some of the important factors of the space environment such as ultraviolet, protons, electrons, etc. are discussed, with particular emphasis on the major problem of the resultant solar input load to surfaces with low solar absorptance-to-emittance ratios.

Title: The San Marco 1-A scientific satellite
Publication: IAC 1965 congress proceedings, 16th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  13–18 October 1965, Athens, Greece
Abstract:
The San Marco Project, stems from an agreement signed by representatives of Italy and the United States on September 5, 1962.
Basic objectives of the co-operative venture in space is to perform high altitude measurements of atmospheric and ionospheric characteristics in the equatorial region.
Under terms of the agreement between the two countries, NASA is providing the launch vehicles, use of its facilities, and training for Italian personnel.
The Italian Space Commission of the National Council of Research of Italy is responsible for the design, fabrication and testing of all payloads and experiments including construction of the satellite structures, the special electronic circuiteries and devices, the telemetry and the command system, as well as for the orbital launchings.
The Italian Space Commission also is establishing the equatorial range, including the two mobile platforms, and such tracking and data acquisition facilities as are peculiar to project San Marco and which are not available from NASA.
The project, as it is well stated in the Memorandum of Understanding between NASA and ISC, will culminate in the launching of a satellite into an equatorial orbit. This launch, using a NASA Scout Vehicle, will take place from the so called San Marco Range, consisting of two towable sea platforms (similar to a certain extent to Texas Towers), located near the Equator on the continental shelf off the East coast of Africa.
The technical agency responsible for the development of the San Marco Project is the Centro Ricerche Aerospaziali of the University of Rome. This laboratory (CRA) is a space center equipped with various facilities, including a large space environment simulator, for the design construction and grounding testing of the scientific satellites. The CRA is located in Rome and is directed by Prof. Luigi Broglio, who is also the general Director of the San Marco Project.

Title: The influence of shell behavior on the design of large antennas
Publication: IAC 1965 congress proceedings, 16th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  13–18 October 1965, Athens, Greece
Abstract:
The most important structural requirement placed on large and highly accurate antennas is a very stringent restriction on the permissible change in the shape of the reflecting surface. “Large” in this context means diameters greater than fifty feet and “stringent” means that changes in shape are to be kept below approximately 1/16 of the operating wavelength. This leads to a deflection criterion on the order of 0.075 in. for operating frequencies of 10,000 Me. A design requirement of this severity on the shape of such a large structure is highly unusual and not much information exists to assure its attainment.1
The main structural components of an antenna consist of a parabolic reflecting surface and a space-framework on which the reflector is mounted. If properly constructed, the reflector is a thin paraboloidal shell of revolution It is assumed that the antenna will be protected from wind loads by a radome so that tne primary source of applied load is the dead weight of the structural components themselves. Long standing methods of analysis have been applied to study the structural capability of the space-frame,7 but only very simple treatments of the reflecting surface have been conducted. Even with closed form solutions obtained by various approximate analyses, the accurate calculation of the deflections of the reflector is not easy since many complicated analytical expressions are involved.2,3,4 Consequently, the intrinsic capabilities and advantages of shell actions have yet to be fully exploited. To this end a series of computer programs called LLAPS (Lincoln Laboratory Analyses of Paraboloidal Shells) has been developed by Lincoln Laboratory of Massachusetts Institute of Technology to calculate deflections as well as stresses of paraboloidal shells of revolution under the influence of gravity loads. Shells of a homogeneous material or of layer media including sandwich type construction can be handled. By means of these programs, the digital computer is utilized to evaluate the closed form solutions of the membrane, shallow shell and asymptotic approximations of general theory of thin elastic shells. Descriptions of these methods of solution and the solutions themselves have been published as Lincoln Laboratory reports and in part in Ref. 5. The present work discusses the implications of some of the results obtained by these programs. Our effort can be divided into three principal aspects. By introducing the concept of a moved focus, we establish in the first part of the paper a measure of the structural performance of the reflector and show that the structural capability of the shell, when viewed in proper- context, is far better than that which appears at first sight. Next the effect of several design parameters on the structural behavior of the reflector is studied. Lastly, we discuss the existing method of construction of the parabolic reflector and offer an alternate concept suggested by the shell behavior. We confine ourselves to homogeneous and isotropic shells. The behavior of sandwich shells will be discussed in a future publication.

Title: A curriculum in engineering science directed toward astrautics
Publication: IAC 1964 congress proceedings, 15th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  7–12 September 1964, Warsaw, Poland
Abstract:
Most of the other lectures in this session on the impact of astronautics on engineering education have treated individual subjects in the engineering curriculum. Each has shown the changes that have taken place in the scope of the particular subject as a result of present interest in astronautics. This lecture, on the other hand, is concerned with the curriculum as a whole. For example, which courses should a student in engineering take? In what ways does the selection of courses to compose an engineering curriculum differ from that of 20 years ago ? How does the philosophy of the curriculum today differ from that of 20 years ago?
Important changes have taken place in our concept of what an engineer is expected to do, what he must know, and how he should be educated. In particular, the courses that an engineering student studies today are not the same as twenty years ago. He is expected to do much more independent study to supplement his formal course work. Above all, he is expected to be much more creative as a student and to display much more initiative in formulating his particular program of study.
The points of educational philosophy stressed in this paper are subsequently illustrated by analysis of the educational program in aerospace propulsion at Princeton University. But, these points of educational philosophy are not limited to Princeton’s curriculum in aerospace propulsion, nor are they limited to Princeton University. They represent a growing trend in all technical disciplines and in many other universities.
The following remarks summarize in the opinion of the author the main points of educational philosophy and practice that distinguish technical education today from that of twenty or thirty years ago. These relatively new features have resulted from the stimulus given to engineering education by the emergence of the new fields of nuclear power, high frequency communications, automation, high speed aeronautics, and astronautics. Education for these new fields (especially astronautics) necessitated important changes in the curriculum. Some of the trends are as follows:
(1) Emphasis on basic engineering sciences and reduction of emphasis on design practice in the university. The student learns practical engineering and design when he goes to work in industry.
(2) Greater emphasis for the engineer on mathematics and theoretical subjects. This gives the student greater versatility and greater capacity to attack new types of engineering projects later in his career.
(3) Broad study in diverse disciplines instead of limited study in a single department. This is important at both undergraduate and graduate levels. The idea is that modern engineering developments require simultaneous consideration of several disciplines; an engineer trained in only a single narrow discipline cannot carry out such developments.
(4) Constant advancement and modernization of course content. The student becomes flexible and independent in his study habits; he learns that knowledge of a subject is not limited to a single book or to a static curriculum.
(5) More advanced study for the engineer in the sciences of physics and chemistry, in place of some narrowly specialized engineering courses.
(6) Greater allowance for the student’s individual interests and abilities in selection of courses. The curriculum is not rigid.

Title: Ground support equipment and launch installations at John F. Kennedy Space Center, NASA, for the manned lunar landing program
Publication: IAC 1964 congress proceedings, 15th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  7–12 September 1964, Warsaw, Poland
Abstract:
The magnitude of the Manned Lunar Landing Program has led to the evolution and adoption of a new launch operations concept to cope with the requirements of the program. Major factors contributing to the need for a new approach include the greatly increased size and complexity of the Apollo Saturn V space vehicle, the requirement for unprecedented reliability, and the flexibility of handling varying launch rates. It has been determined that these needs can best be satisfied by the adoption of a “mobile” launch concept.
As compared with the established practice of vehicle assembly, checkout, and launch at a fixed launch site, the “mobile concept” embodies space vehicle transfer in an assembled and checked out condition to the actual launch pad. Advantages of this new concept are assembly and checkout in a protected environment, reduction of actual “pad time” with a consequent increase in launch rate capability, and the ability to adapt to expanding program requirements.
Major facilities at Launch Complex 39, where the “mobile concept” is being implemented, include: (1) a Vertical Assembly Building, for assembly and checkout of the space vehicle; (2) a Launcher-Umbilical Tower, upon which the vehicle is erected vertically for checkout, transfer, and launch; (3) a Crawler-Transporter, to move the space vehicle and Launcher-Umbilical Tower to the launch pad; (4) an Arming Tower, to provide space vehicle access at the Launch Pad; and (5) the Launch Pad area.
Necessary equipment to assemble the space vehicle stages and payload is provided in the 525-foot high Vertical Assembly Building. The building will consist of a Low Bay area and a High Bay area. The Low Bay area contains eight stage preparation and checkout bays. Erection of the vehicle begins when the S-IC stage is positioned on the Launcher Umbilical tower within the High Bay area. After initial preparation in the Low Bay area, the S-II and STVB stages are transferred to the High Bay area and erected. Erection is completed when the Instrument Unit and the Apollo Spacecraft are positioned atop the launch vehicle.
Systems checkout is performed concurrently in the High Bay and, following validation of all stages, a combined-systems test and a simulated-flight test are performed. After all tests have been performed satisfactorily in the High Bay, the vehicle is ready for transfer to the Launch Pad.
Vertical transfer of the space vehicle to the Launch Pad is provided by the 5.5-mil- lion-pound Crawler-Transporter capable of carrying a load of 12-million pounds. In addition, it is used to transfer the Arming Tower between a parking area and the Launch Pad.
Remote control of launch operations, using automatic checkout techniques is performed from a Launch Control Center which is located adjacent to the Vertical Assembly Building. Data is transferred between the Launch Control Center, the Vertical Assembly Building, and the Launch Pads by digital data transmission networks. Automatic checkout will increase reliability, decrease pad time, and provide rapid trouble shooting of the space vehicle on the pad.
At the pad, prior to countdown, all systems are verified and a second simulated- flight test is performed. Countdown is then initiated, propellant loading accomplished, and astronaut embarkation takes place. Final systems checks are conducted and the vehicle is launched.
The provision of these launch facilities at Launch Complex 39 has progressed through the programming, planning, criteria development, and design stages and is now under construction. Construction is well underway at the vertical assembly building area. An extensive pile driving operation has been completed, foundations have been poured, and steel erection has begun. It is expected that Vertical Assembly Building construction will be completed in early 1966. Launcher-Umbilical Tower erection is now in progress and Crawler-Transporter fabrication is underway. Three Launcher-Umbilical Towers will be operational by mid-1966, and two Crawler-Transporters will be operational in early 1965. At present, one of the two planned Launch Pads is under construction, and a massive surcharge operation is underway for the second.

Title: Selected studies of space broadcasting
Publication: IAC 1964 congress proceedings, 15th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  7–12 September 1964, Warsaw, Poland
Abstract:
Seven years ago, at the VUIth IAF Congress in Barcelona, the author discussed the Communication Satellite in some detail.1 This 1957 paper concluded with a visualization of a large communication center in space, and noted that such a station was beyond the reach of rocket technology of that time.
The years which have followed the launching of the first Sputnik have produced a steady improvement in space technology. As a result, the aspects of the Communication Satellite which relate to the point-to-point relaying of telephone and telegraph messages are now matters of immediate engineering design. The other aspect of the communication satellite, that of direct broadcast to the home, has [not progressed as rapidly ; in fact, the progress which has been made has been in the nature of improvements in “the state of the art” rather than progress in space broadcasting itself. However, this accumulated progress is such that the space broadcasting is now a short term matter; experimental broadcasts are feasible with equipment now available,2 and small scale operational broadcasts could be accomplished with a design and fabrication program of one to three years duration.
In this early paper, it was noted that the question of desirability of communication satellites depended on complex economic factors, and on sociological and political factors. These factors are now reasonably well understood for the relay service (telephone and telegraph traffic). However, they are quite different for the broadcast service. In particular, before space broadcasting becomes common, it appears that acceptable solutions must be found to three groups of problems :3
a) The technical problem of providing a high quality broadcast service from space.
b) The problem of providing a compatible service, which arises from differences in broadcast standards around the world.
c) The problem of assuring equitable operation.
Considering the fact that space broadcasting is a short term possibility, it appears desirable to study these three problems and their interrelations; this is the purpose of this paper. Since the problems are complex, the study must be limited; this is done by limiting consideration to selected areas of Earth which are reasonably typical, and considering the problems of these areas.
Study will be limited to television broadcasting. Technically and operationally, this is the most difficult service, and if it is found feasible, the feasibility of other types of broadcasting would seem to be shown also.
To show the differences in the problems, a developed and developing area are examined first; the mainland U.S.A. and the sub-continent of India are used as examples. This is followed by an examination of a multinational area, Africa being chosen as the example. In each case, attention is given to the present situation, to factors affecting the problem, and to the requirements for suitable coverage.

Title: Evaluation and testing of the "relay" satellite
Publication: IAC 1963 congress proceedings, 14th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  25 September–1 October 1963, Paris, France
Abstract:
Relay is a microwave repeater designed and built by the Radio Corporation of America for the United States National Aeronautics and Space Administration.
It is appropriate to briefly review the design of the communications aspect of the satellite. Its completely redundant microwave system provides a 10 watt output that yields a margin of more than 6 db for TV transmission over a range of 9500 km. Originally, it was estimated that the limited bandwidth afforded.by the ground based klystrons would inhibit the available signal to noise ratio of the detected FM signals received on Earth. Consequently, the deviation is tripled within the satellite before retranslation and transmission. Cubing the signal poses an additional problem. The satellite is required to relay “east-to-west” and “west-to-east” signals simultaneously. The inevitable differences in levels of these signals are exaggerated (tripled their ratio in db) because of the multiplication. The automatic gain control would, of course, discrirnjnate against the weaker signal. The two sets of signals are therefore separated and amplified to equal levels before they are mixed and transmitted together in the traveling wave tube. The entire subsystem is designed using solid state components with the obvious exception of the TWT’s. The latter item weighs 3i lb, provides and output of II w at an efficiency of 21% and a gain of about 35 db.
The satellite geometry makes the use of an isotropic antenna difficult; a toroidal pattern was chosen and, in doing so, a simple light weight structure was evolved that provided excellent decoupling between the two transmitter ports and between the transmitter and receiver sections. The pattern is “bent” towards the nose of the bird by a set of radial wires imbedded in a polyurethane disc.
The redundant repeaters along with the supporting command and telemetry subsystems are all housed in a 172 lb 8 sided prism-like structure 32 in. high and about 29 in. wide.
The physical tests specified for Relay were designed to approximate the environment experienced by the spacecraft during handling, launch, and orbital flight. A complete microwave transmitter and receiver was installed in a van to allow traffic tests to be made with the satellite in the center of the loop. The (radiated) power of the unit was sufficient for the transmission and reception of signals to and from the spacecraft at the gantry at the Atlantic Missile Range.
The satellite was launched from Cape Canaveral on December 13, 1962 at 6 : 30 EST in an almost “perfect” orbit (orbital elements as of April 25, 1963 : perigee—1315 km, apogee—7445 km, inclination—47.5°, anomalistic period—185 min). As the temperature within the satellite stabilized at those values which were commensurate with the space environment, the spacecraft’s power supply failed. A faulty series transistor in a voltage regulator leaked seriously because of the low ambient temperature (the satellite’s earliest orbits yielded partial eclipses). The continuous drain on the batteries lowered the bus voltage to a level (about 15 v) that made operation of the communication system impossible. This failure was duplicated in an experiment on the prototype spacecraft in the laboratory. As the orbit shifted into one that was without eclipse, the faulty regulator recovered. With the exception of one additional “anxious” but short period, the satellite has been used continuously, exploiting the communications repeater for periods between 1 and 2 hr a day. Much of the operation has been devoted to communication engineering experiments (group delay, noise loading, distortion, baseband response, television test signals, etc.). In addition, several public demonstrations have proven the technical feasibility of providing excellent broadband transmission using a microwave communications satellite.

Title: Same title as paper # 1963-26
Publication: IAC 1963 congress proceedings, 14th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  25 September–1 October 1963, Paris, France
Abstract:
Manned space operation requires an adequate human maintenance subsystem to support the crewmen in the vehicle. The phrase “human maintenance subsystem”, as utilized here denotes the total support requirements of man and includes a satisfactory environment, suitable food, the collection and processing of waste, optimum hygiene and sanitation, and crew accomodations and workspace designed to insure the effective utilization of man as a component of the system.
Man must be considered as a component of the total engineering system. As such, he also requires preventive maintenance. The full value of modern technology will be realized through effective design for man/machine compatibility. When man is a component of an enegineering system, the provision of more than the actual necessities required for life sustenance is necessary. For example, in the hygiene associated with space flight, the system under consideration includes a compact shower to provide cleanliness for the crew. Some people will consider this to be an extravagance beyond the necessities of manned space flight, but tests to date have shown that such a system is well received and indeed adds to the effective and efficient operation of the man in closed systems for prolonged periods of time.
A program was laid down to design and fabricate a human maintenance subsystem which would satisfy the needs of five men for a period of 30 days’ duration. The program was developed under the direction of the National Aeronautics and Space Administration of the United States. It is one of a series of systems being developed by NASA to provide support for humans, extending from a minimal time in space of approximately one week up to and including protracted periods of months and perhaps years.
The design of such systems has included the potential for expansion dependent on the ability of the boosters in the program to carry increased weights and volumes of materials. In this paper we do not attempt in any manner or means to say that this is the best system for the 150 man-day period under consideration. The discussion will, indeed, point out some of the errors of the early work, together with such facts as are available regarding the actual opefsation of the integrated hardware, thus providing a system that meets the general specifications laid down for such a system.
The human maintenance subsystem as dtsigned, fabricated, and tested in this program consisted of the following items integrated into a working, closed system.

Title: Same title as paper # 1963-92
Publication: IAC 1963 congress proceedings, 14th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  25 September–1 October 1963, Paris, France
Abstract:
Meteorological satellites are unique in their system requirements. Carrying a variety of sensors, these satellites provide the greatest capability for data collection, and must therefore be flexible in their system design.
From the point of view of system performance, the meteorological satellite program has been the most successful space program to date; all launchings have resulted in successful performance, and have yielded enormous quantities of data. So far, seven TIROS satellites have been launched and operated, and TIROS VI and VII are now in routine operation.

Title: World communication satellite system
Publication: IAC 1962 congress proceedings, 13th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  19–23 September 1962, Varna, Bulgaria
Abstract: The paper describes a study by the above company of a communication satellite system to provide world coverage with particular reference to the global interests of the British Commonwealth and European countries. The study assumes that a global communication satellite system is already in some form of operation before the European system, and the traffic studies have been carried out on this basis, thus influencing the catchment areas of the traffic. Several techniques have been used to estimate the traffic and data is given on the traffic within the catchment areas which could be expected, if the service was provided predominantly for the British Commonwealth. In this case over a twenty year period an average growth rate of 9.6% per annum (overall growth factor of 6. 35) of telephone traffic is estimated. This is believed to be conservative and would in any case be greatly increased when the full catchment area to include European interests is added. To meet the peak demand levels anticipated, the initial operational satellite would be provided with a capacity equivalent to five hundred high quality two-way telephone circuits, and the available bandwidth could be used either for telephones, telegraph etc. or partially for a television link, together with a few telephone circuits etc. as an alternative. As the program develops and traffic demand increases, the satellite capacity would rise to at least two thousand high quality two-way circuits in addition to simultaneous television links. Different forms of traffic loading are considered audit is shown that the main revenue is based on the telephone and telegraph services. The service requirements are carefully considered, emphasis being given to the need for flexibility in the operation of the system, in view of the circuit locations, and a method is proposed to achieve extremely flexible telecommunication operation by the satellites, allowing for both large and small blocks of telephone circuits. The system design is discussed first with reference to the relative merits of low, medium and synchronous altitude orbits. If the apparently fundamental problem of time delay is substantiated, it is proposed that the first form of commercial operational system to meet the above European requirements would best make use of a pattern of nine equally spaced, station keeping satellites located in the same circular, orbit moving east in relation to the earth at an altitude of 7,480 nautical miles. Certain advantages of synchronous satellites are recognized and the possibility of a mixed system discussed. In substantiating the choice of a nine satellite system as an example of an operational system, various factors are reviewed which must yet be resolved in detail before final decisions can be reached that this is the best combination of orbit height and number of satellites. Such factors include the single hop requirement, ( particularly with respect to the transatlantic route and the associated depth of the Atlantic terminals into Western Europe ), this parameter having powerful bearing on the choice of system. The broad description of the satellite's specifications is given, together with certain design trends on the form the satellite may take. Several different forms of ground stations are visualised working with the satellite system; tnese include main relay stations, and high and low capacity terminal stations. All stations would make use of steerable parabolic antennae of various diameters, as opposed to horn antennae. The specifications of these stations are described, together with the necessary operational facilities, such as computing centers. The proposal is based on the use of the three-stage rocket vehicle now under development with the European Launcher Development Organisation, using the British "Blue Streak" rocket as the first stage, which will be capable of placing at least 800-lb satellites into the 7,480nautical mile orbit. The particular requirements for the vehicle in this application are discussed, together with the suitability of Woomera as opposed to a new equatorial launching site. The cost of the various parts of the system have been established in detail incorporating, for example, each individual launch attempt of the order of L 1.4m. , including the satellite. Within the first phases of the program, it is expected that the satellite life will increase to at least four years duration, and this can be expected to improve as the program develops. Parametric studies have been made on the effects of such factors as satellite life, showing the influence of this on the cost of the system over a twenty year period. Development costs of the rocket vehicle are not discussed in the paper, but the satellite system development, deployment and operation costs are given, together with revenue figures over the twenty year period, which is expected to gross some L 700 million. The extent of probable European interest in'the development and operation of such a system is discussed with respect to the present situation.

Title: Exobiological instrumentation
Publication: IAC 1961 congress proceedings, 12th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  1–7 October 1961, Washington, United States
Abstract:
Exobiological studies will require a variety of automated experiments designed for life detection and the investigation of the physical and chemical properties of living systems in extra-terrestrial environments. Exobiological experiments may be divided into four general classes.
1. Visual inspection of the macro and micro planetary environment.
2. Organic and inorganic chemical analysis.
3. Measurement of chemical changes produced by sample specimen, e.g., metabolic activity.
4. Direct biological experiments, i.e., growth and culture of organisms.
A major consideration in instrument design for automated biological experiments will be sample collection and sample processing techniques. The samples must be collected from completely unknown environments under unknown conditions; therefore, sample collection instrumentation must be designed for maximum versatility.
Telecommunications bandwidth requirements for most exobiological experiments will be low, except for visual experiments.
Typical examples of planned exobiological experiments will be discussed.

Authors: ['R J Gnkel', 'D N Lascody', 'D S Merriles']
Title: Impulsive midcourse correction of an interplanetary transfer
Publication: IAC 1959 congress proceedings, 10th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  31 August–5 September 1959, London, United Kingdom
Abstract:
Impulsive Midcourse Correction of an Interplanetary Transfer. A survey of possible ballistic trajectories from Barth to another planet, with particular attention to sensitivity to initial condition errors, indicates that initial condition tolerances can be maximized by careful choice of the trajectory to be used. The possibility of midcourse correction to compensate for initial errors is considered and the relationship between correction impulse requirements and sensitivity to initial conditions is established. A method of utilizing available correction impulse to obtain the desired amount of correction is determined.
Inferential methods based on a two-dimensional model are used for the basic survey with the effect of third dimension estimated a posteriori. A more detailed analysis of some “maximum tolerance” trajectories is obtained by using a three-dimensional open integration simulation of the solar system. A comparison of results shows the suitability of approximate methods for determining basic trends, but indicates the necessity for using more accurate solutions for design purposes. This extends to these interplanetary trajectories a conclusion reached in a previous paper concerning a lunar shot.

Es wurden Inferenzmethoden, die sich auf ein zweidimensionales Modell gründen, ftir eine Voruntersuchung benutzt, wonach der EinfluB der dritten Dimension a posteriori abgeschatzt wurde. Impulsion correctrice à mi-courso pour transfert interplanétaire. Une étude des possibilités de trajectoires balistiques de la Terre à une autre planète montre que les tolérances sur les conditions initiales peuvent être rendues maximum par un choix judicieux de la trajectoire utilisée. La compensation des erreurs initiales par une correction à mi-course est envisagée et les corrections d’impulsion mises en relation avec la sensibilité aux erreurs initiales. Une méthode pour l’utilisation de l’impulsion disponible en vue d’obtenir la correction désirée est établie.
Une étude préliminaire est basée sur un modèle à deux dimensions, les effets de la troisième dimension étant estimés a posteriori. Une analyse plus détaillée de quelques trajectoires à tolérance maximum est obtenue par une intégration pas à pas du problème tridimensionnel du système solaire. La comparaison des résultats montre que les méthodes approchées rendent compte de façon satisfaisante des tendances générales mais que des solutions plus précises sont nécessaires pour les besoins d’une application spécifique. Ce résultat étend aux trajectoires interplanétaires une conclusion déjà formulée dans un article précédent pour une trajectoire lunaire.

Title: Recent development and design of the ion rocket engine
Publication: IAC 1959 congress proceedings, 10th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  31 August–5 September 1959, London, United Kingdom
Abstract:
Recent Developments and Designs of the Ion Rocket Engine. Recent developments of ion rocket engines have proceeded rapidly in the last two years under research programs sponsored by the Air Force Office of Scientific Research. In order to understand the trend of this progress a brief summary of the basic relationships governing the operation of electrical propulsion systems are summarized. Fundamental design parameters of ion rocket engines are tabulated for both English and metric systems.
The cross-sectional area of the engine is estimated by considering a flat-plate electrode configuratioii and the modifications imposed on this idealized situation by the presence of an aperture through which ions are emitted.
The relationship of engine design, vehicle design, and the mission results from the characteristic velocity required to accomplish the objective. Methods of mission analysis are referenced, but not discussed in detail. These methods result in characteristic velocity requirements which in turn establish the specific impulse or exhaust velocity the engine must develop.
The specific impulse cannot be arbitrarily chosen if the maximum payload is to be transported in the vehicle. The variation of payload with specific impulse is demonstrated with some typical examples. The overall variation depends upon the weight of the vehicle per unit power developed and the efficiency of conversion of primary energy into directed kinetic energy in the exhaust jet. The analytical relationship among the characteristic velocity, weight per unit power of the vehicle, efficiency and the specific impulse to obtain maximum payload is graphically presented. The maximum payload for a mission accomplished with an electrically powered vehicle is estimated from these data.
The characteristic velocity of the mission also determines the operating time of the electrical rocket engine. In general it is desirablè to use as low a specific impulse powerplant as possible in order to reduce the operating time ; however, the operating time is also dependent upon the thrust-to-weight ratio of the vehicle. This ratio depends on the capability of the yehicle to generate adequate amounts of power. The limiting thrust-to-weight ratio has been summarized graphically for several types of veiiicles including ion, plasma, and chemical rockets and modem aircraft. Comparative maximum payloads of chemical and ion rockets are presented in terms of the mission characteristic velocity.
The experimental program and techniques for verifying these analyses on a specific type of ion rocket engine conceived at Rocketdyne are presented. The experiments are conducted in high vacuum environments. The ion thrust chamber discussed in this paper uses electrostatic acceleration of ions generated from surface contact ion sources. Preliminary evaluation of the results of the program indicate that a flyable prototype engine can be produced within a few years under the impetus of a progressive development program.

Jiingste Entwicklungen und Entwiirfe eines lonenraketenmotors. Entwicklungen des lonenraketenmotors haben in den letzten zwei Jahren unter dem vom Air Force Office of Scientific Research gefôrderten Programm groBe Fortschritte gemacht. Um die Richtung dieses Fortschrittes zu verstehen, wird eine kurze Zusammenfassung der grundlegenden Beziehungen gegeben, die die Operation des elektrischen Antriebssystems beherrschen. Fundamentale Entwurfsparameter des lonenraketenmotors werden in englischen und metrischen Systemen tabuliert.
Die Querschnittflache des Motors wird mit Hilfe einer Flachplatten-Elektroden- Anordnung geschatzt, aber auch der Modifikationen, die durch die Gegenwart einer Offnung, durch die lonen ausgesendet werden, auf diese idealisierte Situation einwirken.
Die Beziehung zwischen dem Maschinenentwurf, Fahrzeugentwurf und dem Auf- trag folgt aus der charakteristischen Geschwindigkeit, die benôtigt wird, um das Ziel zu erreichen. Methoden einer Auftrags-Analyse sind angegeben, werden aber nicht im einzelnen besprochen. Diese Methoden fiihren zu charakteristischen Geschwindig- keitsbedürfnissen, die ihrerseits wiederum den spezifischen împuls aufstellen oder die Auspuffgeschwindigkeit, die der Motor entwickeln muB.
Der spezifische Impuls kann nicht willkürlich gewâhlt werden, wenn eine maximale Nutzlast im Fahrzeug transportiert werden soil. Die Yerânderung der ISTutzlast mit dem spezifischen Impuls wird an Hand einiger typischer Beispiele demonstriert. Die Gesamtverànderung hângt ab von dem Gewicht des Fahrzeuges pro Einheit erzeugter Kraft und der Leistungsfahigkeit der Umwandlung von ursprünglicher Energie in gerichtete, kinetische Energie in der Auspuffdüse. Die analytische Beziehung zwischen der charakteristischen Geschwindigkeit, Gewicht pro Krafteinheit des Fahrzeuges, Leistungsfahigkeit und dem spezifischen Impuls, um eine maximale Nutzlast zu erhalten, wird graphisch dargestellt. Die maximale Nutzlast für eine Mission (Auftrag), die mit einem elektrisch angetriebenen Fahrzeug unternommen wird, wird mit Hilfe dieser Daten geschatzt.
Die charakteristische Geschwindigkeit der Mission bestimmt ebenfalls die Arbeits- zeit des elektrischen Raketenmotors. Im allgemeinen ist es wünschenswert, eine môglichst wenig spezifische Impuls-Kraftanlage zu benutzen, um die Arbeitszeit zu verringern; doch hângt die Arbeitszeit auch von dem Schub-Gewichtsverhâltnis des Fahrzeuges ab. Dieses Verhâltnis ist abhângig von der Fâhigkeit des Fahrzeuges, angemessene Mengen von Kraft zu erzeugen. Das begrenzende Schub-Gewichtsver- hâltnis wurde für verschiedene Typen von Fahrzeugen einschlieBlich der lonen-, Plasma-, chemischen Raketen und modernen Flugzeuge graphisch zusammengefaBt. Vergleichbare maximale Nutzlasten von chemischen und lonenraketen werden als Ausdruck der charakteristischen Geschwindigkeit der Mission angegeben.
Das experimentelle Programm und die Techniken zur Bestâtigung dieser Analysen, die an einer spezifischen Type einer lonenrakete bei Rocketdyne erhalten worden sind, werden wiedergegeben. Die Expérimente wurden im Hochvakuum ausgeführt. Die lonenstoBkammer, die in dieser Abhandlung diskutiert wird, benutzt elektrostatische Beschleunigung der lonen, die von einer Oberflachenkontakt-Ionenquelle erzeugt werden. Vorlâufige Berechnungen der Ergebnisse des Programms zeigen, daB eine fliegbare Prototyp-Maschine in einigen Jahren, unter dem Antrieb eines fortschritt- lichen Programmes, erzeugt werden kann.

Progrès récents et études dans le domaine des propulseurs ioniques. Une progression rapide des études de propulseurs ioniques a été faite pendant les deux dernières années sous l’égide du Bureau des Projets Scientifiques des Forces Aériennes. Pour mieux comprendre la nature de ce progrès, l’auteur donne un résumé des relations fondamentales qui gouvernent le fonctionnement des systèmes à propulsion électriques. Les paramètres d’études de base des propulseurs ioniques sont présentés en unités anglaises et métriques.
Le maître-couple du moteur est calculé à partir d’une électrode-plaque en tenant compte des corrections nécessaires, la configuration idéalisée étant affectée par la présence d’un orifice prévu pour l’émission ionique.
Les relations entre le dessin du moteur et du véhicule et sa mission dépendent de la vitesse caractéristique imposée par l’objectif à atteindre. Des références pour les méthodes d’analyse de mission sont données, sans discussion détaillée. Ces méthodes permettent de définir la vitesse caractéristique qui, à son tour, établit l’impulsion spécifique ou la vitesse d’éjection du propulseur.
L’impulsion spécifique ne peut être choisie d’une façon arbitraire si le véhicule doit transporter une charge payante maximum. Quelques exempless typiques illustrent les variations de charge payante en fonction de l’impulsion spécifique. La variation totale dépend du poids du véhicule par unité de puissance développée et du rendement de la conversion de l’énergie primaire en énergie cinétique dirigée à l’éjection. Les rapports analytiques entre la vitesse caractéristique, la puissance massique, le rendement et l’impulsion spécifique nécessaires pour obtenir une charge payante maximum sont illustrés graphiquement. La charge payante maximum pour une mission accomplie par un véhicule à propulsion électrique est calculée à partir de ces données.
La vitesse caractéristique de la mission détermine également la durée de fonctionnement du propulseur électrique. En général il est désirable d’utiliser un propulseur à impulsion spécifique aussi basse que possible afin de réduire la durée de fonctionnement ; cependant, la durée de fonctionnement dépend également de la poussée massique du véhicule. Ce rapport est gouverné par la capacité du véhicule de produire une puissance suffisante. Les valeurs limite de la poussée massique ont été résumées graphiquement pour plusieurs types de véhicules comprenant les propulseurs ioniques, plasmas, fusées à propergols chimiques ainsi que les avions modernes. Des comparaisons de charges payantes maxima de fusées chimiques et propulseurs ioniques sont données en termes de vitesses caractéristiques de mission.
Sont aussi présentés : le programme expérimental et les techniques de vérification d’analyses d’un propulseur ionique d’un modèle établi par Rocketdyne. Ces expériences ont lieu dans un vide très poussé. La chambre de poussée décrite dans la présente conférence fonctionne par l’accélération électrostatique d’ions produits par un système de surfaces de contact. Sous réserve d’un programme de travail énergique, l’évaluation préliminaire des résultats acquis démontre qu’il serait possible de construire en quelques années un prototype de propulseur capable de fonctionner en vol.

Title: The effect of the earth's oblateness and atmosphere on a satellite orbit
Publication: IAC 1956 congress proceedings, 7th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  17–22 September 1956, Rome, Italy
Abstract: Over the past several years, we of Martin have analyzed papers devoted to the mathematical description of the orbit of an earth satellite (Ref. 1 is an example of these publications). Each publication has resulted in continuous progress toward a better understanding of the complex motion of this type of satellite. Although, without a doubt, this understanding was of maximum assistance to our advance design group working on the preliminary configuration of satellite launching vehicles, we noted that the use of these studies was limited. These limits were based on certain conditions, conditions imposed by employment of certain simplifying assumptions in the solution of the mathematical expressions.

Title: Materials for rocket frame and motor construction
Publication: IAC 1953 congress proceedings, 4th  International Astronautical Congress (IAC),  3–8 August 1953, Zurich, Switzerland
Abstract: To materialize the design of a space- or rocket- ship it is required as in all applications of the engineering art, that suitable materials be selected among those physically available to the constructor. The suitability of a material may be determined by its meeting the operational requirements, its adaptability to the technological processes of fabrication, and also its price of purchase on a normal market. The properties and characteristics (chemical, physical, etc.) of the available materials impose some restrictions on the boundless exercise of the creative human mind whose ingenuity in the design of machinery must always reckon with the feasibility of making his invention take substantial shape. The price factor also assumes a most important place in the selection of materials, for, aside from military inspired projects, all other activities in the engineering field must be based on sound evaluation of economic nature.
